chapters.title: RCE Language Specification, draft 0.9: Overview
chapters.question: In the overview's tiny example, what is the name of the event?

sections.html:
Abstract. RCE, the Reality Code Engine, is a small programming language whose programs mean one thing everywhere. It exists so that programs can be written, checked, changed and run by machines, in the era of code written by models, with no model in the loop that decides what a program means. A program is turned into a Form: a state machine given by its states, its events, a step function that maps a state and an event to a new state and an outcome, and the log of events. Every runtime that runs the Form must produce the same results bit for bit, and the rules that make this so are checked by machine.

Figure (informative). The pipeline from source to Form, log, emit targets and host. Source: docs/figures.

Three plain points:

  1. Same answer on every target. Arithmetic, text, floats and concurrency have one defined meaning; there is no undefined behaviour.
  2. Every program ends. Loops, recursion and iterators are bounded, so the step function always returns.
  3. Memory is safe by construction. Ownership, second-class borrows, regions and linear handles rule out use-after-free and data races.

Tiny example (a counter that never goes negative: a Dec at zero keeps the state):

RCE
state Counter
    n: i64 = 0
event Dec
step Counter on Dec
    check n > 0
    n -= 1

Reading map. Files are in spec/book/ and are meant to be read in order:

FileWhat it covers

01-notation.mdhow grammar and typing rules are written; what conformance means
02-lexical.mdcharacters, comments, tokens, keywords, literals, indentation
03-syntax.mdthe full grammar of declarations, types, statements, expressions
04-programs.mdmodules, the program's Form, scope
05-types-ownership.mdtypes, contexts, typing rules, ownership, borrowing
06-regions-effects-extensions.mdarenas, concurrency, traits, comptime, foreign functions, linear types, device regions, iterators
07-form-evaluation.mdthe Form of a program, evaluation, exact edge cases of every primitive
08-steps-loops-concurrency.mdthe step function, errors, hashing, loops, tasks, examples
09-wellformedness.mdthe list of rules a program must pass to be accepted
10-theorems.mdthe theorems and what is proved in Lean
11-decisions.mddesign decisions and the changes per draft
12-tooling.mdthe rce command line and language server
13-references.mdsources
14-draft06-concurrency.mdAppendix C: the concurrency part of the language, and the release rule (C.15: a release label names exactly one spec commit)
15-handler-spec-profile.mdAppendix D: the engine profile, handler specs and fits, including reads, joins and scans
16-host-contract.mdAppendix E: the host contract (one admitter, durable log, capabilities, fabric entries, placement)

INDEX.md lists every file with its hash; READ-PROTOCOL.md says how an agent proves it read the spec. RCE-SPEC.md is all of these files joined into one, generated by rce-book build.

Status. Draft 0.9, 2026-10-17. Status: for review. Appendix F is specified and implemented in part (F.12) and applies the 2025+ language survey and the security study (transactional calls, contracts, ghost code, written termination measures, information-flow labels with robust declassification, a World capability, caretaker revocation, typed shell and prompt output, constant-time functions, declared budgets, hash-pinned builds, templates, if let, trait laws and lexical hygiene), and states as non-goals the four constructs that would break a theorem (effect handlers, switchable contracts, mutable aliasing across par, runtime reflection). The reference checker implements a part of it (Tier 0 hygiene, World, definition hashes with rce api-diff, transactional calls; F.12 lists the rest, which it reports as requiring change: reserved, not implemented), the Lean files, the emitters and the tree-sitter port do not, and every theorem it adds (T42 to T56) is stated (F.9); T48, T51 and T53 are proved of models (RCE/Discharged.lean), and the other twelve are unproved. There is one language: this text. Drafts 0.5 to 0.9 are labels of past commits of it, not alternatives; # rce-version: is a release label that is tolerated, ignored and not hashed (2.7), and a label names exactly one spec commit (C.15). The language of this text is what the reference checker and the Lean files enforce and prove for concurrency (Appendix C), and a program that an earlier commit accepted may require change under this one when a rule was added; an implementation of a release implements that release's text. The core is mechanized in Lean 4 (spec/lean/, section 8), a reference type and well-formedness checker (spec/checker/, rce-check) implements sections 4, 5 and 7 including the admission gate of 6.9 (examples, checks, comptime and constants are evaluated), tree-sitter/ is a tree-sitter port of the grammar checked against the LALR(1) tables of section 3, and grammar-level random programs are checked by rce-fuzz (spec/checker/). The production compiler has not been built from this document yet. Changes made while mechanizing are listed in 9.1 to 9.4. Draft 0.4 follows the language review in spec/LANGUAGE-REVIEW.md; draft 0.5 applies the changes that review proposed and draft 0.4 deferred (9.4). The changes per draft are in 9.1 to 9.7, and the decisions taken for draft 0.9 by derivation, with the open questions each closed, are in 9.7 and 9.8.

RCE is defined by this document. A program is a text; its meaning is a Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) (section 6). Runtimes, emitters, harnesses and editors are not part of the language: they are implementations, and an implementation conforms when it accepts exactly the programs this document accepts and gives each one the meaning this document gives it.

Document status. This specification is the only normative text. SURFACE.md (the native surface design) and the proposals in spec/proposals/ are informative: two normative texts with two grammars could disagree, and only one of them is checked by machine. The programs in SURFACE.md must still be accepted by the reference checker (spec/checker/tests/surface_status.rs). The Form signature is 6.1.

The normative grammar is section 3, and it is also the machine-readable one: rce-spec-check (in spec/checker/, Rust only) reads the EBNF of section 3 from book/03-syntax.md, builds its LALR(1) tables and fails on any shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict, then parses every program in spec/examples/ and requires every program in spec/examples/change/syntax/ to be reported as requiring change, by the LALR(1) tables, the Rust parser and the tree-sitter port alike, then runs rce-check over the same files (all examples together form one program and must be accepted; the 13 syntax rejects, the 49 programs in spec/examples/change/types/ and the 17 in spec/examples/change/admission/ must be reported as requiring change). Current result (draft 0.9, the printed output of rce-spec-check, compared with this text by scripts/claim-counts.py check): the section-3 grammar has 0 conflicts (104 rules, 512 productions, 1028 states); with the additions of C.2, 0 conflicts (118 rules, 581 productions, 1206 states); with C.2 and F.13, 0 conflicts (123 rules, 611 productions, 1273 states), accepting the 18 Appendix F examples; grammar 62/62 accepted, 13/13 requiring change; checker 62/62 accepted, 13/13 and 66/66 requiring change (17 of them inadmissible). Until 2026-10-12 the same grammar was held in spec/rce.lark and checked with Lark (0 conflicts, 533 rules in Lark's expansion); that file is retired. rce-fuzz N SEED generates random type-directed programs from the grammar's productions, with targeted near-misses. 100,000-program run (8 parts × 12,500, seeds 1001–1008, spec/fuzz/RESULTS.md, with the former Python generator and Lark): all 100,000 parsed by LALR(1), exactly one Earley parse each, all accepted by rce-check; 516,012/516,012 rule near-misses and 392,362/392,362 syntax near-misses reported as requiring change; 0 failures. That run used the draft 0.4 generator. From draft 0.5 the generator also covers extern, arena bound, structural recursion, f32, lane-wise arrays, device regions, byte text, u64, select, linear structs, LOOP_LIMIT and iterators; a 1,000-program run (seed 2026) of it has 0 failures. The Rust generator, with the section-3 LALR(1) tables as a third parser: 1,000 programs (seed 7), 0 failures, tree-sitter and LALR(1) agree on all 4,977 syntax mutants.

chapters.title: 1. Notation and conformance
chapters.question: In the grammar notation, what does a Repetition `{ ... }` mean, in the spec's words?

sections.html:
This section fixes how the rest of the spec is written and what it means for an implementation to follow it. EBNF (extended Backus-Naur form) is a notation for grammars; an inference rule states that a conclusion holds when its premises hold. For example Option = "[" Expression "]" . says an option is an expression in brackets.

Grammar notation. EBNF in the style of the Go specification:

Grammar Production, Expression, Term, Factor, Group, Option, Repetition
Production=name "=" Expression "." .Expression=Term { "|" Term } .Term=Factor { Factor } .Factor=name ∣ token [ "…" token ] ∣ Group ∣ Option ∣ Repetition .Group="(" Expression ")" .Option="[" Expression "]" .(0 or 1)Repetition="{" Expression "}" .(0 or more)\begin{array}{rcl}\textsf{Production} & = & \texttt{name}\ \texttt{"="}\ \texttt{Expression}\ \texttt{"."}\ . \\ \textsf{Expression} & = & \texttt{Term}\ \{\ \texttt{"|"}\ \texttt{Term}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{Term} & = & \texttt{Factor}\ \{\ \texttt{Factor}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{Factor} & = & \texttt{name}\ |\ \texttt{token}\ [\ \texttt{"…"}\ \texttt{token}\ ]\ |\ \texttt{Group}\ |\ \texttt{Option}\ |\ \texttt{Repetition}\ . \\ \textsf{Group} & = & \texttt{"("}\ \texttt{Expression}\ \texttt{")"}\ . \\ \textsf{Option} & = & \texttt{"["}\ \texttt{Expression}\ \texttt{"]"}\ .\quad\textcolor{gray}{(0\ \text{or}\ 1)} \\ \textsf{Repetition} & = & \texttt{"\{"}\ \texttt{Expression}\ \texttt{"\}"}\ .\quad\textcolor{gray}{(0\ \text{or}\ \text{more})} \\\end{array}ProductionExpressionTermFactorGroupOptionRepetition​=======​name "=" Expression "." .Term { "|" Term } .Factor { Factor } .name ∣ token [ "…" token ] ∣ Group ∣ Option ∣ Repetition ."(" Expression ")" ."[" Expression "]" .(0 or 1)"{" Expression "}" .(0 or more)​
Plain text of this block
Production  = name "=" Expression "." .
Expression  = Term { "|" Term } .
Term        = Factor { Factor } .
Factor      = name | token [ "…" token ] | Group | Option | Repetition .
Group       = "(" Expression ")" .
Option      = "[" Expression "]" .      (0 or 1)
Repetition  = "{" Expression "}" .      (0 or more)

Lower-case names are syntactic productions, UPPER names are tokens, and quoted strings are literal tokens. NEWLINE, INDENT and DEDENT are produced by the layout pass (2.6).

Judgment notation. Inference rules are written

Typing rules Name
premise1…premisenconclusion  [Name]\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\text{premise}₁\qquad …\qquad \text{premise}ₙ\end{array}}{\begin{array}{c}\text{conclusion}\end{array}}\;\textsf{[Name]}conclusion​premise1​…premisen​​​[Name]
Plain text of this block
  premise₁   …   premiseₙ
  ───────────────────────── [Name]
         conclusion

Γ is a typing context (name ↦ type, mode), Δ a context of live borrows, Σ the declaration environment (types, kinds, traits, events, errors, regions). "iff" means if and only if.

Conformance. An implementation (a) reports that a text requires change whenever it is not in the language of section 3, or breaks a rule of section 7, with a diagnostic naming the rule; (b) for every accepted program, computes δ, λ and the fold of section 6 exactly, including every edge in 6.3. Behavior the spec does not define does not exist: there is no "undefined behavior" and no "implementation-defined" result. The only implementation freedom is cost (time, memory, energy), never value.

chapters.title: 2. Lexical grammar
chapters.question: Which code point is the horizontal tab, as written in this section?

sections.html: This section says how source text is cut into tokens (the smallest meaningful pieces: names, numbers, keywords, punctuation) and how indentation becomes block structure. Getting this exact is what lets every tool read a file the same way. Example: let x = 0x1F # note is the tokens let, x, =, 0x1F; the comment is dropped.

sections.title: 2.1 Source text
sections.html: A source file is UTF-8 encoded Unicode text. A byte-order mark requires change. Line ends are LF or CR LF; a bare CR requires change. The horizontal tab U+0009 requires change anywhere in a file (layout is by spaces only, 2.6). A file that does not end in a line end is read as if it did.

sections.title: 2.2 Comments
sections.html: # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. A comment is part of the line end that follows it, so a line holding only a comment is blank for layout. There are no block comments. (# never occurs inside a token other than a string.)

sections.title: 2.3 Tokens
sections.html:
Tokens are identifiers, keywords, operators and punctuation, and literals. Spaces (U+0020) separate tokens and are otherwise ignored. Tokenization is maximal munch: at each point the longest token that matches is taken. Two consequences are stated so they are not surprises:

  • a<-b lexes as a, <-, b (a send), never as a < -b. Write a < -b.
  • t.0.1 lexes 0.1 as a float. Write (t.0).1.

sections.title: 2.4 Identifiers and keywords
sections.html:
Grammar NAME, letter, digit
NAME=letter { letter ∣ digit ∣ "_" } .(but not the single character "_")letter="A" … "Z" ∣ "a" … "z" ∣ "_" .digit="0" … "9" .\begin{array}{rcl}\textsf{NAME} & = & \texttt{letter}\ \{\ \texttt{letter}\ |\ \texttt{digit}\ |\ \texttt{"\_"}\ \}\ .\quad\textcolor{gray}{(\text{but}\ \text{not}\ \text{the}\ \text{single}\ \text{character}\ \texttt{"\_"})} \\ \textsf{letter} & = & \texttt{"A"}\ …\ \texttt{"Z"}\ |\ \texttt{"a"}\ …\ \texttt{"z"}\ |\ \texttt{"\_"}\ . \\ \textsf{digit} & = & \texttt{"0"}\ …\ \texttt{"9"}\ . \\\end{array}NAMEletterdigit​===​letter { letter ∣ digit ∣ "_" } .(but not the single character "_")"A" … "Z" ∣ "a" … "z" ∣ "_" ."0" … "9" .​
Plain text of this block
NAME = letter { letter | digit | "_" } .      (but not the single character "_")
letter = "A" … "Z" | "a" … "z" | "_" .
digit  = "0" … "9" .

Identifiers are ASCII. (Text values may hold any Unicode; names may not. This keeps names comparable byte for byte, which the name-free hashing of 6.6 relies on.) _ alone is the wildcard token.

Keywords are reserved and cannot be identifiers:

actor     after     and       arena     as        bound     break
chan      check     comptime  const     continue  default   device
elif      else      emit      error     event     example   extern
fail      false     fn        for       forall    from      if
impl      in        intent    iter      kind      let       linear
loop      match     module    mut       none      not       on
or        pass      pub       recv      return    select    self
send      spawn     state     step      struct    then      to
trait     true      try       type      use       var       while
with      yield

One reserved list. The language has one closed list of reserved words, the same in every module, and nothing selects or extends it. It is: the keywords above; the 23 concurrency words of C.1 (par, branch, nondet, budget, deadline, priority, replicated, interrupt, session, lvar, group, lanes, barrier, scope, atomic, protocol, offer, choose, node, supervisor, strategy, child, restart); the ten words of Appendix F (requires, ensures, decreases, ghost, ct, declassify, endorse, release, label and law); and the type names World, Template, Shell, Prompt, Header, mathint and the eight indexed names of 5.16, which no module may declare (W-NAME-2). A keyword or concurrency word used as a name requires change under the grammar (W-SYN-1). A word of Appendix F whose construct this implementation has (ct, endorse, release, label, requires, ensures, ghost, decreases, and law, which begins the laws of 6.11) used as a name requires change (W-NAME-2) unless it is used as its construct. A reserved word or type name whose construct this implementation does not have (declassify, Template, mathint, and law inside a trait, the trait laws of F.6.6) requires change, with the rule W-RES-1 and the words reserved, not implemented; it is never read as an ordinary name and never silently ignored (F.12). Directly after . a reserved word is a member name, so c.offer() and c.choose(L) remain method calls.

device, iter, linear and yield are new in draft 0.5. lalr is not a keyword: drafts up to 0.4 reserved it in rce.lark and the tree-sitter scanner by mistake, without listing it here; draft 0.5 removes it from both.

catch is also a keyword. Keywords are reserved everywhere except as a member name directly after . (x.type, c.close()), where the grammar's member_name admits them; this is the only place a keyword can be a name (change S3). Note: class, unsafe, null, goto, async and await are not keywords; class and unsafe used as statements are syntax errors, and unsafe, Rc, Arc, RefCell as names require change under rule W-SAFE-1 (section 7) so prototype code that used them is diagnosed clearly.

sections.title: 2.5 Literals
sections.html:
Grammar INT, decimal, FLOAT, exponent, STRING, char, escape
INT=decimal ∣ "0x" hexdig { [ "_" ] hexdig } ∣ "0o" octdig { [ "_" ] octdig }∣ "0b" bindig { [ "_" ] bindig } .decimal=digit { [ "_" ] digit } .FLOAT=decimal "." decimal [ exponent ] ∣ decimal exponent .exponent=( "e" ∣ "E" ) [ "+" ∣ "-" ] digit { digit } .STRING=‘"‘ { char | escape } ‘"‘ .char=any Unicode scalar value except ‘"‘, ‘\‘ and line end .escape=‘\"‘ ∣ ‘\\‘ ∣ ‘\n‘ ∣ ‘\r‘ ∣ ‘\t‘ ∣ ‘\0‘ ∣ ‘\u{‘ hexdig{1,6} ‘}‘ .\begin{array}{rcl}\textsf{INT} & = & \texttt{decimal}\ |\ \texttt{"0x"}\ \texttt{hexdig}\ \{\ [\ \texttt{"\_"}\ ]\ \texttt{hexdig}\ \}\ |\ \texttt{"0o"}\ \texttt{octdig}\ \{\ [\ \texttt{"\_"}\ ]\ \texttt{octdig}\ \} \\ & & |\ \texttt{"0b"}\ \texttt{bindig}\ \{\ [\ \texttt{"\_"}\ ]\ \texttt{bindig}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{decimal} & = & \texttt{digit}\ \{\ [\ \texttt{"\_"}\ ]\ \texttt{digit}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{FLOAT} & = & \texttt{decimal}\ \texttt{"."}\ \texttt{decimal}\ [\ \texttt{exponent}\ ]\ |\ \texttt{decimal}\ \texttt{exponent}\ . \\ \textsf{exponent} & = & (\ \texttt{"e"}\ |\ \texttt{"E"}\ )\ [\ \texttt{"+"}\ |\ \texttt{"-"}\ ]\ \texttt{digit}\ \{\ \texttt{digit}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{STRING} & = & `\texttt{"` \{ char | escape \} `"}`\ . \\ \textsf{char} & = & \texttt{any}\ \texttt{Unicode}\ \texttt{scalar}\ \texttt{value}\ \texttt{except}\ `"`,\ `\backslash `\ \texttt{and}\ \texttt{line}\ \texttt{end}\ . \\ \textsf{escape} & = & `\backslash "`\ |\ `\backslash \backslash `\ |\ `\backslash n`\ |\ `\backslash r`\ |\ `\backslash t`\ |\ `\backslash 0`\ |\ `\backslash u\{`\ \texttt{hexdig}\{1,6\}\ `\}`\ . \\\end{array}INTdecimalFLOATexponentSTRINGcharescape​=======​decimal ∣ "0x" hexdig { [ "_" ] hexdig } ∣ "0o" octdig { [ "_" ] octdig }∣ "0b" bindig { [ "_" ] bindig } .digit { [ "_" ] digit } .decimal "." decimal [ exponent ] ∣ decimal exponent .( "e" ∣ "E" ) [ "+" ∣ "-" ] digit { digit } .‘"‘ { char | escape } ‘"‘ .any Unicode scalar value except ‘"‘, ‘\‘ and line end .‘\"‘ ∣ ‘\\‘ ∣ ‘\n‘ ∣ ‘\r‘ ∣ ‘\t‘ ∣ ‘\0‘ ∣ ‘\u{‘ hexdig{1,6} ‘}‘ .​
Plain text of this block
INT    = decimal | "0x" hexdig { [ "_" ] hexdig } | "0o" octdig { [ "_" ] octdig }
       | "0b" bindig { [ "_" ] bindig } .
decimal = digit { [ "_" ] digit } .
FLOAT  = decimal "." decimal [ exponent ] | decimal exponent .
exponent = ( "e" | "E" ) [ "+" | "-" ] digit { digit } .
STRING = `"` { char | escape } `"` .
char   = any Unicode scalar value except `"`, `\` and line end .
escape = `\"` | `\\` | `\n` | `\r` | `\t` | `\0` | `\u{` hexdig{1,6} `}` .

There are no literal suffixes (1u8 is not a token): the type of a literal comes from context (5.3). A \u{…} escape that is not a Unicode scalar value (a surrogate, or above U+10FFFF) requires change. - is never part of a numeric literal; -1 is negation applied to 1, except in patterns (3.9). true, false and none are keyword literals.

sections.title: 2.6 Layout
sections.html:
RCE uses indentation for blocks, as Python does, and the rule is the same one Python's tokenizer uses:

  1. Inside (…), […] and {…} line ends and indentation are ignored.
  2. Otherwise each line end that ends a non-blank line emits NEWLINE.
  3. The layout pass keeps a stack of indentation widths, initially [0]. On the first token of a logical line with indentation width w (number of leading spaces): if w > top, push w and emit INDENT; if w < top, pop while w < top and emit one DEDENT per pop, and w must then equal top (otherwise the text requires change: "inconsistent dedent"); if w = top, emit nothing.
  4. At end of file, emit NEWLINE if needed and one DEDENT per stack entry above 0.

Blank and comment-only lines produce no tokens. There is no line continuation character; open a bracket instead.

sections.title: 2.7 Release label
sections.html:
A module may carry a release label on its first line, as the comment

RCE
# rce-version: 0.6

The line must start with # in column 0 and hold, after optional spaces, rce-version: and a label; trailing spaces are allowed. The label is tolerated and ignored: it selects nothing, gates nothing, is not hashed, does not appear in the Form, and no value of it requires change. A module without it means exactly what the same module with it means. There is one language, the one this document defines, and every module of a program is in it; modules may use each other whatever labels they carry. Because the label is a comment, the grammar of section 3 and its LALR(1) check do not mention it.

A release label names exactly one spec commit (C.15): the text of this document at that commit. An implementation of a release implements that text and no other, and a later commit that changes the meaning of a valid program of the earlier text is a new release with a new label, never a silent change to an old one. The cost of a standard library method call (C.6.4) is the one cost of that text, in every module and wherever the call is executed from.

chapters.title: 3. Syntactic grammar
chapters.question: Which numbered resolution rule in 3.11 covers `send`? (for example R1)

sections.html:
This section is the complete grammar: which token sequences are programs. Its EBNF is read by the machine check (3.12) and checked to be LALR(1) (parsable left to right with one token of lookahead and no conflicts), so every program has exactly one parse. Example: fn half(x: u64) -> u64 = x / 2 is a function declaration with an arrow body.

The grammar is LALR(1) with no conflicts (checked, 3.12). Where a reader might see two parses, the grammar admits exactly one; the resolutions are listed in 3.11.

sections.title: 3.1 Modules
sections.html:
Grammar SourceFile, ModuleHeader, Path, Item, UseDecl
SourceFile={ NEWLINE } [ ModuleHeader ] { Item } .ModuleHeader="module" Path NEWLINE .Path=NAME { "." NAME } .Item=UseDecl ∣ IntentDecl ∣ ExampleDecl ∣ CheckDecl ∣ LawDecl∣ [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl ∣ TypeDecl ∣ StructDecl ∣ KindDecl∣ TraitDecl ∣ FnDecl ∣ ActorDecl )∣ StateDecl ∣ EventDecl ∣ ErrorDecl ∣ StepDecl ∣ ImplDecl∣ ExternDecl .UseDecl="use" Path [ "as" NAME ] NEWLINE .\begin{array}{rcl}\textsf{SourceFile} & = & \{\ \texttt{NEWLINE}\ \}\ [\ \texttt{ModuleHeader}\ ]\ \{\ \texttt{Item}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{ModuleHeader} & = & \texttt{"module"}\ \texttt{Path}\ \texttt{NEWLINE}\ . \\ \textsf{Path} & = & \texttt{NAME}\ \{\ \texttt{"."}\ \texttt{NAME}\ \}\ . \\ \textsf{Item} & = & \texttt{UseDecl}\ |\ \texttt{IntentDecl}\ |\ \texttt{ExampleDecl}\ |\ \texttt{CheckDecl}\ |\ \texttt{LawDecl} \\ & & |\ [\ \texttt{"pub"}\ ]\ (\ \texttt{ConstDecl}\ |\ \texttt{TypeDecl}\ |\ \texttt{StructDecl}\ |\ \texttt{KindDecl} \\ & & |\ \texttt{TraitDecl}\ |\ \texttt{FnDecl}\ |\ \texttt{ActorDecl}\ ) \\ & & |\ \texttt{StateDecl}\ |\ \texttt{EventDecl}\ |\ \texttt{ErrorDecl}\ |\ \texttt{StepDecl}\ |\ \texttt{ImplDecl} \\ & & |\ \texttt{ExternDecl}\ . \\ \textsf{UseDecl} & = & \texttt{"use"}\ \texttt{Path}\ [\ \texttt{"as"}\ \texttt{NAME}\ ]\ \texttt{NEWLINE}\ . \\\end{array}SourceFileModuleHeaderPathItemUseDecl​=====​{ NEWLINE } [ ModuleHeader ] { Item } ."module" Path NEWLINE .NAME { "." NAME } .UseDecl ∣ IntentDecl ∣ ExampleDecl ∣ CheckDecl ∣ LawDecl∣ [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl ∣ TypeDecl ∣ StructDecl ∣ KindDecl∣ TraitDecl ∣ FnDecl ∣ ActorDecl )∣ StateDecl ∣ EventDecl ∣ ErrorDecl ∣ StepDecl ∣ ImplDecl∣ ExternDecl ."use" Path [ "as" NAME ] NEWLINE .​
Plain text of this block
SourceFile   = { NEWLINE } [ ModuleHeader ] { Item } .
ModuleHeader = "module" Path NEWLINE .
Path         = NAME { "." NAME } .
Item         = UseDecl | IntentDecl | ExampleDecl | CheckDecl | LawDecl
             | [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl | TypeDecl | StructDecl | KindDecl
                         | TraitDecl | FnDecl | ActorDecl )
             | StateDecl | EventDecl | ErrorDecl | StepDecl | ImplDecl
             | ExternDecl .
UseDecl      = "use" Path [ "as" NAME ] NEWLINE .

sections.title: 3.2 Intent

Block      = NEWLINE INDENT Stmt { Stmt } DEDENT .
Stmt       = SimpleStmt | LetStmt | VarStmt | IfStmt | WhileStmt | LoopStmt
           | ForStmt | MatchStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt
           | EmitStmt | FailStmt | SpawnStmt | SelectStmt | ArenaStmt
           | DeviceStmt | YieldStmt | ComptimeStmt | CheckDecl | PassStmt .
SimpleStmt = Expr [ AssignOp Expr | "<-" Expr ] NEWLINE .
AssignOp   = "=" | "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/=" | "%=" | "&=" | "|=" | "^=" | "<<=" | ">>=" .
LetStmt    = "let" Pattern [ ":" Type ] "=" Expr NEWLINE .
VarStmt    = "var" NAME [ ":" Type ] "=" Expr NEWLINE .
IfStmt     = "if" Expr Block { "elif" Expr Block } [ "else" Block ] .
WhileStmt  = "while" Expr [ Bound ] Block .
LoopStmt   = "loop" [ Bound ] Block .
Bound      = "bound" Expr .
ForStmt    = "for" Pattern "in" Expr Block .
MatchStmt  = "match" Expr NEWLINE INDENT Arm { Arm } DEDENT .
Arm        = Pattern [ "if" Expr ] ArmBody .
ArmBody    = "->" InlineStmt | Block .
InlineStmt = SimpleStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt | PassStmt | EmitStmt | FailStmt | YieldStmt .
ReturnStmt = "return" [ Expr ] NEWLINE .
BreakStmt  = "break" NEWLINE .      ContinueStmt = "continue" NEWLINE .
PassStmt   = "pass" NEWLINE .       EmitStmt     = "emit" Expr NEWLINE .
FailStmt   = "fail" Expr NEWLINE .  SpawnStmt    = "spawn" Expr NEWLINE .
YieldStmt  = "yield" Expr NEWLINE .
SelectStmt = "select" NEWLINE INDENT SelectArm { SelectArm } DEDENT .
SelectArm  = "recv" Pattern "from" Expr ArmBody
           | "send" Expr "to" Expr ArmBody
           | "after" Expr ArmBody
           | "default" ArmBody .
ArenaStmt  = "with" "arena" NAME [ Bound ] Block .   (capacity, 5.7)
DeviceStmt = "with" "device" NAME [ Bound ] Block .  (accelerator region, 5.13)
ComptimeStmt = "comptime" Block .

The grammar accepts any expression left of =; rule W-PLACE (section 7) then requires it to be a place (a variable, field, index or tuple member path). This is how Python handles the same problem and keeps the grammar LALR(1).

sections.html:
Precedence, loosest first. All binary levels are left-associative except comparison and range, which are non-associative (at most one operator).

sections.title: 3.10 Statement and expression boundaries
sections.html: A Block always begins with NEWLINE INDENT, so a block can never be confused with an expression. A one-line form exists for the common cases: fn f(x: T) -> U = e, step S on E -> e, and Pattern -> stmt in match and select.

sections.title: 3.11 How apparent ambiguities are resolved
sections.html:
Each is resolved in the grammar itself, so there is no precedence declaration and no conflict to resolve at parse time.

  • R1 dangling else. else only follows a Block (statement if) or is mandatory (if … then … else … expression). A statement if ends at its DEDENT, so the next else at the same indentation belongs to it.
  • R2 try … else against if … then … else. The branches of an if expression and the operands of try are CatchExpr, which cannot contain a bare try or if. if c then try a else b is a syntax error; write if c then (try a else b) else d.
  • R3 comparison chains. 0 < a < 10 is a syntax error (non-associative). Write a in 0..10.
  • R4 assignment against equality. = is a statement form, never an expression; (x = 1) is a syntax error.
  • R5 generic call against index. f[T](x) parses as index(f, T) then a call; name resolution (4.3) turns an index of a generic function or type by type arguments into instantiation, as in Go.
  • R6 impl generics against slice types. impl [T] … would be ambiguous with the slice type [T], so impl parameters need forall: impl forall[T: Show] Show for List[T].
  • R7 labels. In argument and pattern lists NAME ":" is always a label. Map literals {k: v} are in a different bracket, so {a: 1} is a map whose key is the variable a (write {"a": 1} for a text key).
  • R8 variant patterns against bindings. A Path pattern is a unit variant if name resolution finds a variant of that name in scope, otherwise it binds a fresh variable (Rust's rule). W-PAT-1 reports that a binding which shadows a variant name requires change, so a misspelled variant is never silently a binding.
  • R9 send. <- after an expression at statement level is a send; in prefix position it is a receive. The two never meet: a <- <- b is "send the value received from b to a".
  • R10 the words of a law. always, every and attest are words of the grammar only at the start of a line inside a law block, and applied and a kept with no : only as the whole outcome of an every step line; everywhere else each is a NAME, so no identifier is reserved for them. A bool field named applied is read in that outcome as (applied). law itself is reserved (2.4).

sections.title: 3.12 Machine check
sections.html:
rce-spec-check (in spec/checker/, Rust only):

  1. reads every rule of this section from its code blocks (the annotation column beside a rule is prose and is skipped), expands the EBNF the way Lark did ([ X ] and { X } inlined as with and without, { X } as one left-recursive helper rule), builds the LALR(1) tables and fails on any shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict (verified: adding | AddExpr "+" AddExpr to AddExpr makes it fail with 3 conflicts); current result (draft 0.9): 104 rules, 512 productions, 1028 states, 0 conflicts (scripts/claim-counts.py check compares these numbers with the output of rce-spec-check);
  2. parses the 62 programs in examples/ (the 60 files there and the 2 of examples/26_use_module/), with and without their final newline; all must parse;
  3. parses the 13 programs in examples/change/syntax/ (tab indent, chained comparison, if expression without else, try in a then branch, inconsistent dedent, class, assignment inside an expression, empty kind, state with no fields, step without on, example without ->, unterminated string, a law with two claims); all must be reported as requiring change.

Each program is parsed three ways (the LALR(1) tables on the reference lexer's tokens, the Rust parser, and the tree-sitter port) and all three must agree.

tree-sitter/ is the same grammar for tree-sitter (grammar.js, with layout, bracket depth, reserved-keyword NAME and longest-match numbers and <- in src/scanner.c). spec/checker/tests/tree_sitter_sync.rs keeps it in sync: for every .rce file under spec/, the tree-sitter parser accepts the file exactly when the Rust parser does, on every CI run.

chapters.title: 4. Programs, names and scope
chapters.question: What is the outermost scope called? (one word)

sections.html: This section says what a whole program is: a set of modules, the names each module can see, and the Form the program denotes. A module is one source file; scope is the region of text where a name can be used. Example: use std.text makes the module std.text visible as text.

sections.title: 4.1 Modules and packages
sections.html: A source file is a module. Its path is given by module a.b.c or, if absent, by its file path relative to the package root with / read as . and the .rce extension removed. use p.q makes module p.q visible under the name q; use p.q as r under r. Items are private to their module unless marked pub. Import cycles require change (W-MOD-2). The modules std.text, std.collections and std.math are built in and always resolvable (S4), and so is every module of the standard library (stdlib/lib of the repository, pinned by hash in its manifest, and pinned by a program as the dependency stdlib, F.5.3): use enc, use data.events and the others resolve with no file given, no directive and no flag, in every tool (rce lib lists them). A library module's own check, example and intent items are not part of a program that imports it; its items are. use is the only way to bring one module's items into another: a line #!lib NAME, which earlier tools read as a second way, is a comment like any other. A program is the set of modules given together, and use must name one of them or a built-in module (W-NAME-1).

sections.title: 4.2 The program's Form
sections.html:
A Form module is a module (with what it imports) that declares at least one state, event or actor. The Form of the program is built from all Form modules reachable from the root (6.1). A module with only fn, types, const and impl is a library module: it has no Form of its own and denotes a set of pure functions.

A program whose root declares fn main() and no state is a command: it denotes the Form with one region Main of unit type, one event Start(args: List[text]), and δ given by running main (6.8).

sections.title: 4.3 Scope
sections.html:
Scopes nest: universe (built-in types and functions, 6.3–6.4) ⊃ package ⊃ module ⊃ item (generic parameters, parameters, state fields inside steps) ⊃ block. Declarations at module level are visible throughout the module regardless of order (so const N may follow its use). Inside a block a name is visible from its declaration to the end of the block. Shadowing a name from an enclosing block is allowed with let; shadowing a parameter, a state field or a module-level name in the same item requires change (W-NAME-2).

Namespaces: one namespace for values (variables, functions, consts, variants, events, errors) and one for types (types, kinds, traits, states, actors). Event, error and variant constructors live in both: as types (for patterns and payload typing) and as constructor functions.

chapters.title: 5. Static semantics
chapters.question: What is the name of the example kind used to illustrate error sets?

sections.html: This section gives the static semantics: the rules checked before a program runs. A type is the set of values an expression may have; ownership says which variable is responsible for a value, and a borrow is a temporary reference to it. Example: after let b = a where a is a List, using a again requires change because the list moved to b.

usize is a u64 used for lengths and indexes. f32 (draft 0.5) is computed in f64 and rounded once to f32 after each operation (6.3 N7), so every target gives the same bits. Float literals are f64; an f32 value is written x as f32, and f32 and f64 never mix without a cast. Box[τ] is List-like owned indirection of one element, needed only for recursive kinds; a &Box[τ] (or &mut Box[τ]) argument is accepted where &τ (&mut τ) is expected (deref coercion, draft 0.4). Every type has a kind of ownership (5.5): Copy, Move, or Borrow.

Integer ranges. An integer type denotes the mathematical integers in its range: iN = [−2^(N−1), 2^(N−1)−1], uN = [0, 2^N−1]. Arithmetic is checked against the declared type's range (6.3). Arithmetic on u64 and usize uses the Form's unsigned operations (6.3 N8, draft 0.5), so the whole range [0, 2^64) is available; drafts up to 0.4 trapped any u64 result at or above 2^63 (D7).

Text is byte-indexed (draft 0.5). s.len_bytes() is the number of UTF-8 bytes (s.len_chars() the number of characters; unqualified len on text requires change, W-LEN-1), s[i] is the byte at offset i as a u8, and s[a:b] is the text between byte offsets a and b, which must both be character boundaries (otherwise trap("not a char boundary")). Iterating for c in s still yields one-character texts. Go, Rust and Zig all index text by byte; the draft 0.4 code-point indexing made s[i] O(n).

Lane-wise arithmetic (draft 0.5). For arrays a, b : [τ; n] of one numeric τ and one comptime length n, a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b (and a % b for integers) apply the operator lane by lane and have type [τ; n]. Each lane follows the scalar rules (overflow and division by zero trap). Different lengths, or a non-numeric τ, require change (W-SIMD-1). An implementation may use vector instructions; the result is defined by the lanes, so it is the same on every target. A list literal is a List unless it meets an array type of the same length, as an integer literal is i64 unless it meets another integer type.

Type aliases. type A = τ (and type A[α₁, …, αₙ] = τ) without where gives τ a second name: A, with its parameters substituted, is the type τ in every rule. It is not a nominal type, since N above ranges only over structs, kinds, actors and states. So a parameter c: A with type A = chan τ′ is a chan parameter and makes its function a task function (5.2), and a value of type A is accepted wherever τ is and the reverse. Example: with type Pipe = chan (u64, text), fn feed(p: Pipe, n: u64) may send on p and be spawned (spec/checker/tests/alias.rs).

Refined types (extension, all versions). type R = τ where p declares R as the values of τ that satisfy the predicate p, in which self names the value. τ is an integer type, text, or a List, Map, Set or array type. p is in a decidable fragment: comparisons (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) between self (integer τ), self.len() (text, in UTF-8 bytes as in 5.15, or a collection) and integer literals; the character classes self.isdigit(), self.isalpha(), self.isspace(), self.isempty() of a text; and and, or, not. Anything else is W-REF-1. where is contextual: no type is followed by a name, so the word stays an ordinary identifier. A refined value is checked exactly where a value is checked against its declared integer range (6.3, 6.4 step 3): at a typed let or var, a parameter, a field or payload constructor, a field initializer and the write-back of a state field. The check fits the value to τ first, then evaluates p; if p is false the result is trap("refinement: value is outside R"). So an event whose payload is outside its refined type does not apply and keeps the state before any step runs, as an out-of-range integer payload does, and a step whose new state breaks a field's predicate keeps the state (6.4, T8). R <: τ: a refined value is used wherever τ is. Derivation: validation that the type does not record can be skipped (soundness), a predicate checked at one boundary has one outcome (determinism), and the refinement reuses the one boundary the language already has, the range check, rather than a second mechanism (one meaning per construct). The fragment is decidable in time linear in p and in the value, so the check has a fixed cost class (energy observability); full dependent types are excluded by the same derivation, since an undecidable obligation would make acceptance itself unbounded. Example: type Pct = u8 where self <= 100; event SetVolume(pct: Pct); SetVolume(pct: 101) keeps the state with refinement: value is outside Pct, and a step computing level + 60 on level: Pct = 60 keeps the state. Lean: RCE/Refine.lean (holds_total, fit_sound, refine_preserved, refine_kept_unchanged, admit_sound; T35).

Error sets. In τ ! ε, ε is a finite set of declared error names, written as one error name or as the name of a kind whose variants are all errors (type ParseErrs = … is not needed; declare kind ParseErrs with variants ParseFailed(at: u32) and Empty). Subtyping: τ ! ε₁ <: τ ! ε₂ iff ε₁ ⊆ ε₂, and τ <: τ ! ε (a plain value is a success).

sections.title: 5.2 Contexts and modes
sections.html:
A typing context Γ maps each variable to (τ, m) with mode m ∈ {let, var, field} and a liveness flag (live, moved). A step body runs in context step(R), a function body in fn, a comptime block in comptime, and an actor handler in actor(A). Effects are tied to the context:

Contextmay emitmay failmay spawn/send/recv/selectmay read state
fn (pure)noyes (if return type is τ ! ε)nono
task fn (has a chan parameter)yesyesyesno
fn mainyesyesyesno
step(R)yesyessend only (to actors and declared channels)fields of R only
actor(A) handleryesyessend onlyfields of A only
comptimenoyes (compile error)nono
call a foreign extern fn (5.11)only from fn main and task functions

A function called from a step does not inherit the step's effects; only the step body itself emits or sends. A function with a chan parameter is a task function: it may emit, send, receive, select and spawn, and it can be called (or spawned) only from main or another task function. Every other fn is a pure function of its arguments; a pure function, a step or a handler cannot call a task function (W-EFF-1). spawn f(ā) requires f to be a task function (W-SPAWN-1). (Change S2: draft 0.1 made every fn but main pure, which left nothing that spawn could start.)

Tail values. In a block-bodied function, if the last statement is an expression statement, or a match or if/else whose every branch ends in one (recursively), those expressions are the function's result and are typed against its return type ([Tail]; change S5). Elsewhere an expression statement's value is discarded, and an error union may not be discarded.

sections.title: 5.4 Types of declarations
sections.html:
• state R with fields fᵢ : τᵢ = eᵢ: every τᵢ is an owned value type (no borrows, no channels, no region types, no functions); every eᵢ is a comptime constant expression (W-STATE-2). R's type is the record {fᵢ : τᵢ}.
  • event E(fᵢ : τᵢ) and error E(fᵢ : τᵢ): payload types are data types: base types, tuples, arrays, List, Map, Set, options, structs and kinds built from data types. Events may additionally carry chan τ (a reply channel) when received by an actor.
  • step R on p if g -> e: in context step(R), the fields of R are bound as var, p is typed against the event sum, g : bool, and e must have the type of R's single field (only allowed when R has exactly one field; W-STEP-3). With a block body, the body is a statement list; the final state is the values of the field variables at the end of the block.
  • actor A with fields and handlers: like a state whose steps are the handlers, plus an address type A (a Copy handle) that supports a <- msg.

sections.title: 5.5 Ownership
sections.html:
Every value has exactly one owner: a variable, a field, a collection slot, a channel buffer, or the state. Types fall in three ownership kinds:

Copy   : bool, integers, f32, f64, (), chan τ, actor handles, fn values,
         and tuples/arrays/structs/kinds all of whose components are Copy
         and whose size is fixed.
Move   : text, List, Map, Set, Box, options/tuples/structs/kinds containing a Move component.
Borrow : &τ, &mut τ, [τ] (slices exist only borrowed).

Rules:

  O1  Use of a Move variable moves it ([Var-Move]); a moved variable cannot be
      read, borrowed, or moved again until reassigned.
  O2  Assignment `x = e` to a var drops the old value of x first and makes
      x live.
  O3  `copy(e)` duplicates a value of any data type (deep copy); it is the
      only way to duplicate a Move value. (Copy-on-write is an
      implementation choice, not visible.)
  O4  At the end of each block, live owned values introduced in it are
      dropped in reverse order of introduction. Drop has no user-visible
      effect (there are no destructors), so drop order is unobservable.

sections.title: 5.6 Borrowing
sections.html:
RCE borrows are second class (as in Hylo and Swift's inout): a borrow can be created only as a function argument or as the operand of a for, a match, a method receiver, or a let whose scope ends before any conflicting use. A borrow cannot be stored in a field, a collection, a channel message, an event, a state, a closure that escapes, or be returned: with one exception: a function whose return type is a borrow (-> &[T]) must return a borrow derived from a parameter, and the result is tied to that parameter (R-RET). This removes lifetime annotations entirely.

Δ is a set of live borrows (ℓ, k, path) with k ∈ {shr, mut}. Paths are x, x.f, x[_] (any element), ordered by prefix (x ⊑ x.f).

Typing rules Borrow-Shr, Borrow-Mut

Two paths overlap iff one is a prefix of the other; x[i] and x[j] always overlap (indexes are not compared statically). The borrows among the arguments of one call are made together, so f(&mut s.a, &mut s.b) complies with the Form, while f(&mut s.a, &mut s) and f(&mut xs[i], &mut xs[j]) require change under W-OWN-2. A borrow ℓ ends at the end of the call or statement that created it (R-END), for a let borrow at the last use of its name, or for R-RET at the last use of the returned value. Because borrows never outlive the statement that made them except through a let borrow or R-RET, Δ is empty at every statement boundary outside those ranges, which makes the check a local, linear pass.

let borrows. A borrow made by let a = &p or let a = &mut p is live from the let to the last statement of the same block that uses a or a name bound from a. In that range a use of a path overlapping p that the rules above forbid (writing, moving or &mut-borrowing it under either kind of borrow, reading or borrowing it under a &mut borrow) requires change under W-OWN-2: let a = &mut n; n = 5; bump(a) requires change, and let a = &mut n; bump(a); n = 5 complies with the Form. A write through a is a write to the place p (writeVia of the Lean model of T6), so let a = &mut n; bump(a); emit n emits 1. An index in p is evaluated once, at the let.

Shared XOR mutable (theorem T6 relies on this): at every program point, for every path p, either Δ holds no mut borrow overlapping p, or it holds exactly one and no shared borrow overlapping p.

Not relaxed in draft 0.9. A limited relaxation, in which a reference is invalidated only below steps that are not independent of it (the group borrowing of the Valen language), is sound in the form studied, but its preservation of T6 is not proved. The rules above are unchanged; the obligation is T56 (Appendix F, F.9, stated and unproved), and the rule is adopted only after that lemma is proved in Lean. Relaxing W-PAR-1 is not sound and is excluded (F.2).

chapters.question: What kind of channel does a capacity of 0 give? (one word)

sections.html: This section continues the static rules for features that control where values live and what code may do: regions (arenas freed as a block), concurrency, traits, compile-time code, foreign functions, and the draft 0.5 linear types, device regions and iterators. Example: with arena r bound 4096 gives a block its own memory of at most 4096 canonical bytes, freed when the block ends.

sections.title: 5.7 Regions (arenas)
sections.html:
with arena r introduces region r for the block. A type τ @r is allocated in r.

Typing rules Arena

  r ∉ free-regions(type of any value assigned to a place outside the block)

with arena r bound n gives r a capacity of n bytes (n : u64, evaluated once at block entry). Capacity is counted in canonical bytes, the length of the canonical JSON of each value allocated in r, so the limit is the same on every implementation. An allocation that would take r past n is trap("size limit"), and the state is kept as for any trap. Without bound the capacity is unlimited except by N9. The reference evaluator measures the values bound in the region after every statement of the region's body. So nothing allocated in r escapes the block; copying out (copy(x), or pushing a Copy element) is how results leave. Each step body runs inside an implicit region step freed when the step returns; state fields are not region-typed (they live in the state's own storage).

sections.title: 5.8 Concurrency
sections.html:
• chan[τ](n) creates a channel with capacity n (a comptime or runtime usize; 0 means rendezvous) and type chan τ; τ must be a data type or a chan. Channels are Copy handles.
  • c <- v moves v into the channel. <- c has type τ? (none when c is closed and empty).
  • spawn f(a₁…aₙ) requires every argument to be a data value or channel (not a borrow, not region-typed): arguments are moved into the task (W-SPAWN-1). Tasks share nothing but channels and actor handles, so data races cannot be written.
  • select arms: recv p from c (c : chan τ, p : τ?), send v to c, after n (n : u64 logical ticks), default. At most one default, at most one after.

sections.title: 5.9 Traits
sections.html: A trait declares associated types and function signatures. impl Tr for T must define every member with a signature equal to the trait's after substituting Self := T (W-TRAIT-1). Coherence: at most one impl of a trait for a type in the whole program, and an impl must be in the module of the trait or of the type (orphan rule, W-TRAIT-2). Generic functions are monomorphized (no dynamic dispatch, no vtables), so trait method calls are resolved statically. Built-in traits: Eq, Ord, Hash, Show, Copy, Data, derived structurally for every type whose components have them (f64 is Eq and Ord with the total order of 6.3, since NaN never exists).

sections.title: 5.10 Comptime
sections.html: An expression or block marked comptime, every const initializer, every array length, every state field initializer, and every argument for a comptime parameter is evaluated during compilation by the dynamic semantics of section 6 (with the same edge semantics). A comptime evaluation that traps or exceeds its fuel (6.7) is a compile error. A comptime fn may only be called at comptime. Comptime results become constants in the Form IR. Comptime evaluation cannot read files, clocks, environment or network (W-CT-1), so compilation is deterministic.

sections.title: 5.11 Foreign functions
sections.html:
extern "C" fn f(p₁: τ₁, …) -> σ declares a function implemented outside RCE with the platform C calling convention. It has no body. Rules (W-FFI-1):

  • The ABI string is "C". A foreign function is not comptime, not generic and has no self.
  • Each parameter type is bool, an integer type, f64, &text (passed as a pointer to UTF-8 bytes and a byte length), &[τ] or &mut [τ] with τ one of those scalars (pointer and element count). Borrows are second class (5.6), so the foreign callee holds them for the duration of the call only; no copy is made.
  • The result type is a scalar or (). No memory allocated by foreign code is ever owned by RCE, and no RCE allocation is freed by foreign code, so the two sides never need to agree on an allocator.
  • A foreign function may be called only from fn main and task functions (W-EFF-1), never from a pure function, a step, a handler or comptime, and it cannot be spawned (W-SPAWN-1). δ therefore never calls foreign code.
  • A foreign function is not a value: its name may appear only as the callee of a direct call (W-FFI-1). The context rule above is checked at the call, so a value would let a pure function receive a foreign function from main and call it.
  • Each call is recorded in the log as Foreign(f, arguments, result). Replay supplies the recorded result instead of calling f, so the run of a command remains a function of its inputs and its log (T1, T3), with foreign results counted as inputs.
  • The memory behaviour of the foreign code is outside the language: T6 holds for the RCE side on the assumption that the callee touches only the buffers it was given, writes only through &mut buffers, and keeps no pointer after it returns. This is the trust boundary; it is named by the extern keyword at the one place it occurs.

sections.title: 5.12 Linear types (draft 0.5)
sections.html:
linear struct H declares a type whose values must be used exactly once. It is meant for handles to outside resources (a file, a socket, a device buffer) that must be released once and only once. Rules (W-LIN-1):

  • A linear value is moved, never copied: copy(h) requires change, and the type is not Copy whatever its fields are.
  • Every linear local, parameter included, is consumed (moved into a call, returned, or sent into a foreign function) exactly once on every path: a linear local still live at the end of its block, at return or at fail requires change, and so does one consumed on some branches of an if or match but not others.
  • A linear value is not moved inside a loop body unless it was created in that iteration.
  • A linear type may not appear inside a collection, an array, an option, a channel, a state or actor field, an event or error payload, a struct field or an iterator's element type. So no data structure can hide a second copy or drop one.
  • A foreign function (5.11) may take and return a linear struct whose one field is an integer or bool; the C side sees that scalar. This is how open/close pairs are typed.

Reading a field (h.fd) does not consume the value. Lean: RCE/Linear.lean (linear_exactly_once).

sections.title: 5.13 Device regions (draft 0.5)
sections.html: with device d [bound n] is a region (5.7) whose contents an implementation may place in accelerator memory. In addition to the arena rules, a device region holds fixed-size values only: no List, Map, Set, text, slice, channel or iterator may be bound in it, and its body may not emit, spawn, send, select, yield or call a foreign function (W-DEV-1). The body is therefore pure arithmetic on scalars, tuples, structs of those and arrays (with lane-wise operators), which is what accelerators run. Its meaning is the same as the block run on the CPU, so the region is only a placement hint; bound counts canonical bytes as for arenas.

sections.title: 5.14 Iterators (draft 0.5)
sections.html:
A function whose result type is iter τ is an iterator function. Its body is a block that produces values with yield e (e : τ) and ends by falling off the end or by return with no value. Rules (W-ITER-1):

  • An iterator function is pure (no chan parameter, no effects), and yield appears only in one.
  • A value of type iter τ may only be the operand of for or the receiver of .collect() (which returns List[τ]). It cannot be stored, passed or returned, so an iterator is never shared or resumed twice.

The meaning is the push model of Go 1.23 range-over-func: the loop body runs at each yield, break in the body stops the iterator, and return in the body returns from the enclosing function. The number of yields per run counts against the loop limit (6.7), so yield number LOOP_LIMIT + 1 is trap("loop bound"), and an iterator always terminates. Python generators and Rust iterators are pull-based and can be resumed from anywhere; the push form keeps delta total without any suspended state.

sections.title: 5.15 Standard library, effects and I/O
sections.html:
Standard library (normative). The standard library is closed: it is exactly the builtin methods below plus the concurrency methods of 5.8 and Appendix C (close, join, offer, put, wait, freeze, pscan, pscan_incl) and the num.rs primitives of 6.3. A method not in the table is W-NAME-1 at check time, so no program reaches an unknown method at run time. Every method in the table is pure and deterministic: it reads its receiver and arguments, and a method that "changes" a receiver (push, insert, sort, ...) updates only that receiver variable; none performs I/O. The table is checked against the reference evaluator (spec/checker/tests/stdlib_costs.rs).

ReceiverRCE typeMethods
Intintegers (iN, uN, usize)abs, checked_add, checked_div, checked_mul, checked_sub, max, min, saturating_add, saturating_mul, saturating_sub, tostr, wrapping_add, wrapping_mul, wrapping_sub
Ff64abs, ceil, floor, max, min, round, sqrt, tostr
Boolbooltostr
Texttextchars, contains, endswith, isalpha, isdigit, isempty, isspace, join, len, len_bytes, len_chars, lines, lower, raw, reverse, sha256, split, startswith, strip, toint, tostr, upper, words
F32f32abs, tostr
Geniter τcollect
ListList[τ], [τ; n]append, clear, contains, filter, fold, get, isempty, len, map, pop, push, reverse, sort, sum, utf8, with
MapMap[k, v]contains, get, insert, keys, len, merge, remove, values
SetSet[τ]contains, insert, inter, len, tolist, union
Optτ?isnone, issome, or

raw exists only on Text[C] (5.16). Text has len_bytes and len_chars and no unqualified len, which requires change (W-LEN-1, F.5.2).

Sets and map merge (normative). A Set[τ] is its own value, not a List[τ]: it holds its elements in canonical order without duplicates (7.1), so two sets with the same elements have the same representation (RCE.Canon.set_canon), and list methods do not apply to it. It is shown and embedded in the Form (7.1) as that list. set_of(xs) makes one from a List[τ]. s.len() is the number of elements and s.contains(x) whether x is one of them. s.union(t) is the set of the elements of either, s.inter(t) of the elements of both, s.insert(x) sets s to s.union(set_of([x])) (a var receiver), and s.tolist() is the elements as a list in that order. m.merge(n) on two Map[k, v] has the keys of either; a key in both maps to m[k] ⊔ n[k] by the Merge of v (a user impl Merge, or the built-in instance, C.11.5), and the result is in canonical key order. union, inter and merge borrow their argument. These are the join (and, for inter, the meet) of the set and pointwise map lattices, so a merge written from them is certified (C.11.5).

Hashing (normative). t.sha256() on a text t is the SHA-256 digest (FIPS 180-4) of the UTF-8 bytes of t, written as 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, as a text. It is pure, total and the same on every target; it is the digest 6.1 and 6.8 apply to canonical JSON, so a program given the canonical JSON of a value as text computes the same hash as the Form log and the content-hash ids. It is in the linear class of C.6.4.

Bytes to text (normative). b.utf8() on a List[i64] b is the text whose UTF-8 encoding is exactly the bytes of b. It traps, and so keeps the state for the event it runs in (T8), when an element is outside 0..255 or the bytes are not well-formed UTF-8 (RFC 3629: no overlong forms, no surrogates, nothing above U+10FFFF); it never substitutes characters, since that would change content silently. A leading byte-order mark is kept. It is pure, total on well-formed input, the same on every target, and in the linear class of C.6.4.

Effects and I/O (normative). By derivation from least privilege, a program has no ambient authority: there is no file, clock, network, environment or randomness primitive. The only ways values enter are the events of E (6.1) and, in fn main and task functions, channel receives and foreign calls (5.11); the only ways values leave are emit (λ) and sends. Each of these is an effect of the context table above, so the checker, not run-time behaviour, decides which code may do I/O. Inputs that are not events (a select nondet choice, a foreign result) are logged, so replay is deterministic (T1, T21). A capability that is not in this list cannot be added by a library, because the library is closed.

Cost semantics. Each standard library call costs c_call plus the work of its complexity class on the sizes of its receiver and argument (C.6.4); see C.6 for the budget rules.

sections.title: 5.16 Indexed values
sections.html:
In every module four type names and four contexts belong to the language: Text[C], Secret[τ], Cap[A], Guarded[τ, A], and Html, Url, Sql, Json. No module may declare an item with one of these names (W-NAME-2). Each is a type index: the value is a value of the base type (text, τ, (), τ), and the index is a static fact the checker carries. Indices are erased at run time, so δ, the log and the emitters are unchanged except for the encoders. Derivation (spec/proposals/CORE-PROPERTIES.md, P1): one meaning per construct requires that a text which is HTML in one place and SQL in another be two types; least privilege requires that authority be a value, not an ambient fact; soundness requires that the checker, not a convention, enforce both. The three indices are one mechanism: a value carries an index, and it crosses an index only by a named, total, costed construct.

Context-typed text (W-CTX-1). Text[C] for C one of the contexts is text whose structure (markup, query syntax) is fixed by the program. It is made only by C.lit(s), where s is a string literal (program text is trusted: its author wrote it), and by C.encode(t) for a text t, which escapes every metacharacter of C. a + b joins two values of one context; any other operator, or + with plain text or another context, is W-CTX-1. x.raw() gives the text of a Text[C] as text (going back only re-enters through encode). An event payload carries plain text only (W-CTX-1): context text cannot come from outside. emit may carry Text[C]; a host sink for C takes exactly that type. The encoders (normative, every runtime): Html maps & < > " ' to & < > " '; Url percent-encodes every UTF-8 byte except A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ with uppercase hex; Sql gives a standard SQL string literal, the text between single quotes with each ' doubled; Json gives a JSON string literal with " \ newline, return and tab escaped and other code points below U+0020 as \u00xx. Consequence (T36): every structural metacharacter of a Text[C] value comes from a literal, so untrusted text cannot form markup or query syntax. SQL injection and cross-site scripting are not expressible. Example: Sql.lit("WHERE name = ") + Sql.encode(b) with b = O'Brien is WHERE name = 'O''Brien'; Sql.lit("WHERE name = ") + b is W-CTX-1.

Secrets (W-SEC-1). Secret[τ] is opaque. A secret value comes only from an event payload field of a Secret type: there is no constructor and no literal of a secret type, so a credential cannot be written in the program (hard-coded credentials are not expressible; comparing a secret with a literal is W-TY-1). The only operations are binding, storing (in a state field, a struct, an option), passing and ==/!= between two secrets of one type, whose boolean is the one release. Any other operator or method on a secret is W-SEC-1. A value that can hold a secret may not be emitted, sent on a channel, carried by an error payload (a kept outcome is an output, 6.1) or passed to a foreign function (W-SEC-1). So λ never carries a secret (T36, noninterference up to the equality bits). The log D holds admitted events with their payloads, as any store of the program's inputs does; it is not an output.

Capabilities (W-CAP-1, W-CAP-2). Cap[A], for A a declared struct, is the authority A as a value. It appears only as the type of an event payload field or of a parameter (W-CAP-1): it cannot be stored in a state, struct, collection, option or channel, so authority lives for one event and is never ambient. It cannot be constructed by an expression: the host that admits an event attests the capability (written () in an event list or example), exactly as it supplies every other input, and the attested event is logged. Guarded[τ, A] is the type of a state field only (W-CAP-1); reading it gives a τ, it keeps τ's range checks (6.3), and a step that writes it (assignment, &mut borrow, a mutating method, or the arrow form of its only field) must match only events whose payload has a field of type Cap[A] (W-CAP-2). So a missing authorization check is not expressible: a log of events without the capability never changes the guarded field (T36).

chapters.title: 6. Dynamic semantics: the mapping into the Form
chapters.question: Which JavaScript function is named for rounding to binary32?

sections.html: This section gives the dynamic semantics: what a program computes, as a mapping into the Form. It also lists the exact edge behaviour of every primitive (overflow, division by zero, float rounding, text indexing), which every implementation must reproduce. Example: -7 / 2 is -3, and i64.MIN / -1 traps with "overflow: 9223372036854775808 is outside i64".

sections.title: 6.1 The Form of a program
sections.html:
Let the program declare regions R₁…Rₖ (state and actor declarations; actors also carry a mailbox), events E₁…Eₘ and errors X₁…Xⱼ. Its Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) is:

Figure (informative). Where the Form sits between the checker, the log D and the emitters. Source: docs/figures.

  • S = ⟦R₁⟧ × … × ⟦Rₖ⟧, where ⟦R⟧ is the set of records {fᵢ : ⟦τᵢ⟧} of R's field types, with the initial state s₀ = (r₁⁰, …, rₖ⁰), rᵢ⁰ the record of field initializers (evaluated at comptime). Actor regions add a mailbox queue and a held-message queue (Form law 3).
  • E = the disjoint union of the events' payload sets: E = ⊎ₗ {Eₗ} × ⟦payload(Eₗ)⟧, plus the built-in Tick(n: u64) and the task events of 6.8.
  • δ : S × E → S × O* (state and the outputs of the step) is defined in 6.4. It is a total function (T2).
  • λ maps each step to its output sequence O*: values emitted, and for an event that does not apply the record Kept(X, payload).
  • D is the log: the sequence of admitted events e₁, e₂, …, each entry with its outcome (applied, or kept with X). The fold law: the state after the log is sₙ = foldl(δ₁, s₀, D) where δ₁ is the state component of δ.

Canonical signature (normative). This is the one signature; the engine profile (D.6), the engine IR (FormIr::step) and the language interpreter are instances of it, and any other text (proposals, papers) defers to it. S = Σc × Σd (control regions, data: regions, clock, input count, relations); δ : S × E → S × O* total; λ = π₂ ∘ δ; δ₁ = π₁ ∘ δ. An entry of D is the record {seq, event, prev_hash, state_hash, hash} where seq is the 0-based index, event is {type, payload}, prev_hash is the hash of the previous entry (64 zeros for the first), state_hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the positional form of the state after the step, and hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash} with event in its positional form. The positional form (T7) replaces every declared name by a position: the state is the list of its regions in declaration order, each the list of its field values in declaration order; a record of a declared struct, event or error is the list of its field values in declaration order; a variant record is [k, [fields]] with k the variant's index in its kind; an event is {type, payload} with type the event's index among the module's events and payload the positional record; every other value embeds as the table below says. A record of a type the module does not declare (a host.* record, a label) and the built-in Tick keep their names, since no renaming of the program touches them. The stored event and the readable state keep their names, so a log is readable without the module; a log or trace that repeats the hashed forms does so under hashed ({event, state}), which is derived. A log may also carry outcome, out and state; these are derived and must equal replay (T1), so they are not hashed. An event that does not apply (T8) is recorded with its unchanged state and ends the example log. Both producers are tested against this rule (spec/checker/tests/form_signature.rs, tests/form_signature.rs), and tests/nameless.rs checks that a renamed program has the same hashes; RCE/Positional.lean proves that the positional form, and so the state hash and the entry chain under any hash function, is unchanged by the renamings of 10.6 (T7).

Values ⟦τ⟧ are the Form's JSON-shaped values (form/types.rs): integers (i64), floats (finite f64), text, bool, null, lists, records. The embedding of RCE types into them is fixed:

RCE typeForm value
boolbool
iN, uN, usizeint, with the range of the RCE type checked at every write
f64float, finite, type kept (6.3 N1)
texttext (sequence of Unicode scalar values)
()null
(a, b, …), [τ; n], List[τ]list
Set[τ]list, sorted by canonical order, no duplicates
Map[k, v]list of [k, v] pairs sorted by canonical order of k
struct / state recordrecord (keys sorted, as canonical JSON)
kind variant V(f: …)record {"$v": "V", f: …}; unit variant: {"$v": "V"}
τ?null for none, the value for some (and some(none) requires change: τ may not itself be an option, W-TY-2)
chan τ, actor handlerecord {"$chan": id} / {"$actor": id}, id the content hash of 6.6

Canonical order of values (used by Set, Map and select): null < bool < int < float < text < list < record; ints by value; floats by IEEE 754 totalOrder (-0.0 < 0.0); text by code point; lists and records lexicographically. It is a total order (NaN does not exist, N3 F4) and it agrees with state identity: two values are equal in it exactly when their canonical JSON is equal. Derivation: Set and Map keys are compared by this order, so an order that called two observable values equal (-0.0 and 0.0 under IEEE ==, or 1 and 1.0 by numeric value) would silently merge distinct keys; the type tag and totalOrder keep every distinct state a distinct key.

6.1.1 Canonical JSON bytes (normative)

Every hash of 6.1 (state_hash, hash), the value limit of N9 and every trace written as JSON are taken over the same byte sequence, the canonical JSON of a Form value. This subsection defines it byte for byte. It is derived from one requirement: two implementations must produce the same bytes for the same value, and the bytes must decode to that value and to no other (6.3 N1), because replay rebuilds state from D.

The output is a UTF-8 byte sequence with no byte order mark, no whitespace outside text and no trailing line end. By the kind of value:

  1. null, bool. null, true, false.
  2. int. The exact value in decimal: an optional -, then digits with no leading zero (0 is 0), no +, no exponent, no fraction. The range is -2^63 to 2^64 - 1 (6.3 N2). An integer is never written as a float and a float is never written as an integer.
  3. float. Finite binary64 only (NaN and infinities are not Form values, 6.3 N3). Let x be the value.
    • x = 0: 0.0, or -0.0 when the sign bit is set.
    • Otherwise take the shortest decimal digit string d1 d2 … dn that reads back as x (round to nearest, ties to even). When two digit strings of that length both read back as x, take the one closer in value to x; when they are equally close, take the one whose last digit is even. Let e be the decimal exponent of d1 (x = ±d1.d2…dn × 10^e).
    • If 10^-4 ≤ |x| < 10^16: decimal notation with no exponent. A sign - when x < 0, then the digits with the point placed after e + 1 digits; zeros are added to fill the integer part, and 0. followed by -e - 1 zeros starts a value below 1. The result always has at least one digit after the point (10.0, not 10).
    • Otherwise: a sign - when x < 0, d1, then .d2…dn only if n > 1, then e, then e as a decimal integer with - when negative and no + and no leading zero (1e16, 1.5e-7, 5e-324).
  4. text. ", then each Unicode scalar value in order, then ". " is written \", \ is \\, U+000A \n, U+000D \r, U+0009 \t. Any other value below U+0020 is written \u and four lowercase hexadecimal digits, so U+0008 is \u0008 and U+000C is \u000c. Every other scalar value, including U+007F, U+2028, U+2029 and /, is written as itself in UTF-8. Text is not normalised: é (U+00E9) and é (U+0065 U+0301) give different bytes.
  5. list. [, the canonical JSON of each element in order separated by ,, ].
  6. record. {, then each field as the canonical JSON of its key (as text) : the canonical JSON of its value, separated by ,, then }. Fields are in ascending order of key by Unicode code point (equivalently, by the bytes of the UTF-8 encoding). Keys are distinct.
  7. Set and Map. As their list embeddings of 6.1, in the canonical order of 6.1, then rule 5.

Relation to RFC 8785. The JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785, sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.3) fixes whitespace, literals, the escaping of control characters and the sorting of object members, and takes number serialisation from ECMAScript. Rules 1, 5 and the absence of whitespace agree with it. Rules 2, 3, 4 and 6 differ, each for a stated reason, so an RFC 8785 library does not produce these bytes and must not be used to hash a Form value:

CaseRFC 8785This sectionReason
float with no fractional part1010.0an int and a float must decode differently (N1)
negative zero0-0.0the sign is observable state (N3 F6)
10^-6 and 10^210.000001, 1e+211e-6, 1e21one fixed rule with no +; the thresholds are 10^-4 and 10^16
integers above 2^53not exact in an ECMAScript number; RFC 8785 section 3.1 says to use textdecimal digits, exact to 2^64 - 1the language has u64 and i64 (N2)
U+0008, U+000C\b, \f\u0008, \u000cone escape form for every control character not named in rule 4
member orderUTF-16 code unitscode pointsthe same unless two keys first differ at a supplementary-plane character against one in U+E000 to U+FFFF (the RFC's own sort data differs)

Golden vectors. spec/data/canonical-json-vectors.json holds 77 vectors: a value, the exact canonical text, and the SHA-256 of its UTF-8 bytes. It covers every rule above, the boundaries 10^-4 and 10^16, the extremes of i64, u64 and binary64, the sort data of RFC 8785 section 3.2.3, five of the number rows of RFC 8785 Appendix B, and the bytes behind one state_hash and one hash. Two programs check it: spec/checker/tests/canonical_json.rs against the reference implementation, and scripts/canonical-json-vectors.py check, an encoder written from this subsection alone. A third implementation is conformant when it reproduces every canonical text and digest.

Resolved items. Two differences between the reference implementation and this subsection were found by the vectors and are fixed.

  • Tie rule. Rust's shortest-digit routine ({:e}) breaks an exact tie between two shortest candidates to the odd digit: for 1424953923781206.25 (binary64 0x43143ff3c1cb0959) it gave 1424953923781206.3, where the rule of rule 3 (as ECMAScript's String(x) and Python's repr) gives 1424953923781206.2. The reference now takes the shortest digit count n from {:e} and then the n-digit decimal closest to x, ties to even (interp::shortest_e, used by float_json, float_text and emit/rt.rs). The vectors float-1424953923781206.2 and the four float-tie-* vectors (round down, round up, and their negatives) pass.
  • Second writer. rce trace now writes text through the same jstr as the hashed writer, so U+0008 and U+000C print as \u0008 and \u000c and a trace shows the bytes that were hashed. The test the_trace_writer_agrees_with_the_hashed_writer covers every vector. A decision between this text-based form and a length-prefixed binary form is deferred until measured (the form defined here is the one all existing hashes use).

sections.title: 6.2 Evaluation
sections.html:
Expressions are evaluated by a big-step judgment ⟨e, ρ, σ⟩ ⇓ r, where ρ maps variables to values, σ is the store of vars and fields, and the result r is one of

  • ok(v, σ′): a value and updated store,
  • trap(m): a defined failure of the Form. The trap texts are exactly those of 6.3 ("overflow: V is outside T", "division by zero", "shift amount out of range", "non-finite float", "index K out of range", "slice index out of range", "slice bounds reversed", "not a char boundary", "size limit", "value limit"), "loop bound" (6.7) and "budget" (C.5),
  • fail(X, v): a user error raised by fail or propagated by try,
  • control signals ret(v), brk, cont (statements only).

Evaluation order is fixed: left to right, operands before operators, arguments before the call, receiver before arguments. and/or short-circuit. There is no other source of nondeterminism in expressions.

Selected rules (the rest are the standard ones for a strict language):

Typing rules E-Arith, E-Arith-Trap, E-Try-F, E-TryElse, E-Catch
