  • R3 completed: the reference evaluator counts arena and device bytes (canonical JSON of the values bound in the region, after every statement) and traps "size limit".
  • lalr is no longer reserved (2.4).
  • The four Form runtimes of the engine (Rust crate and WASM through num.rs, Python, JavaScript for XState and SCXML) must agree on the new ops. They are in the engine crate, not in this repository, and no test published here compares them.

Known open questions (not decided here): the standard library surface beyond the num.rs primitives; foreign interfaces other than the C ABI (WASM component model, GPU kernels); how an RCE module is used as a fit (the handler spec and fit formats themselves are now Appendix D); whether emitters should lower device regions and lane-wise operators to real accelerator or vector code (today they run them on the CPU, which 5.13 allows).

sections.title: 9.5 Changes in draft 0.7
sections.html:
• Size-scaled standard library method costs (C.6.4), the one meaning change recorded in C.15 (a new release of the whole text; the per-module version selection of that draft was retired by decision 64).
  • Errata for every version, listed in C.15: closed standard library and no ambient I/O (5.15), &mut write-back on fail in the emitters (6.2, the earlier T33 rule, since retired) with nested calls flattened by an order-preserving ANF pass (T34), exact u64 at or above 2^63 (6.3 N2), the fallible-return literal fix (5.1), saturating budget arithmetic (C.6), the hash-chained Form log (6.1).
  • Refined types (5.1, W-REF-1, T35): type R = τ where p with p in a decidable fragment, checked where the declared integer range is checked. Derived from soundness and one meaning per construct (spec/proposals/CORE-PROPERTIES.md, P2). Closes the replacement-matrix rows "improper input validation" (defined: requires change at entry) and "dependent specifications" (defined for the decidable fragment; undecidable obligations excluded by derivation). An extension for every version (C.15).
  • sha256 text method (5.15): SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes as 64 lowercase hex digits, linear cost class (C.6.4), in the reference evaluator and the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes. Derived from self-hosting: the hash-chained log (6.1) and content-hash ids (6.8) must be computable by an RCE program. An extension for every version, since it only admits programs that required change before (C.15).

sections.title: 9.6 Changes in draft 0.8
sections.html: • Version 0.8 (2.7, 5.16, C.16): 0.7 plus indexed values, context-typed text Text[C], opaque Secret[τ], capabilities Cap[A] and Guarded[τ, A] fields, with W-CTX-1, W-SEC-1, W-CAP-1, W-CAP-2 and T36. A new version because the names it takes (Text, Html, ...) could be a 0.7 program's own declarations, whose meaning would change. Derived from one meaning per construct, least privilege and soundness (spec/proposals/CORE-PROPERTIES.md, P1). Closes the replacement-matrix rows SQL injection and XSS (excluded), missing authorization (excluded), hard-coded credentials and information exposure (excluded).

sections.title: 9.7 Changes in draft 0.9
sections.html:
Version 0.9 (2.7, Appendix F) is specified and not yet implemented. Each item below is applied in the tier order of its dependencies; the derivation is in Appendix F next to the rule, and every theorem is stated and unproved (F.9).

  • Tier 0. Stale text corrected (errata for every version): decisions 8, 11, 12, 21 and 29, the Copy list of 5.5 (f32 added), the former W-VER-1 (removed: the release label is tolerated and ignored, 2.7, decision 64) and 2.7 (0.8 and 0.9 named), the overview status and its checker figures. Under version 0.9, unused values, dropped non-unit results and unused stores require change (F.3.2), and adds lexical hygiene: hidden and bidirectional characters, shadowing of any enclosing local, qualified variants, longest-token lexing (F.3.3).
  • Tier 1. World capability for foreign calls (F.4.1); information-flow labels with the kept-outcome channel and robust declassification (F.4.2, T42, T43); definition hashes and rce api-diff (F.4.3, T50); transactional calls (F.4.4, T47).
  • Tier 2. File-system capabilities and caretaker revocation (F.5.1, T51); typed shell and prompt output and strict input (F.5.2, T44); the hash-pinned manifest (F.5.3, T54); ct fn (F.5.4, T45); declared budgets (F.5.5, T52).
  • Tier 3. Templates t"..." (F.6.1); requires and ensures (F.6.2, T46); ghost (F.6.3, T49); decreases (F.6.4, T48); if let (F.6.5); trait laws, tested not proved (F.6.6).
  • Tier 4. The broker contract for the lethal trifecta (F.7, T55).
  • Rules derived from the sources' later items (F.8): closures, types, calls, operators, containers, indexing, classes, errors, reflection and derive, compile-time code, linear values, tooling, release gate.
  • Non-goals (F.2): effect handlers, switchable contracts, mutable aliasing across par, runtime reflection, and the other constructs listed there, each with its reason.
  • Not adopted until proved: relaxed sequential borrows (5.6, T56).
  • Version number. The proposal list was drafted under the name "draft 0.6"; 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8 are taken, so this is 0.9 (C.15: a version number is never reused).

sections.title: 9.8 Decision log for draft 0.9 (open questions, decided by derivation)
sections.html:
Each row decides one question left open by the survey and security study. The principle named is one of the five in Appendix F: least privilege (a), soundness (b), determinism (c), totality (d), one meaning per construct (e). No row rests on taste: where no principle decides, the existing text stays.

QQuestionDecisionDerivation
1Which effects are undoable for a transactional callWrites to owned values and emit into the pending output are undoable; send, receive, spawn, foreign calls, World operations, host entries and consuming a linear handle are not; a path from a non-undoable effect to a fail requires change (W-TX-1)(c): a restore must be total and need no handler; (b) T8
2Measure for mutual recursionOne lexicographic tuple for the whole group (F.6.4)(d): one well-founded order for the group, as 6.7 already uses
3Is tool metadata hashedNo. Comments, formatting, declaration order and attributes are not hashed; the version, signature, contracts, measure, ghost clauses, labels and referenced hashes are(c) and T7: a hash is the meaning, nothing else
4? in par armsRequires changeT16: ? leaves the arm early, so an arm is not an expression with one result
5Advisory formatCanonical JSON object signed with Ed25519 over its SHA-256(c): reuse the canonical JSON of 6.1; Ed25519 signatures are deterministic
6Map iteration orderAscending canonical key order of 7.1already 6.7 and the C.15 erratum; (c)
7Half-open slices and inclusive rangesUnchanged: slices as in 6.3 N8, ranges keep .. and ..=(e): both already have one meaning; no principle favors removing one
8Comparison-chain sugarNot adopted; a chain is a syntax error (R3, section 3)(e): one meaning, and a chain would need a second reading of the operator
9NaN payload and libm strategyNeither exists: non-finite results trap, transcendentals are RCE code in math (F9)already decision 51; (c)
10Value-indexed typesNot adopted beyond comptime array lengths and the type indices of 5.16(d): a value in a type needs a decidable fragment, and none is specified
11Linear types in the specThey are (5.12, W-LIN-1, T12); a linear handle is not undoablealready in the spec; (b)
12Inductive predicatesNot adopted; a predicate is a ghost pure total bool function(d): inductive definitions need positivity and continuity checks no theorem needs
13Are doc comments hashedNo doc comments exist (decision 2, # comments only), so nothing is hasheddecision 2; (e)
14Maximal-munch token ruleAdopted as a requirement on the lexer, checked in F.11(c): the same text must tokenize the same everywhere
15First-class type invariantsA refined type has R.check(v) -> R?; no witness clause; no implicit conversion; opaque outside its module(b) T35: a value of R is only made by a checked path
16Argument labelsKept (decision 18) and checked: a wrong label requires change(e): a label that is not checked has two meanings, the written and the real one
17Constant conditionsAn if, elif, while or guard on a comptime constant requires change (W-UNUSED-2)(e): one branch is dead code; P8
18Display traitShow of 5.9; a template field of a non-text type must implement it(e): one display conversion, explicit; no new trait
19Map equality independent of orderYes, because the representation is canonical(c): equality and iteration agree by construction
20User-definable deriveNot offered; derive is the built-in closed set of 5.9T7: a user derive needs reflection
21Literal default type when unconstrainedUnchanged: integer literals default to i64, float literals are f64 (5.3, 5.1)(c): the default is a fixed rule; requiring change adds no safety
22Expression fields and nested quotes in t"..."Not allowed: a field is an identifier or a field path, no quotes inside a field(e) and S8: a field needing a nested lex has two readings
23Inductive type syntax and its decreases ruleNo new syntax: a recursive kind with Box, strictly positive because fn types cannot occur in data (W-TY-2)(d): positivity follows from W-TY-2
24Is the kept outcome the empty enumNo: the kept outcome is not a value and has no type(e): a bottom type brings subtyping, which RCE does not have
25Fixed-size arrays as value parameter or ghost lengthArray length stays a comptime constant [τ; n]; contracts may use len(d): no value-indexed types (Q10)
26Spelling of the Copy and Discard boundsNo new spelling; Copy is the built-in of 5.5 and generics stay affine (decision 41); a type parameter is not instantiated by a linear type(b) T12
27Canonical form of propositionsA contract is hashed as the canonical parsed tree of its expression; no rewriting or solver normalization(c): a hash must not depend on a solver
28Source span in the kept record of a contract violationNo; the record has the rule or clause, the definition hash and the clause index(c) and T7: a span depends on whitespace
29Layout-sensitive vector typesNot adopted; lane-wise fixed arrays only (decision 43)no principle decides; the existing text stays
30Any foreign boundary in 0.9Yes, the C ABI of 5.11 as a World operation, declared in the manifest(a): authority is a value; (c) T32
31Big integer or ghost mathematical integermathint, ghost and contract code only; no runtime big integer(d): an unbounded integer has size-dependent cost, which budgets cannot bound
32Wording for reactive programsA total step function driven by the host (6.1, Appendix E); no while true(d)
33Unsatisfiable contracts: static or first callStatic in the decidable fragment (W-CON-1); otherwise enforcement makes every call trap, keeping the state(b), (d): decide what is decidable, never succeed vacuously
34Comment formsOnly # line commentsdecision 2; (e)
35Implication spelling in contractsNone; write not a or b(e): or short-circuits, so the form is already guarded
36Digit separators in literalsOne _ between digits, as 2.5 already says(e): one canonical form, already specified

sections.title: 9.9 Reconciliation of the published text with draft 0.9
sections.html: The published text and the engine development tree were joined at draft 0.9. No version number was reused or redefined: versions 0.7 and 0.8 keep the meaning they had in the published text, and 0.9 is the version of Appendix F. Where both trees had reworded the same stale sentence (decisions 8, 11, 12 and 29 above), the wording that states the original rule and then its revision was kept, because it says what the rule was and what it is now. The canonical JSON text of 6.1.1 and its vectors, and the claim counts of the published text, are kept as published. The figures quoted in the overview, the syntax chapter and the tooling chapter are the printed output of rce-spec-check on this tree, checked by scripts/claim-counts.py check.

chapters.title: 10. Tooling: the `rce` command and the language server
chapters.question: Which JSON-RPC error code does the language server return for a request it does not know? (a number)

sections.html: This section defines the tools that read RCE programs: the rce command and the language server it contains. It adds no rules to the language; it says what each tool prints and returns for a given input. Example: rce run counter.rce "Inc, Dec, Dec" prints the state after each event and shows that the step of the third event keeps the state, with exit status 1.

sections.title: 10.1 Principles
sections.html:
1. Determinism. Every subcommand of 10.2 to 10.10 is a function of its arguments and the bytes of the files it reads. Two runs on the same input give the same output bytes and the same exit status. None of them reads the clock, the network, environment variables or random numbers. The same binary also carries the host commands (rce host ...) and rce db, defined by Appendix E; the host loop reads the clock (the frame period of Tick) and the network by design, and logs what it reads as inputs (HC-2, HC-14), so this item does not describe them. The handler-spec staleness rule W-HS-CUR-2 takes a time as an input and is part of the engine profile (D.9, D.10), not of these subcommands.
  2. No model in the loop. No subcommand and no language server request calls a language model, a remote service or any learned component. A diagnostic, a run, a test verdict, an emitted file and a formatted file come only from the rules of sections 2 to 7.
  3. One checker. rce check, rce test, rce run, rce emit and the language server all use the same parser, type checker and admission gate (6.9) as the reference checker rce-check. A file accepted by one is accepted by all.
  4. Exit status. 0 means success. 1 means a program requires change, an example or check failed, a run reached a kept step, or fmt check found a file to change. 2 means a usage error: unknown subcommand, wrong number of arguments, unreadable file, or an unknown emit target or construct an emitter does not translate (10.5). 3 means a question the command could not decide within its bound: rce equiv and rce change when exploration reached fuel before either equivalence or a distinguishing event sequence was established, and rce law when the bound LAW_FUEL left a law undecided (10.11). 4 means a run the host cannot perform: a run of fn main in which an lvar passes from one task to another needs task threads, and the host cannot start one (10.3).

rce is one binary, built from the reference checker crate in spec/checker (crate rce-spec-check, cargo build --release --bin rce). The language commands of this section are implemented in spec/checker/src/cli.rs (entry point cli::main), with their tests in spec/checker/tests/. This rce carries the language commands only; the Form command line (rce form ...), which reads the Form spec format rather than RCE programs, is not part of this build, and rce form exits with status 2.

The tables of 5.15 (which methods each receiver has) and C.6.4 (the work class of each method) are not typed into the checker a second time: it reads them from spec/data/spec-data.json, which rce-spec-data generates from this book. The two tables are cut from it into spec/data/spec-tables.json, the file compiled into rce, the checker and its wasm build; rce-spec-data check fails when either file differs from what the book gives.

sections.title: 10.2 `rce check FILE|DIR...`
sections.html:
All FILEs form one program: use resolves among them and then in the built-in standard library (4.1). A DIR is a package: it stands for its .rce files, recursively, in sorted order, and reads nothing outside it (the multi-module example is the package spec/examples/26_use_module/, so rce check spec/examples/26_use_module checks it alone). Each file is parsed, type checked (section 5) and admitted (6.9: every const, comptime block, check and example is evaluated). For each file, in the order given, one line is printed:

ok FILE
recommended FILE: line N: RULE message
requires change FILE: line N: RULE message [METHOD][; line M: RULE message [METHOD] ...]

Every requires change report names its rule from section 7 and ends with the rule's method from the table of 7.1: [altered by rce fmt] when rce fmt writes the change (10.6), else [requires change]. A recommended line follows the ok line of an admitted file, one per recommended change. Exit status 1 if any file requires change, else 0.

sections.title: 10.3 `rce run FILE [EVENTS]`
sections.html:
The file must pass rce check alone; otherwise one requires change line is printed and the status is 1.

With EVENTS. EVENTS is written exactly as the event list of an example line (3.2, EventRef { "," EventRef }), for example "Inc, Inc, Dec" or "Deposit(amount: 50), Withdraw(amount: 20)". Let s₀ be the initial state (6.1) and e₁ … eₙ the events. For k = 1 … n the command computes

(sₖ, oₖ) = δ(sₖ₋₁, eₖ)

where δ is the step function of 6.4 and oₖ is the sequence of values the step emitted (λ). It prints line 0 as 0 (initial) STATE, then for each k the line k EVENT STATE followed by one line emit VALUE per element of oₖ, in order. STATE lists every region as Region { field = value, ... }, regions separated by ; , in declaration order. If the step for eₖ keeps the state, the line is k EVENT kept: ERROR, sₖ = sₖ₋₁ (T8), and the next event is applied to that state, as on the host (HC-21). The status is 1 when the step of some event keeps the state, and 0 otherwise. An event name that is not declared is a usage of a wrong event list: one requires change line, status 1.

For the counter spec/examples/01_counter.rce:

$ rce run 01_counter.rce "Inc, Inc, Dec, Dec, Dec, Inc"
0 (initial) Counter { n = 0 }
1 Inc Counter { n = 1 }
2 Inc Counter { n = 2 }
3 Dec Counter { n = 1 }
4 Dec Counter { n = 0 }
5 Dec kept: Underflow
6 Inc Counter { n = 1 }

Without EVENTS. The module must declare fn main() with no parameters. The command evaluates its body by the rules of section 6 and prints emit VALUE for each value emitted, in order. If the body traps or fails, the last line is kept: REASON and the status is 1. Calls to foreign functions (5.11) are not executed by the reference evaluator and trap. If there is no fn main(), the command says so and the status is 1.

The evaluator is the reference interpreter of the checker, with the fuel bound of 6.7 and the VALUE_LIMIT of 6.3. It is a definition of meaning, not a fast runtime. The body runs on the tick runtime of 6.8 and Appendix C, whose log of the run is the trace of fn main in rce trace (10.9).

The reference tick runtime runs each task, fn main included, on its own thread of the host, or as a state machine of its one scheduler (conc::Tasks). A task held as a state machine is the list of answers the scheduler has given it: at each move the scheduler runs the task's body from its start on a fresh evaluator, replays those answers in order, and takes the first step not yet answered as the task's next request. A body is a function of its arguments and its answers, so every earlier step repeats exactly, and the log of the run (10.9) is the same, entry for entry, as with threads (spec/checker/tests/emit_run.rs, main_traces_without_threads_equal_the_reference, on 66 runs). A par whose branches wait on lvars runs, in such a task, its branches in source order, each until it ends or reaches a wait not yet satisfied, and runs a stopped branch again from the fork after a pass in which a put changed an lvar; a pass with no change fails the waits, as the threaded par does when every waiting branch is idle (T29). Where the host cannot start a thread, such as WASI preview 1 (rce built for wasm32-wasip1), every task is a state machine and every par runs this way, so the run needs no thread and prints what it prints on any host.

One run still needs task threads: one in which an lvar (C.11.8) passes from one task to another, as a spawn argument, in a message to a channel or an actor, or as a task's result. A state machine runs its earlier steps again at every move, so it would read a shared lvar at a later state than the step it belongs to. On a host without threads such a run stops at that step: the command prints nothing on standard output and one line on standard error, FILE: fn main needs task threads, which this host does not provide (HOST: an lvar passes from one task to another), HOST being the host's target, and the status is 4. Whatever output the run had produced before that step is not printed. The tick runtime written in the core, which rce run-core would run, is still the next slice of the proposal one-emitter.md (section 13, 10.12).

sections.title: 10.4 `rce test FILE|DIR...`
sections.html:
The test cases of a module are its example lines and its check items, including those inside intent blocks. rce test admits the files as rce check does, which evaluates every case (6.9, W-INT-1). It prints, per file,

ok FILE (E examples, C checks)
FAIL FILE: line N: RULE message[; ...]

with E and C the numbers of cases in that file, then a total line P passed, F failed. Exit status 1 if F > 0. A test verdict therefore equals the admission verdict: a module whose examples do not hold is not a program (section 7).

sections.title: 10.5 `rce emit TARGET FILE`
sections.html:
TARGET names an output. The file must pass rce check on its own; for core it may instead be a core module, a JSON object whose format is rce-core/1, which is read only if it is well formed (rules W1 to W6 of the proposal spec/proposals/one-emitter.md, ONE-3).

TARGETOutput
formthe Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) as one line of JSON (6.1), then a line end
corethe core module of FILE, format rce-core/1 (the module lowered once, or the core module read), as one line of canonical JSON (6.1.1), then a line end (informative: the core is the proposal one-emitter.md, ONE-1)
rustone Rust 2024 source file with a main
pythonone Python 3 source file
jsone JavaScript module (ES2020 or later, BigInt) for Node
scalaone Scala 3 source file with a @main for the JVM (Java 19 or later)

The Form JSON lists objects in canonical order (6.1), so it is a deterministic function of the program text.

The four program targets are the ones this checker emits. The language places no bound on targets, and it is designed so that every language is both an output of the Form (a target, printed through a per-language table) and an input (a lift, the reverse map, from the language's grammar and a semantics table), each passing the same gate, the reference trace of every example program byte for byte (T9). That design (spec/proposals/rce-form.md, informative) is not built; of the four program targets, rust, python and js pass the gate today. The registry of targets and the one-emitter mechanism are the proposal spec/proposals/emit-targets.md (informative); a target that the table cannot pin to 6.3 is observation-only, never a projection.

The program emitters. rust, python, js and scala translate the checked module, not the Form. Each output is self-contained. Its first line is a comment naming the program hash (10.8: the SHA-256 over the definition hashes of F.4.3, name-free and layout-free) and the checker version and commit that printed it, so an emitted file is tied to its source. It starts with a runtime that defines the values of 6.3 and their operations, following the reference evaluator (spec/checker/src/interp.rs) value by value. That includes the integer range checks, the trap messages, canonical map key order and the display of floats and text. After the runtime comes one target function per RCE function, method, step and constant. An expression becomes calls to runtime helpers with its operands in evaluation order; if, while, loop, for and match become the target's own control flow, with one counter per loop against its bound. Values are never changed in place: an assignment to a.f[i] rebuilds the value, as the reference evaluator's assign does.

The Rust output follows the shape of the verified emitter of T9 (spec/lean/RCE/Emit.lean): one value type, Result with ? for traps and kept steps, and i128 arithmetic checked against each integer type's range. The theorem of T9 is about the Lean model of that emitter. The emitter in rce is tested against the reference evaluator; it is not proved.

The Scala output is the functional-language target. Its values are the same dynamic values as the JavaScript output's (integers as BigInt with their type, floats as JVM Double, whose arithmetic is IEEE 754 binary64 with round to nearest even and no contraction since Java 17, and whose toString is the shortest round trip since Java 19). Loops are while loops, and break and continue are control exceptions caught at the loop, so no RCE loop grows the stack; the observations run on one thread with a 2 GiB stack.

What an emitted program does. Run it, and it prints the module's observations: one line per constant, per check, per function without parameters (other than main), per event of each example (the state after it, its outputs, or the kept record), and finally the outputs and result of fn main. These are the lines emit::observe computes with the reference evaluator, so that a target and the reference can be compared line for line.

Embedding an emitted program. An emitted file is also the step function of the module, for a host to call (Appendix E: the host contract is met around δ). Imported rather than run, it prints nothing: the Python file prints its observations only under __name__ == "__main__", and the JavaScript module only when node runs that file itself; the JavaScript module exports initialState, delta, showState, show, construct, fuelReset, chk, Kept, the value classes Int, F, Rec, Lst, Mp and Opt, EVENT_FIELDS, formValue and fvJson, and loads where there is no process (a browser), where steps run and tasks and par do not. The Rust file, used as a module (#[path = "FILE"] mod m;), makes initial_state, delta, show_state and event_fields public. A host calls the initial state once and delta(state, event) once per input, after resetting the fuel (HC-7a); delta returns the next state and the outputs, or reports the step as kept with the reason's display text. examples/interop/ holds such hosts (an asyncio and a FastAPI service in Python, a tokio service in Rust, a node:http service and a React component in JavaScript) and examples/interop/check.py, which requires each host's transcript to equal rce run FILE EVENTS byte for byte.

How the emitters are tested. spec/checker/tests/emit.rs emits all 62 programs of spec/examples/ (the 60 files and the 2 of 26_use_module) in all three targets. To exercise function bodies, it first adds probes: for each function and method, up to three calls on small sample arguments built from the parameter types, plus one example that sends every event. It then runs each output (rustc, python3, node) and requires its output to equal the reference evaluator's, line for line. On 2026-10-16, with rustc 1.98.1, Python 3.13.5 and Node 20.19.2, all 58 agree on all three targets, with 474 observation lines per target. (The dated runs below were made when the corpus was 51 programs, and 55 for Scala, with 299 and 361 observation lines.) Four programs (14, 15, 34, 47) contain only concurrency and give no observation. A separate program (tests/emit_edge.rce) covers range traps, loop bounds, &mut write-back, closures and float display. The Scala target has its own test in the same file: on 2026-10-14, on the Apple M5 Max below, with Scala 3.10.0 run by scala-cli 1.18.0 on OpenJDK 27, all 55 programs of the current corpus (with the package files of example 26) agree with the reference, 0 not printed, 361 observation lines, and the edge program agrees on all four targets. Its oracle is RCE_SCALA (default scala-cli). That agreement is for this examples corpus only. On the larger conformance suite (conformance/), a run on 2026-10-28 with Scala 3.10.0 on OpenJDK 21, which compared each trace by its head only, passes 1,459 tests with 0 failures, and 520 are not applicable to an emitter; the Scala emitter has not yet been run with the whole-trace comparison of the emit baseline (conformance/README.md). The targets a test run covers are named as data, one word per line, in spec/checker/tests/emit_targets.txt (rust, python, js, scala), never by an environment variable or a flag. Every test that runs emitted programs runs them on each covered target it uses and fails when a covered target's toolchain does not start; a target the file does not name is reported as not covered by the run, never counted as a pass, and a test of that target alone is reported as ignored. The file names rust, python and js, the toolchains of the continuous integration runs; Scala is covered by adding its word. The oracles used were Python 3.13.5 and Node 20.19.2. The test reads the oracle paths from RCE_RUSTC, RCE_PYTHON and RCE_NODE (default rustc, python3, node on the path) and prints each oracle's version. On 2026-10-12 the same tests were also run on an Apple M5 Max (macOS 27.0.1, arm64) with rustc 1.98.1, Python 3.14.5 and Node 26.11.1: 51 of 51 agree on each of the three targets, 0 not printed, 0 skipped, 299 observation lines per target, and the edge program agrees on all three.

Fuel. Each emitted program counts fuel (6.7) at the reference evaluator's charge points: one tick per evaluated expression, per executed statement, per call of a user function or method, and per element of a list comprehension and of map, filter and fold. A temporary introduced by the emitter's own lowering is not charged. The limit is 50,000,000; it is reset before each observation, as the reference starts a new evaluator for each, and running out traps with the message "comptime fuel exhausted". The words fuel N set the limit to N and fuel-trace prints fuel K after each observation, K being the ticks used. These two words exist for the test below; the default program takes no argument.

The log D. With the word trace, an emitted program also prints the log D (6.1) of each example. Before the line of each event that δ applied or kept comes its entry, d applied HASH BODY or d kept HASH BODY, where BODY is the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash} over the positional forms and HASH is its SHA-256; after the example's last event comes trace HEAD, the hash of the last entry (64 zeros when there is none). emit::observe_trace computes the same lines with the reference evaluator, the fuel lines of fuel-trace included. The head commits to the events and the state hashes only. The state shown after each event, the outputs, the reason an event was kept and the fuel are not hashed, so a trace is compared whole: every line of an example's block, the entries of D included. The emit adapters of conformance/ answer a trace with that block, and the harness compares it line for line with the block rce-conform prints for the same program and events.

spec/checker/tests/fuel.rs compares the ticks used, line for line, on the 50 programs of the emitter tests (with probes) against emit::observe_fuel of the reference evaluator, in all three targets. It then runs ten programs at every limit from 0 up to 300 and at 400 evenly spaced limits above, up to one more than the program uses, and requires each target to trap at the same observation with the same output as the reference run at the same limit. Within one observation, the emitted order of ticks can differ from the reference where the emitter evaluates arguments before entering a call; the trap observation and the total are what the test fixes. The Scala target is in the same test (the emitted file is packaged once into a jar and run with java -jar); on 2026-10-14 it agreed on all 54 programs of that corpus and at all 1,366 swept limits (a run that covered Scala alone).

Running fn main. Run with the word run, an emitted program instead evaluates fn main with tasks, channels, select, actors and par on a runtime of its own: every task is a thread (a worker in JavaScript), and one scheduler admits their moves tick by tick in the order of conc::run_main, the reference of rce run without EVENTS. It prints emit VALUE per output and the line outcome Done, outcome Deadlock or outcome Stopped: REASON. A module without fn main() prints the reference's message ("nothing to run") on standard error and exits with status 1, as rce run does. Fuel follows the reference's pools: each task has its own, starting full (its first ticks are the call of its function and one per argument); actor handlers share the scheduler's pool; a par branch or for ... par chunk starts from its parent's remaining fuel, and the branches are charged back in source order, so the trap falls where the reference's sequential run puts it. With trace as well, the program prints the trace of fn main (10.9) before the outcome line: per entry of the run's log, in order, the line d applied HASH BODY (d kept HASH BODY for a Kept entry), BODY the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash} of that step and HASH its SHA-256, then trace HEAD.

spec/checker/tests/emit_run.rs compares the three runtimes with conc::run_main on a corpus of task programs. Among them are the four concurrency examples 14, 15, 34 and 47, each run with a fn main from spec/checker/tests/drivers/ appended to its unchanged text. Its test main_traces_agree_on_every_target compares the traces of fn main of the three runtimes with the reference's, line for line, on 66 runs: that corpus, the supervised actors of the same file, example 37, two session programs of spec/conc06b/accept/, the partition cases and program events, which together write an entry of every kind of 10.9. spec/checker/tests/fuel_run.rs runs seven of these programs at every fuel limit where the reference's result changes and at the limit before it (258 runs over the three targets), and requires the same outputs and outcome.

Limits of the emitters.

  • In the observations, channels, spawn, select, actors and extern functions trap with the same message as in the reference evaluator ("not available at comptime"); they run only under run. extern functions trap there too.
  • A par whose branches wait on an lvar runs its branches at the same time in the reference (ParMode::Threads). Derivation. The governing law is schedule independence: a par must be observationally equal to one fixed sequential order, source order (C.4). Fuel is additive over sequential composition, so the sequential run traps at the first branch i where the uses of branches 1..i sum past the fuel left at the fork. The reference therefore gives each branch a copy of that fuel, sums the branches' uses in source order after they finish, and traps with "comptime fuel exhausted" at the first branch whose running sum passes it, before that branch's own result is taken. The trap point is the sequential one. A split of the fuel before the fork would make the set of programs that trap depend on the split rule and would agree with no sequential order, with no gain in soundness, so it is not used. The cost of running branches ahead is bounded: at most k times the fuel left at the fork is evaluated for a par of k branches, of which the excess over the sequential run is discarded. A wait charges no fuel while blocked, so a branch's use does not depend on the schedule. The emitters run such a par by restart and restore the fuel and the budgets of an abandoned attempt (par_snap, par_restore), so each branch is charged once, for its completing attempt. spec/checker/tests/fuel_run.rs checks this at every change point on two programs (lvarpar, and lvartrap, where a late division by zero must lose to the fuel trap when fuel runs out first).
  • Deep recursion ends with the target's own stack error.
  • A call that writes back its receiver or a &mut argument (xs.push(x), f(&mut a)) is translated only as a whole statement or as the right side of let, var, an assignment, return, emit or fail. Elsewhere, rce emit does not yet print the program: it exits with status 2 and names the construct. Every example program is printed.
  • When a function whose result is a union fails, its &mut arguments are not written back. The reference evaluator writes them back.
  • The Python output has been checked with Python 3.13.5 and 3.14.5, and the JavaScript output with Node 20.19.2 and 26.11.1. Other versions have not been run.
  • The Scala output has been checked with Scala 3.10.0 only, on OpenJDK 27 (the examples corpus) and OpenJDK 21 (the conformance suite). With run it runs fn main through its task runtime, the same tick scheduler as the other targets, and prints that there is nothing to run when no fn main() is declared. A par runs its branches in source order on one thread (by restart when they wait on lvars), as the JavaScript output does when a local cannot go to a worker.

For an unknown target, or a program that one of these emitters does not translate, rce emit prints nothing on standard output, prints the reason on standard error, and exits with status 2. It never prints a partial file.

sections.title: 10.6 `rce fmt [check] FILE...`
sections.html:
rce fmt rewrites each file into canonical layout. Let tok(t) be the token sequence of text t produced by the lexer and layout pass of 2.6, with line numbers dropped. The formatter is a function fmt on texts with:

  1. Meaning preserved. tok(fmt(t)) = tok(t). The formatter checks this equality on every file before writing it; if it would fail, the file is left unchanged, a requires change line is printed and the status is 1.
  2. Canonical layout. In fmt(t): a block that is k levels deep starts its lines with exactly 4k spaces; no line has trailing spaces; there are no blank lines before the first line, no two blank lines in a row, and the file ends with exactly one line end. A comment-only line takes the indentation of the next code line. A line that continues inside an open bracket keeps its position relative to the line that opened it.
  3. Idempotence. fmt(fmt(t)) = fmt(t). This is tested on every program in spec/examples/ and on the formatter's tests; it is not proved.

A text that requires change under the lexer (2.6, W-LEX-1, W-LEX-2) requires change under fmt with the same reason. A file that requires change under rce check can still be formatted.

Altered rules. Before the layout, fmt writes the rewrite of every report whose rule's method is altered (7.1): W-UNUSED-1 and W-DROP-1. The rewrites are those of the table of 7.1. A new name is the first of n, n1, n2, … that is not already a name in the text. Each rewrite is written only when the static reports of the new text are those of the old text less the one it answers; otherwise the report is printed as requires change FILE: line N: RULE message [not altered: …] and the status is 1. No line is added or removed, except that a match arm written on one line, P -> e, whose e is a W-DROP-1 report becomes the block arm P with the one statement let _ = e, since let is not an expression. A second run writes nothing (tests/three_methods.rs). Item 1 holds for the layout step; the altered step changes exactly the places its rewrites name.

With check, no file is written; each rewrite is printed as would alter FILE: line N: RULE what, each file whose layout would change as would reformat FILE, and the status is 1. Without it, each rewrite is printed as altered FILE: line N: RULE what, and each changed file is written and printed as formatted FILE.

rce fmt nameless FILE prints the name-free projection of one file to standard output and writes nothing. Every identifier the module declares is replaced by a positional name in order of first declaration, by kind: regions r0, r1, …, events e0, …, errors x0, …, functions f0, …, types t0, …, kind variants k0, …, fields, parameters and locals v0, …. Keywords, built-in types, standard library names, string contents and intent text are unchanged; the wildcard _ and a _ prefix are kept, as are main, the built-in traits and their methods, the host events and the named constants of 6.7. A use is renamed by its position as well as its name. After ., a call is renamed only when it names a method of the module's own impl blocks, since a call after . reaches a function of the module in no other way (5.15): a standard library method, or a function of another module, keeps its name even when the module declares a function, field or local of that name. After ., a name that is not called is renamed only as a field of the module's own types. A label NAME: in parentheses is renamed only when the callee is the module's own function, type, variant, event or error. A field name that a type of a standard library module the program uses (directly or through that module's own use lines) also declares keeps its text wherever it names a field, since a receiver's type is not known to the projection; it is still renamed where it names a local. Function calls by name are renamed at their call sites. The projection is deterministic and idempotent, and it has the same outcomes, outputs, ids and log hashes as the source: rce trace of the two is equal step for step except in the readable event field, since 6.1 hashes the positional forms (T7). A name the projection does not recognise as declared is left as written, so the output is accepted whenever the input is for every example (tests/nameless.rs), and for every one of the 1,876 files of the repository that rce check admits on their own. The expressions inside a template's {…} (F.6.1) are projected like code, and the authority structs DirRead and DirWrite keep their names and their field root, which the checker reads by name (F.5.1). It is the text of the concept record's complement (6.6).

sections.title: 10.7 The language server: `rce lsp`
sections.html:
rce lsp speaks the Language Server Protocol 3.17 over standard input and output (JSON-RPC 2.0 messages framed by Content-Length headers). It keeps the full text of each open document; it does not read other files.

MessageBehaviour
initializereplies with capabilities: full-text sync (textDocumentSync = 1), formatting, hover, definition, document symbols, and completion triggered by .
textDocument/didOpen, didChangestores the text and publishes diagnostics for that document
textDocument/didCloseforgets the text and publishes an empty diagnostic list
textDocument/formattingreturns one edit replacing the whole text with fmt(t), the canonical layout of 10.6 without the altered rewrites, or no edit if t is canonical or requires change
textDocument/hoverthe type or declaration of the name at the position, or null
textDocument/definitionthe location of that name's binding or item, or null
textDocument/completionthe names that can be written at the position
textDocument/documentSymbolthe document's items, each with its fields, variants or methods
shutdownreplies null
exitends the server: status 0 after shutdown, 1 without it
any other requesterror -32601, method not found

Diagnostics. For a document with text t, the published diagnostics are exactly the reports rce check gives for t that the text requires change, one per report, with severity Error and source rce. A report line N: ... covers line N − 1 in the protocol's 0-based numbering, from column 0 to the start of the next line. use resolves among the module paths of all open documents.

Names. Hover, definition, completion and symbols all read one index of the document. The index is built from the parsed module and from the bindings the type checker declares while it checks the module: each local binding, with its line and its inferred type. A document that does not parse has an empty index, so these requests answer null or an empty list.

  • Hover on a local binding shows name: T, with the type T the checker inferred. On an item it shows the item's declaration: the line of a function, constant, event or alias, or the whole block of a kind, struct, state or trait. On a variant, field or method it shows that line.
  • Definition gives the line of the binding or item, and the column where the name appears on it.
  • Completion after . offers user methods, fields and the builtin methods of the reference evaluator. Elsewhere it offers the local bindings of the enclosing item, the module's items, variants and fields, and the keywords. Each list is filtered by the part of the name already typed.
  • Document symbols list the items in order, with fields of structs and states, variants of kinds and methods of impls as children.

Limits: the AST has no columns, so a name is found by scanning its line, and columns are counted in Unicode scalar values rather than the UTF-16 units of the protocol; the two counts differ only on a line with a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. A local is visible from its line to the end of its enclosing item: block scope is not tracked, so a binding of a closed block is still offered. Names are resolved within one document, not across use.

Because diagnostics come from the same checker, an editor shows a program as clean exactly when rce check accepts it (10.1, principle 3).

sections.title: 10.8 What is not yet implemented
sections.html:
• The program emitters do not run concurrency or actors in their observations, only under run, and never run extern functions (10.5).
  • The language server resolves names within one document, without block scope, and counts columns in Unicode scalar values (10.7). It has no rename, references or semantic tokens.
  • rce run uses the reference interpreter; there is no compiled runtime.
  • Idempotence of fmt is tested, not proved.
  • Version 0.9 (Appendix F) is implemented in part (F.12). rce hash, rce api-diff OLD NEW (F.4.3) and rce v09-status exist: rce hash FILE|DIR... prints the definition hash, kind and name of every named item (pub marks an export) and, last, the program hash (program: the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON list, sorted, of the definition hashes of the name-free projection (10.6) of the program, with every unnamed item (steps, impls, examples, checks) hashed by its masked text, under the domain rce-program/1; name-free, layout-free and order-free, so a program and its renaming have one hash and a changed step body changes it), rce api-diff OLD NEW prints one row per change of the exports (compatible or breaking, then kind and name, then the change; status 1 when any row is breaking) and rce v09-status prints the implemented and the unimplemented rules. rce manifest DIR writes the manifest of a directory (F.5.3: every .rce file as a module pinned by the hash of its canonical text, canonical JSON; a directory whose modules import the built-in library gets the one dependency stdlib, pinned by the hash of the library's manifest) and rce manifest-check verifies one. The standard library is pinned this way (stdlib/lib/MANIFEST.json), and the checker carries that manifest with the library. rce lib prints the library's hash after the modules, then each module whose text differs from its pin (status 1); while such a difference exists, rce manifest writes no stdlib pin and rce manifest-check accepts none. The broker contract (F.7), the provenance record and the build cache of F.5.3, and the emitter messages of F.5.4 for a construct not yet printed do not exist yet. Results are reproducible from the inputs alone (10.1).

sections.title: 10.9 `rce trace FILE [EVENTS]`: reference traces (informative)
sections.html:
The trace format lets an independent projector (another compiler or runtime of the same Form) show that it agrees with the reference evaluator step by step. It adds no meaning: every field is a field of the log D of 6.1, so a trace is the log, and conformance to 6.1 implies conformance to the trace.

rce trace FILE prints one trace per example of the module, in source order (the same logs rce emit form puts in logs), then, when the module declares fn main(), the trace of its run (below); rce trace streams FILE PATH prints one trace per event list of PATH (one list per line, in the syntax of an example line; a line starting with # is skipped), named stream@k, in one run of the checker, with streams carrying their number; with EVENTS (the syntax of an example line, as in 10.3) it prints one trace of that event list. A module that requires change, or a trace of EVENTS that yields no step, is status 1. The output is one JSON object (format rce-trace/2; rce-trace/1 differed in hashing the named forms, before the T7 resolution of C.15), compact, with sorted keys:

FieldMeaning
format"rce-trace/2"
filethe file name, without directories
eventsthe EVENTS argument, or null
genesisthe first prev_hash: 64 zeros (6.1)
traceslist of {source, steps}; source is "example@L" (the example's line), "events" or "main"; a "main" trace also has outcome (below)
steps[i].seqrequired: 0-based index in the trace
steps[i].eventrequired: {type, payload}, payload values as in 6.1
steps[i].state_hashrequired: SHA-256 (lower-case hex) of the canonical JSON of the positional form of the state after the step (6.1)
steps[i].prev_hash, steps[i].hashthe 6.1 chain: hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash} with the positional form of the event
steps[i].outcome"applied" or {kept: error name}; derived, not hashed
steps[i].hashed{event, state}: the positional forms the two hashes are over (6.1), so a reader recomputes both without the module; derived

A kept step is a step of its trace, with outcome {kept: error name} and the unchanged state's hash (T8), and the next event is applied to that unchanged state, as on the host (HC-21); a trace ends only with its event list. A projector conforms on a module when, for every trace, its steps have the same seq, event and state_hash as the reference, in order and with none missing or extra; when it also emits prev_hash, hash or outcome they must be equal too. Since state_hash covers the whole state, equal hashes mean equal states without exchanging them.

The trace of fn main. Its run is the one rce run FILE performs without EVENTS (10.3): fn main() on the tick runtime of 6.8 and Appendix C, with no link, event or restart input and the default seed of select nondet. The scheduler writes a log of the run (C.11.4), one entry per action, and a step of the trace is one entry, in the order written. Within a tick the order is the scheduler's: link inputs, then program events, then the actors (transactions, then one message per actor in id order), then each task's pending operation in task order (higher priority first, then id). Every choice in that order is a function of ids, payloads and per-select counters (6.8), so the trace is a function of the program, as the run is (T1), however the tasks are placed on threads or held as state machines (10.3). The text of an entry is K or K(A), A showing values as emit lines do (10.3):

EntryWritten when
Spawn(task ID, priority P)a spawn is admitted, before the new task first moves
Done(task ID)a task's function returns, traps, fails or is cancelled
Emit(V)a task emits V, or a committed handler emitted V
Send(V)a send of V is admitted: to a channel, to an actor, by a select arm, inside atomic, or by a committed handler
Backpressurethe channel of a send is full: the sender is held (6.8)
Recv(V), Recv(none)a receive or a select arm takes V, or finds the channel closed and empty
Closea channel is closed
Atomicthe sends of an atomic block are admitted together (C.11.10)
Choice(task ID, select line L, execution K, arm A)a select nondet takes arm A (C.5)
Cancelled(task ID)a deadline of the task has passed at its communication step (C.6.2)
Deliver(V)an actor's handler takes the message V
Kept(R)an actor's handler kept its state for reason R, or another handler of the same transaction was not committed (T30)
Restart(CHILD, ID, R, tick T, K), Stopped(supervisor S)a supervisor restarts a child or stops (C.11.11)
Input(V), Unhandled(V)a program event arrives, and no actor handles it (HC-6)
Partition(A, B), Heal(A, B), Held(A -> B)a link input, and a message held at a partitioned link (C.11.4)

The last two rows need inputs of the run, so they occur only in a trace of a run given those inputs (spec/checker/tests/emit_run.rs gives them). A step's event is {type: K, payload: A}, with payload null for an entry K; its state is [tick, actors]: the tick at which the entry was written (the first tick is 1) and, for every live actor in id order, [ID, [v₁, …]], its field values in declaration order in the positional form of 6.1. hashed holds the two, state_hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the state, and prev_hash and hash chain from the genesis as an example's entries do. outcome is {kept: R} for a step Kept(R) and "applied" for every other step; as in an example's trace, a kept step does not end it: the trace ends where the run ends. The trace's outcome is "done", "deadlock" or {stopped: REASON}, as rce run ends. An entry's event is display text, which names declared types (Ping(n: 7, reply: <chan>)), so renaming a declaration changes the hashes of a main trace, where an example's (T7) stay the same. With trace, an emitted program run with run prints the trace of fn main as lines of D (10.5). The core evaluator (10.12) does not run fn main on the tick runtime, so it prints no trace of fn main.

On a host that cannot start a task thread (10.3, WASI preview 1) the tasks are state machines of the scheduler and the trace of fn main is the same as on any host; the cross-architecture parity job (.github/workflows/xarch-parity.yml) compares the five examples with fn main() on wasm32-wasip1 as on the other targets. Only a run in which an lvar passes from one task to another needs task threads (10.3): on such a host its trace of fn main is absent, {"source": "main", "outcome": {"absent": REASON}, "steps": []}, REASON being the line of 10.3 after FILE: . The other traces are printed as on any host, standard error has one line FILE: no trace of fn main: REASON, and the status is 4. A projector conforms on such a module only on a host that runs it.

spec/traces/ holds the reference traces of the example corpus: one file per top-level example (the package 26_use_module/ has no state machine), plus two event-list traces, 01_counter.events.json (the counter on a longer list) and 16_multi_region.events.json (two regions stepped by one event, which has no example lines). Five examples declare fn main(): 02, 13 and 37 run to done, and 40 and 48 stop at their first foreign call, which the reference evaluator does not execute (10.3). Examples without a state machine or fn main() have an empty traces list. spec/traces/rce-trace-diff.py REFERENCE OTHER (Python 3, standard library only) compares two trace files or two directories of them and prints exact match or the first divergence (trace, seq, field, both values); exit 0 on full match. spec/checker/tests/traces.rs checks that the fixtures are current, that every step is on the 6.1 chain, and that the runner finds a planted divergence.

sections.title: 10.10 `rce index [vectors N] FILE|DIR...` and `rce search CATALOG QUERY`: the brick catalog (informative)
sections.html:
rce index checks the files as one program (10.2) and prints one JSON object (format rce-catalog/1, compact, sorted keys) with one entry per top-level function of each module (the pub ones when the module marks any pub, else all; methods are not bricks), sorted by module and name. A use item names a module given with the files or one of the built-in library (4.1), and a file is listed as requiring change in the catalog exactly when rce check reports that it requires change. An entry holds module, name, file, line, generics, params (name and type), ret, key (the type with generic parameters renamed t0, t1, ... in order of first occurrence), hash (SHA-256 of the module path and the canonical text of the function alone, so layout and position do not change it), checked (the verdict of its file) and lowering ({"term": T}, the D.7 lowering, or {"kept": reason}). The catalog's hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of its entries; pending_files maps each file that requires change to its diagnostics. With vectors N, vectors maps a lowered brick's hash to up to N {"args", "out"} or {"args", "trap"} records of the reference evaluator on inputs generated from the parameter types by a fixed rule (an input that needs more than 200000 interpreter steps gives none, as the store-passing terms do more work than the interpreter); they are outside the catalog hash. rce-brick-verify CATALOG (src/form/brick.rs) evaluates each lowered term on its vectors and reports, per brick, agreement or the first disagreement: a result must be equal, a trap must be an error.

rce search reads a catalog and a query A -> R or (A, B) -> R, where one-letter lowercase names are type variables, and prints RANK module.name : key per match, best first. A brick matches when its arguments and result unify with the query's, in some order of the arguments. RANK is 0 for a type equal up to renaming of variables, 1 for an instance, plus 2 when the arguments match only in another order. Ties break by module and name. Both commands are deterministic: equal inputs give equal output bytes.

sections.title: 10.11 `rce dim [fuel N] [control] [json] FILE`: behaviours and redundancy (informative)
sections.html:
rce dim checks the file (10.2) and measures the quantities of 6.10 on its Form, with its use imports linked. It explores reach(P) breadth-first from s₀: at each state it applies every instance of the explored alphabet, defined here. Each payload field has a column of candidate values: first the boundary set of 6.3 for the field's base type (the type's minimum, −1, 0, 1 and maximum for a signed integer; 0, 1 and the maximum for an unsigned one; −1.0, 0.0 and 1.0 for a float; (); false and true; the texts "" and "a"; for T?, none and some of each value of T; for List[T], the empty list and the list of the second value of T's set), then the field's harvested values. A field of another type has no boundary set, and its event is not explored (the report lists it).

Literal harvesting finds the literals a program compares a field with. A field's value is followed from the step pattern (or actor handler) that binds it, through let and var bindings whose value is the name itself, copy(x), &x, x as T, or if c then x else y with x or y followed, into the arms of a match on it (or on a tuple position that holds it), and into a parameter of a function of the module it is passed to, each (function, parameter, field) once. A literal (an integer, float or text literal, a negated one, or a constant whose value is one) is harvested when it meets a followed value in ==, !=, <, <=, > or >=, as a literal or range-end pattern of a step pattern or a match arm, or in the predicate of the field's refined type (5.1) with self the field. A value computed by a method call or an operator (t.split("/"), x + 1) is not followed. The harvested values of an integer field are each harvested integer and its two neighbours within the type's range; of a float field, each harvested float and it ± 1.0; of a text field, each harvested text, and, when both "" and "a" are harvested, the first of "aa", "aaa", … that is not, so some value of the column equals none of the literals. Values already in the column are not repeated; at most 64 are added per field, the smallest in value order, plus that one text. A field of another type harvests nothing. The instances of an event are the Cartesian product of its columns in field order, the first field varying slowest, cut at 4,096 instances per event; an instance that a refined type refuses at construction (T35) is not explored and is listed.

Exploration stops at fuel states (default 100,000) and reports whether the bound was reached. On the explored graph it runs partition refinement (Hopcroft) with the per-step output of λ as the initial partition, giving the number of distinct behaviours among explored states, which is dim(P) exactly when the bound was not reached and a lower bound otherwise. It prints, per program and per region:

states explored     12480    bound reached: no
behaviours          1206     dim(P) (exact)
redundancy          3.37     bits: log2(states) - log2(behaviours)
  region Counter    0.00
  region Audit      3.37
control states      17       dim_c(P)          [control]
shape_ctl           sha256:…                   [control]

A region's redundancy is computed from the projection of the explored graph onto that region's fields. control computes the control quotient of 6.10 on the same explored graph: each step is labelled by its control outcome only (the kept step's error, by declaration index; else the constructors of what was emitted, by declaration index or type class) and never by a value, a name or a state change, so the quotient is a coarser output function on the same deterministic machine and dim_c ≤ dim holds by construction. Predicate equivalence is decided by concrete evaluation on reach(P): exact on the explored set, a lower bound when the bound is reached. The canonical control string numbers the quotient's states by first visit in breadth-first order from s₀ with events in canonical order, one line per (state, event) with the successor's number and the label; shape_ctl is the SHA-256 of its canonical JSON text. It is invariant under renaming (T61, tested by tests/dim.rs against rce fmt nameless). The report also says whether some explored step has a λ output (6.1): an emitted value, or the record of a kept step (has_output in the JSON, with emits and keeps reported separately, since a kept step and an emitted value are two kinds of the program's answer: a kept step leaves the state as it was and records why, an emitted value is an output), and how many distinct output sequences the explored steps carry (distinct_outputs; a silent step is excluded). A program with no such step has one behaviour by definition, so its redundancy is its whole state: the state is in D and readable, and an example may check it, but no future output depends on it. A program whose every output is the same has one behaviour as well. The dimension benchmark reports these strata separately. json prints the same as one JSON object (format rce-dim/1, compact, sorted keys; has_output, emits, keeps and distinct_outputs since 2026-10-24, replacing observable and distinct_labels). The command is deterministic: equal inputs give equal output bytes, and the exploration order is the canonical order of 6.1 on events and payloads. It is informative: no admission depends on it.

rce equiv [fuel N] [json] A B asks whether two programs have the same behaviour (6.10): it links both and explores both from their initial states over the same event instances (the explored alphabet above, with the harvested literals of A and B joined per event, by declaration index, and per field, by position, so x < 5 and x <= 4 are compared on the same values), compares every step by its name-free output (emitted values in their positional form, a kept step by its error's declaration index, T7), refines the two graphs together by those outputs and reads whether the two initial states fall in one class (T58: equivalence is bisimilarity). Status 0 and equivalent when they do; status 1 and different with the shortest distinguishing event sequence and the two outputs at its end, or the event instances one program explores and the other does not. When an exploration reached its bound and the refinement separates the initial states but no distinguishing sequence exists within the explored graph, the separation may come from the unexplored frontier, so the verdict is undecided with status 3, never different. The verdict is over the explored alphabet and, when a bound is reached, to that bound; T59 bounds what agreement to a depth proves. Two programs that differ only on a payload value outside that alphabet (a target that only t.split("/") distinguishes, for example) are called equivalent. A program and its name-free projection (10.6) are equivalent by T7. JSON format rce-equiv/1.

rce change [fuel N] OLD NEW classifies a change to a program by the classes of C.15 and proposal CC-2, comparing the two programs under one text: it prints both program hashes (equal hashes mean a renaming or a reformatting, the same program), the rce api-diff rows (F.4.3) and the behaviour check of rce equiv, and decides: erratum when every export is compatible and every behaviour is kept (status 0; "to the explored bound" when a bound was reached); meaning change when a behaviour changed (status 1: the program's meaning changed); interface change when behaviour is kept but an export is broken (status 1: callers must change); undecided when rce equiv is undecided (status 3: raise fuel); compatible or breaking from the rows alone when neither program is a Form. The decision is the tool's, not a version number's. Laws (6.11) are part of a program's meaning. rce change prints one law row per law of OLD, decided on NEW with NEW's definitions (= the law is unchanged in NEW, ~ edited, - removed), and one + row per law NEW adds. Meaning change (status 1) is then also the verdict when NEW breaks a law of OLD (CC-L1 of spec/proposals/laws.md; the row is followed by the counterexample line) and when a law of OLD is edited or removed (CC-L2), whatever the behaviour check says. A law added to a program whose behaviour is unchanged is an erratum. On the flag game of 6.11, the change that removes the far-edge walls has the same behaviour (no step emits a value or keeps the state), so without its law it was an erratum; with the law it is a meaning change, with the 9-event sequence.

rce law FILE checks FILE as rce check does up to the admission gate, then decides every law of FILE by method D1 (6.11) and prints one line per law: its name, its verdict (holds, fails, undecided or attested), the method and the counts (states, steps, alphabet size and whether it is complete, whether the exploration closed), and for a failing law the counterexample line. An undecided law's line names what left it undecided and the cover an attestation must carry. Exit status 0 when every law holds or is attested, 3 when the only obstacle is the bound LAW_FUEL, 1 otherwise. scripts/t7-equiv.sh runs rce equiv between every corpus program and its name-free projection (T7) and is a continuous-integration step.

sections.title: 10.12 `rce run-core FILE`: the core evaluator (informative)
sections.html:
rce run-core FILE lowers FILE to its core module, as rce emit core does (FILE is an RCE module or an rce-core/1 core module, read only if it is well formed), runs that module with the core evaluator of the proposal one-emitter.md (ONE-1), and prints what the run writes. The core evaluator is an implementation under test, compared with the reference evaluator like any target: the expected bytes of every comparison are the reference trace (10.9), never this output. Exit status 0 when the run ends; 1 when the checker reports that FILE requires change, when a core module is not well formed, or when the run halts; 2 when FILE uses a construct the lowering does not cover, or on an internal error.

The core evaluator observes fn main as one call of its body, as the main block of the proposal's trace (ONE-5) does, not as a run on the tick runtime: the lowering covers no channel, spawn, select, actor or supervisor (status 2), and the core has no scheduler, so rce run-core prints no trace of fn main (10.9). The reference's tick runtime now holds tasks as state machines where the host has no threads (10.3), so the run of fn main happens on WASI preview 1 as on other hosts; that scheduler is written in Rust inside the reference (conc.rs), not in the core. The next slice of the proposal is the same scheduler in the core: the lowering of channels, send, spawn, select, actors, protocols, nodes and supervisors, and the tick, its phases and the log written as core functions, so that rce run-core prints the trace of fn main.

sections.title: 10.13 `rce repair [json] [bound N] FILE [MODULE...]`: the exact-proposer ladder (informative)
sections.html:
rce repair takes a program FILE that requires change (an example or check does not hold, or a static rule reports it) and proposes a changed program. FILE is checked together with the MODULEs, which are the program's other modules (10.2). The command is a ladder of exact proposers: each rung builds candidate programs by a fixed rule from the program, the MODULEs and the built-in library alone, and the checker, the same gate as rce check (6.9), judges each candidate. The ladder stops at the first candidate the checker admits; since the gate runs every example and check, an admitted candidate is one whose examples and checks all hold. No rung calls a model (10.1, item 2). A candidate is the canonical text of an edited module (the source printer of unparse.rs), never a text written by hand, and a candidate equal to one already judged is judged once.

Terms. A definition is a function, a method of an impl, a step, an actor, a constant or a state declaration. A site is one expression of a definition. Intent, example, check and law items, and check, requires and ensures statements, are never edited: they are what a candidate is judged by. The name-free signature of a function is its number of generic parameters, its parameter types and its result type, without the names of the function and its parameters.

Order of definitions. First the definitions that contain a line the report of FILE names (a static rule); then, breadth first, the definitions reachable from the checks that do not hold (the functions they call, and what those call) and, when an example does not hold, the steps, actors and state declarations and what they call; then every other definition, in source order. Sites within a definition are visited in preorder.

The rungs, in order:

  • a. Reuse. The body of one function becomes the body of another function with the same name-free signature, from FILE, the MODULEs or the built-in library (rce lib), with its parameters renamed to the receiving function's. A donor with the same name as the receiving function comes first, then donors by module and name; donors with equal name-free projections (10.6) are tried once, and a donor equal to the receiving function is not tried.
  • b. Lookup by type. The brick catalog (10.10) of FILE, the MODULEs and the library modules FILE uses is searched (rce search order) for (1) a function of the same type as a definition, whose body then becomes return h(p1, ..., pn) on its own parameters, and (2) a function of the same type as the callee of a call, which then replaces that callee. Only functions FILE can name are proposed: its own, and those of a module it uses, through the module's alias.
  • c. Altered rules. The text rce fmt writes (10.6) for the rules whose method is altered in 7.1 (W-UNUSED-1 and W-DROP-1, alter.rs): every rewrite of FILE, in the order rce fmt writes them, and only when the canonical layout accepts the result, as in rce fmt. The candidate is the canonical text of that program, one per run; there is none when rce fmt would alter nothing. A rewrite only names a binding or drops a value that was already dropped, so the candidate has the behaviour of FILE; it is admitted when the reports it answers were the only reason FILE requires change. The edit lists each rewrite as rce fmt reports it (line L: RULE what).
  • d. Bounded enumeration. One small edit at one site: a binary operator replaced by each other operator of its class (+ - * / %, < <= > >=, == !=, and or, & | ^, << >>), the operands of an ordering comparison swapped, an integer literal n replaced by n + 1, n - 1, 0 and 1 (each value at least 0 and different from n), a boolean literal negated, two arguments of a call with two to four arguments swapped (each pair once), and a condition (of if, elif, while, a guard or an if expression) negated, or its not removed. These edits never add or rename a name, so they act alike on a program and on its name-free projection. At most N candidates (bound N, default 2000) are judged in this rung; the bound counts checker calls, not edits skipped as duplicates.

Rungs a, b and c are not bounded by bound: a and b judge at most one candidate per donor or catalog hit, and c at most one candidate.

Output: the rung that closed the program (a reuse, b lookup by type, c altered rules, d bounded enumeration, or none when FILE already complies with the Form), the edit (it names the line of FILE), the diff of the canonical texts (- the old lines and + the new, with line numbers of the canonical text), the number of candidates each rung judged with 0 model calls, the skipped rungs (every rung, when FILE does not parse), and the checker's verdict on the result: ok FILE: admitted; E examples and C checks hold, or, when no candidate is admitted, the report on FILE and not closed FILE. With json the same is one JSON object (format rce-repair/1) that also holds the repaired text, model_calls (always 0), canonical_same_report (whether the canonical text of FILE gets the report FILE gets, line numbers aside) and attempts, one record per candidate judged: rung, definition, edit and the checker's verdict. Exit status 0 when the program is closed or already complies, 1 when it is not closed, 2 on a usage error. The command is deterministic: equal inputs give equal output bytes and the same exit status.

An admitted candidate passes the examples and checks; that does not make it the program that was meant. rce equiv (10.11) and the program hash of rce hash (10.8) say whether a repair has the behaviour or the definitions of a known original; scripts/ladder-run.py reports that split for the task sets that scripts/ladder-tasks.py writes.

chapters.title: Appendix C. Concurrency (draft 0.6 and 0.6b; normative)
chapters.question: How many concurrency words does C.1 add to the keywords of 2.4? (a number)

sections.html: This appendix defines the concurrency part of the language: structured parallelism (par, for ... par), budgets, deadlines, nondeterministic select and priorities (drafts 0.6), and the 0.6b extensions: workgroups, session types, structured spawn, cross-actor transactions, supervisors, nodes, interrupts, LVars and replicated state. It applies to every module; no declaration selects it (2.7). The text is written from what the reference checker (spec/checker, check.rs, check06b.rs, conc.rs, link.rs) and the Lean files (spec/lean/RCE/Par*.lean, Models06b.lean, Session*.lean, TickClock.lean, VClock.lean) actually enforce and prove; where the two differ from an intended design, the checker is what is described. Example: par with two branches that write different variables gives the same result as running the branches in source order.

sections.title: C.1 Keywords
sections.html:
The 23 words below are on the reserved list of 2.4, in addition to the keywords of 2.4, except directly after . (so c.offer() and c.choose(L) remain method calls):

par       branch    nondet    budget    deadline  priority
replicated interrupt session  lvar      group     lanes
barrier   scope     atomic    protocol  offer     choose
node      supervisor strategy child     restart

They are not names in any module: fn f(node: i64) requires change. The reference checker keeps them in parse::DRAFT06_KEYWORDS, separate from parse::KEYWORDS only as a source layout; the reserved list is their union with the words of Appendix F, one list for every module.

sections.title: C.2 Grammar
sections.html:
These productions extend section 3. They are the productions of the tree-sitter port (tree-sitter/grammar.js) and of the Rust parser. A rule below with the name of a section-3 rule replaces it; the others are new. The grammar is the productions of section 3 with these applied, and the same for every module. The machine check of 3.12 builds the LALR(1) tables of section 3 with these rules applied (lalr::book_grammar_06), lexing with the keywords of C.1 reserved, and fails on any conflict; it runs that machine over the concurrency corpora (spec/conc06, spec/conc06b). So T10 (one parse per program) holds for the whole language.
