Item         = UseDecl | IntentDecl | ExampleDecl | CheckDecl | LawDecl
             | [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl | TypeDecl | StructDecl | KindDecl
                         | TraitDecl | FnDecl | ActorDecl | ProtocolDecl )
             | StateDecl | EventDecl | ErrorDecl | StepDecl | ImplDecl
             | ExternDecl | NodeDecl | SupervisorDecl .
StateDecl    = [ "replicated" ] "state" NAME NEWLINE INDENT Field { Field } DEDENT .
EventDecl    = [ "interrupt" ] "event" NAME [ Payload ] [ "priority" Expr ] NEWLINE .
StepDecl     = "step" NAME "on" Pattern [ "if" Expr ] [ "deadline" Expr ] StepBody .
ProtocolDecl = "protocol" NAME NEWLINE INDENT ProtoStep { ProtoStep } DEDENT .
ProtoStep    = "send" Type NEWLINE | "recv" Type NEWLINE
             | "offer" NEWLINE INDENT ProtoArm { ProtoArm } DEDENT
             | "choose" NEWLINE INDENT ProtoArm { ProtoArm } DEDENT
             | "loop" NEWLINE INDENT ProtoStep { ProtoStep } DEDENT
             | "break" NEWLINE .
ProtoArm     = NAME NEWLINE [ INDENT ProtoStep { ProtoStep } DEDENT ] .
NodeDecl     = "node" NAME "{" NAME { "," NAME } "}" NEWLINE .
SupervisorDecl = "supervisor" NAME "strategy" NAME NEWLINE INDENT SupChild { SupChild } DEDENT .
SupChild     = "child" NAME ":" TypePath [ "restart" Bound ] NEWLINE .
BaseType     = TypePath | "(" ")" | "(" Type "," [ Type { "," Type } [ "," ] ] ")"
             | "(" Type ")" | "[" Type "]" | "[" Type ";" Expr "]"
             | "chan" BaseType | "iter" BaseType
             | "fn" "(" [ TypeList ] ")" "->" BaseType
             | "session" TypePath | "lvar" BaseType .
Stmt         = SimpleStmt | LetStmt | VarStmt | IfStmt | WhileStmt | LoopStmt
             | ForStmt | MatchStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt
             | EmitStmt | FailStmt | SpawnStmt | SelectStmt | ArenaStmt
             | DeviceStmt | YieldStmt | ComptimeStmt | CheckDecl | PassStmt
             | ParStmt | BudgetStmt | DeadlineStmt | GroupStmt | BarrierStmt
             | ScopeStmt | AtomicStmt .
ForStmt      = "for" Pattern "in" Expr [ "par" ] Block .
SpawnStmt    = "spawn" Expr [ "priority" Expr ] [ "->" NAME ] NEWLINE .
SelectStmt   = "select" [ "nondet" ] NEWLINE INDENT SelectArm { SelectArm } DEDENT .
ParStmt      = "par" NEWLINE INDENT Branch { Branch } DEDENT .
Branch       = "branch" NAME Block .
BudgetStmt   = "with" "budget" Expr Block .
DeadlineStmt = "with" "deadline" Expr Block [ "else" Block ] .
GroupStmt    = "with" "group" NAME "lanes" Expr Block .
BarrierStmt  = "barrier" NEWLINE .
ScopeStmt    = "scope" Block .
AtomicStmt   = "atomic" Block .

sections.title: C.3 Footprints
sections.html: The footprint of a statement is the set of place paths (5.6) it reads and the set it writes. Two branches are disjoint when no path written by one is a prefix of, or has as prefix, a path read or written by the other.

sections.title: C.4 `par`
sections.html:
par runs its branches; each branch is a block. The result equals running the branches in source order (T16). Rules:

  • W-PAR-1: the footprints of two branches overlap (write/write or write/read), including through a &mut self method call.
  • W-PAR-2: a branch has an effect other than its own writes (emit, channel operations, spawn, foreign calls), or returns, breaks or continues out of the par.
  • Two branches with one name also require change (W-NAME-2).

Derivation of the rules (confluence). Determinism of a parallel composition is a confluence property: every way of interleaving the branches' steps must reach one result, which is then the result of any fixed order, source order among them. By the Church-Rosser method it is enough to show the diamond: one step of branch a and one step of branch b, taken from the same configuration in either order, reach the same configuration. A step changes only its write set and depends only on its free variables, so the two steps commute exactly when neither writes what the other reads or writes. That is W-PAR-1, derived, not chosen: it is the weakest footprint condition under which the diamond holds for every store. Termination of each branch (T19) and the diamond give confluence (Newman's lemma), so every complete interleaving gives the source-order store (T16). An effect that leaves the store (emit, channel operations, spawn, a foreign call) is observed in the order it happens, so it would make the observation depend on the interleaving even when the store does not; W-PAR-2 removes these. Traps follow the same law: a trap is observed at the first branch in source order that traps, because that is where the sequential run traps; the reference and the emitters place both arithmetic traps and resource traps (fuel, budget) at that branch (book/12-tooling.md 10.5). Mechanized in spec/lean: the diamond on a core with par (RCE.ParSem.diamond), determinism of complete runs (RCE.ParSem.par_det), refinement to a model of the reference evaluator including overflow traps (RCE.ParSem.refine), and the fuel account, whose sum-checked trap point equals the sequential one and whose evaluated work is at most k times the fuel left at the fork (RCE.ParFuel.sumcheck_eq_seq, RCE.ParFuel.overrun_bound). LVars weaken the diamond to quasi-determinism (C.11.8, T29q). Open: the core has no loops, calls or data structures, so the link from the core to the full evaluator rests on the generated vectors (ParVectors.lean) and the differential tests, not on a proof.

sections.title: C.5 Budgets, deadlines and nondeterminism
sections.html:
• with budget n runs the block with a cost budget n: every Form operation charges its cost (C.6.4) and the operation that takes the total past n is trap("budget"), at the same operation on every target. The cost table is the reference evaluator's (interp and conc.rs, charge), listed in C.6.4. W-TY-1 if n is not an integer. with budget n Block else [as e] Else makes exhaustion a value. Derivation. Totality (T2) asks every step to end in a value; a trap that keeps the state is an outcome of the step, not a value the program can act on. To act on it the program needs a point where the trap is caught, and the state at that point must be one that some sequential execution reaches at a well-defined place, or Else observes a state no specification of Block describes. The only such states are the entry of Block and its completion; the trap rules out completion, so a caught trap restores the entry state. Block is therefore atomic: all of its writes or none (the same law as T30 for atomic). Normative rules:
    • A trap("budget") raised while Block runs, by this budget or any enclosing one, is caught by the innermost enclosing budget that has an else. Every write Block made (locals, struct fields, state fields, self) is undone, then Else runs.
    • as e binds e: Exhausted, the builtin struct Exhausted { limit: u64, used: u64 }, where limit is n and used is the units this frame had spent before the operation that would have passed a limit.
    • Charges stay. Cost counts operations performed (C.6.1), so the units spent in Block remain on every enclosing budget. When the trap came from an outer budget, Else charges that budget, its next charge traps again, and the trap reaches the next budget out with an else, or keeps the state.
    • W-BUD-1: Block of a budget with an else holds an effect that a trap cannot undo (emit, channel operations, spawn, select, yield, lvar put or freeze), or returns, breaks or continues out of it.
    • A budget without else behaves as before: the trap keeps the state.
    • The charge rule: a charge is all or nothing, leaves no frame past its limit, and is additive. Every runtime's charge implements the same rule; in this repository the link between those copies is the differential tests, not a proof. The trap falls on the same operation on every target, so whether Else runs, and the value of e, are functions of the program and its inputs, and replay re-derives them. The emitters save every local the block writes at entry (struct fields and state fields are locals of the emitted step) and restore them on the trap. Checked by spec/checker/tests/conc06_run.rs (budget_else_catches, budget_else_with_undoable_effects_requires_change), emit_run.rs (budget_else_*, reference against the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes) and emit06b.rs (budget_else_is_atomic_on_every_target, the limit swept across the block's cost on all four targets).
  • with deadline n runs the block with an expiry n logical ticks after entry; if the block has not completed by then, the else block runs instead (T22). W-DL-1: outside fn main or a task function.
  • select nondet may take any ready arm; the choice is an input and is logged, so replay reproduces it (T21). W-ND-1: outside fn main or a task function. select without nondet keeps the rotation rule of 6.8.
  • spawn f(...) priority p and event E priority p: admission prefers the highest pending priority (T25). W-TY-1 if p is not an integer.

sections.title: C.6 Cost semantics
sections.html:
C.6.1 A cost is a non-negative integer number of units. Cost is a deterministic accounting of Form operations, the same on every target; it is not a measurement of time or energy (est_j is separate).

C.6.2 Charging point. An operation charges its cost after its operands are evaluated and before it acts. If the charge would take any enclosing budget past its limit, the operation is trap("budget") and does not act; otherwise every enclosing budget is charged. So nested budgets see the same operation trap, and a budget n admits exactly the operations whose running total stays at most n.

C.6.3 par and for ... par charge c_fork per branch (or chunk), then each branch's own costs. The branches' costs are summed in source order, and exhaustion is placed where the sequential run would hit it (C.4, T16), so the trap does not depend on scheduling.

C.6.4 The cost table (normative). Operations not listed (literals of scalars, variable reads, assignment, control flow, let) cost 0. The table is checked against the reference evaluator, and the emitted Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes charge the same costs (spec/checker/tests/stdlib_costs.rs).

OperationCost
c_call: call of a user function or a closure4
standard library method (5.15) on receiver size n, first-argument size k4 + work(m, n, k), below
c_chan: channel send or receive8
c_spawn: spawn32
c_fork: one par branch or for ... par chunk16
list literal [a, b, ...], map literal, comprehension with n results4 + n
[x; n]4 + n
index a[i], slice a[i:j], member x.f, tuple member t.01
unary -, ~, not1
and, or1
binary operator on integer, bool or text operands, comparisons1
float (f64, f32) +, -, *2
float (f64, f32) /8

Method work (normative). A standard library method costs c_call plus work(m, n, k); draft 0.6 charged c_call alone, which is not the language of this text. A budget is a proxy for energy, and energy scales with the operations performed, so a method's cost must track its work. Sizes: text is its UTF-8 byte length, a list its length, a set its number of elements, a map its number of entries, any other value 0. n is the receiver's size and k the first argument's (0 when there is none). work(m, n, k) is fixed by the method's complexity class in the reference evaluator:

ClassMethodswork
linear, text receiverstrip, upper, lower, reverse, tostr, chars, words, lines, split, isdigit, isalpha, isspace, contains, startswith, endswith, toint, join, sha256n + k
linear, list receiverreverse, contains, sum, map, filter, fold, utf8n + k
linear, map receiver (maps are ordered association lists)get, contains, insert, remove, keys, values, mergen + k
linear, set receiver (a set is held as its elements in canonical order)union, inter, insert, contains, tolistn + k
n log n, list receiversortn · ⌈log₂ n⌉, with ⌈log₂ n⌉ = 0 for n ≤ 1
constantevery other method of 5.150

The calls a map, filter or fold makes to its function argument are charged as calls in addition (c_call each, plus their bodies). The arithmetic saturates at the largest i128, so it cannot overflow; no reachable size comes near it, so the Python and JavaScript runtimes, whose integers are unbounded, give the same numbers. work is monotone: it never decreases when n or k grows. The reference evaluator (conc::method_work) and the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes compute the same function, and the budget boundary falls on the same operation in all of them (spec/checker/tests/method_costs.rs, which also checks monotonicity).

sections.title: C.7 Device kernels
sections.html: Inside a device region (5.13), a module may use par and for ... par with the same rules; the device rules of W-DEV-1 still apply.

sections.title: C.8 `for ... par`
sections.html:
for x in e par runs the iterations as if in order. It is encoded in the reference checker as the marker region $forpar (the AST has no new variant). Rules:

  • W-PAR-3: the body writes a place other than as a reduction (+= *= &= |= ^= on a variable never read in the body) or as slot [i] of a range loop over i.
  • W-PAR-4: the body has an effect, or returns, breaks or continues.

A reduction is evaluated on a fixed tree, which equals the left fold for an associative operation with an identity (T18). The tree is normative, since a float operation is not associative and the bits depend on it: for m >= 2 contributions, the left subtree takes the first h, where h is the largest power of two below m, and the right subtree the rest; one contribution is itself; none is the identity. Derivation: placement must give the same bits on every fabric (HC-12), and the reductions that vector units and GPUs execute are complete binary trees over power-of-two blocks. With this split every left subtree is complete, so the tree decomposes into such blocks and a fabric can evaluate it natively. pscan uses the same split for its up-sweep and down-sweep. One definition, host::tree_split, serves the reference evaluator and the placement executor (place_par, place_sum), and every runtime computes the same h. Checked by spec/checker/tests/host_place.rs (forpar_reference_and_placement_share_the_tree: a non-associative float sum gives the same bits from run_main and from the placement executor for every length up to 40) and by the emitter parity tests. Before 2026-10-15 the reference and runtimes split at ceil(m/2) while the placement executor split at the power of two; the two disagreed in the last bits of float reductions from five contributions on. The Lean model defines the same split, RCE.Par.split m = 2 ^ log2 (m - 1) (checked against host::tree_split on sample lengths), and proves tree_eq_foldl for the tree built with it, so T18 is proved for the tree the code runs. RCE.ParFuel reduces branch uses in that tree: tree_use_eq_sum (the tree total is the source-order sum) and tree_work_eq (the threaded work reduced in the tree is the work of overrun_bound, at most k·F).

sections.title: C.11 Draft 0.6b
sections.html:
• C.11.2 Workgroups. with group g lanes n runs n lanes in phases separated by barrier. W-GRP-1: a group not directly inside a device region. W-GRP-2: barrier other than as a statement at the top level of a group body. W-GRP-3: a lane reads another lane's slot in the same phase, or lanes share a scalar written in the phase.
  • C.11.3 Sessions. protocol P declares a session type; a value of type session P is an endpoint. W-SES-1: an operation not allowed by the protocol state, an unknown label, offer() not matched over its labels, a match that does not handle every label, or branches leaving the endpoint in different states. W-SES-2: an endpoint not at the end of its protocol when it goes out of scope or is closed. W-SES-3: a label that appears twice, a protocol loop with no message before it repeats, or break outside a protocol loop. W-TY-1: a payload of the wrong type. The two endpoints of chan[session P] have the types P and dual(P), where dual swaps send with receive and choose with offer (duality). W-SES-4 (linearity): an endpoint is a capability that exactly one name holds. A protocol operation consumes the endpoint at one state and yields it at the next. A bare use of the name (an argument, a spawn argument, a payload sent on another endpoint, a rebinding) moves the endpoint, and close consumes it; after either the name holds nothing, and a further use requires change (no use after move, send or close). Paths that join must agree on whether an endpoint was consumed, so a branch that moves it while another keeps it in use requires change, as does a loop body that moves an endpoint the loop does not create. With W-SES-2 this makes endpoints linear (affine plus must-close): on every path to the end of its scope each endpoint is at the end of its protocol, closed, or moved to a holder that takes the obligation over. let m = x moves the endpoint to m, which owes the rest of x's protocol; a name bound inside a block goes out of scope at the end of that block, so its endpoint must be finished or passed on there. The checker's protocol automaton (check06b, ProtoCursor) is linked to T28 by vectors (C.13). Linearity is a typing judgment (SessionLin.Ty): the checker's W-SES-1, W-SES-2 and W-SES-4 for bodies of send, receive, close, move and branch are proved sound against it, and a typed body never uses a gone endpoint, never closes an unfinished one and ends with every endpoint gone or done, on every path (T28l). W-SES-5 (session graph a tree): a spawn passes at most one session endpoint, and a body that holds both ends of one channel acts on neither until it has passed one on. The session graph has processes as nodes and channels as edges. A spawn with one endpoint adds one edge to a new node, and sending an endpoint to the holder of the other end of the carrying channel moves an edge along a path, so the graph stays a tree. On a tree, if every channel's two ends are compatible, either every process has finished or some channel has both ends waiting on it and they can step (T28d). Two channels between the same two processes break this: each can wait on a different channel. W-SES-5 by priorities: a program that requires change under the tree rule is accepted when its session graph has a priority order. Each exchange on a channel is an action (channel, step), shared by both ends, and a spawn is a one-step action between spawner and spawned. Each process's actions in program order must strictly increase in priority, and each channel's ends must make the same number of exchanges; the checker finds such priorities exactly when the order the processes impose on actions is acyclic. Then every reachable state is finished or can step, on any session graph, cycles included (T28p): the waiting action of least priority has its partner waiting on that same action. A cycle of waits, as in two channels between two processes used in opposite orders, is a cycle in the order and requires change. The checker reads priorities from programs whose endpoints are created, sent on, received on and passed to spawns at the top level of bodies, over protocols of messages; outside that fragment the tree rule decides. Multiparty global types (T28g): a global type says which role sends to which and in what order, with binary choices; its projection on each role uses plain merge (roles not told of a choice must have the same local type in both branches). Every configuration reachable from the projections of a global type is finished or steps, and a step lands on the projections of a global type again. A global type of messages only gives priorities by event order, so its projections pass the priority rule and compose with the other channels of a program. The checker's projection equals the Lean projection on 200 generated global types (C.13). Full merge and asynchrony (T28a): a role not told of a choice may receive differently in the two branches; its projection merges them into one branching that accepts the labels of both (sends must still agree). Sends never block: each ordered pair of roles has one FIFO queue, so two messages from one sender to one receiver arrive in sending order, and the global type records which labels are in flight. Each role's local type need only accept at least what the projection of the current global type accepts (association). Every asynchronous step of an associated configuration is a step of the global type and stays associated; every receiver accepts the label at the head of its queue; and every configuration reachable from the projections with empty queues is final (all roles done, all queues empty) or steps. The checker's full-merge projection equals the Lean projection on 300 generated global types, and its exploration of the asynchronous runs from each fully projecting one finds no stuck configuration and none whose receiver does not accept the label heading its queue (C.13). Convergence notes. Honda, Vasconcelos and Kubo (ESOP 1998) keep channels in a linear realm and pass them by delegation; their type soundness theorem gives subject reduction and the absence of run-time communication errors, and does not claim deadlock freedom. Gay and Hole (Acta Informatica 2005) give each end to exactly one process by environment addition, end a derivation only at a completed environment (as W-SES-2 does), prove their typechecking algorithm sound for the declarative rules (the shape of chkBody_sound), and for polarity inference forbid using one end of a channel while the same thread holds the other (as W-SES-5 does); they show a typable process over two channels between two processes that deadlocks. Wadler (Propositions as Sessions, ICFP 2012) composes processes by a cut on exactly one channel, which gives deadlock freedom; a cut on two channels admits loops that may deadlock, and he notes that a primitive that creates a channel and returns both ends in a pair may suffer from deadlock. RCE's chan[session P] is such a primitive; W-SES-5 keeps its uses to the one-channel shape at spawns. Kobayashi (CONCUR 2006) annotates each channel use with an obligation and a capability level and proves that a well-typed process is deadlock free (and with time tags, lock free); Padovani (CSL-LICS 2014) gives the linear pi-calculus one priority per channel type, requires each process to use its channels in increasing priority, and proves deadlock freedom, encoding multiparty sessions so that a global type's events give the priorities (his App. C). T28p is this rule on RCE's networks, with one priority per exchange. Honda, Yoshida and Carbone (POPL 2008) introduce global types, projection and the progress of a single well-formed session; T28g is the synchronous, plain-merge form of their result, and T28a keeps their order-preserving queues (their Sec. 2) with the full merge and association of Hou, Yoshida and Kuhn (arXiv:2402.16741, Def. 3.1 and 3.7). The reading ledger is spec/proposals/session-reading-ledger.md. Open: an endpoint and its dual sent separately to the same third process close a loop that W-SES-5 does not see; T28d assumes the tree and the preservation of the tree under delegation is argued above, not mechanized (the priority rule closes this loop when the program is in the fragment it reads); T28p and T28g model rendezvous, and T28a models buffered delivery for global types without recursion or payloads; the checker reads priorities only for straight-line bodies over message protocols, and priorities for global types with choice or recursion are not derived; SessionPrio.decideP is proved sound, not complete (the checker's acyclicity test is the complete decision, linked by vectors); there is no surface syntax for global types; T28l covers message steps and local branching, not choose/offer, loops or recursion (those are covered by the automaton vectors of T28).
  • C.11.5 Merge. impl Merge for T declares a join. Its laws (associative, commutative, idempotent) are an admission obligation (W-CRDT-1, conc::crdt_gate), discharged by a certificate and never by sampling. bottom() is the initial state; the states an LVar can reach are the up-set of it, which the join preserves, so the laws on that up-set are the laws of the type. For a kind of nullary variants the gate evaluates every triple, which decides them (MergeLaws.laws_of_enum). Otherwise the gate reads the body of merge as a term over proven combinators (conc::merge_certs): per field, max or min on an integer, or or and on a bool, union or inter on a Set[τ], merge on a Map[k, v] (pointwise, certified when the Merge of v is: an integer, a bool, a set, a map of such, or a type with a certified impl), or .merge of a field whose type has a certified impl (componentwise product); on a record of one integer field, a selection that keeps o when o.k > self.k and self otherwise (max, or min when the smaller side is kept); and lexicographic on an integer key: self when self.k > o.k, o when o.k > self.k, and otherwise the key with the other fields merged by the rules above. Each term is a Cert of MergeCert.lean, and Cert.semi turns every certificate into a proof of the three laws, so they compose by construction. The lexicographic rule needs its key to be a chain (a total order); without that it is not a join (MergeCert.lex_needs_chain), which is why the key must be an integer. Any other impl requires change, also a lawful one written differently (for example bitwise |), with a message naming the combinators; a search on a finite sample runs first and, when it finds a counterexample, the report names it. The built-in instances (integers under max, bool under or, sets and lists under union, maps pointwise, tuples and records componentwise, none as bottom) have the laws by MergeLaws.lean; that sorted lists without duplicates represent sets and maps canonically is Canon.set_canon and Canon.map_canon, and that the canonical order they are sorted by is a strict total order is ValOrder.lt_total. A componentwise instance exists only when every component has one: a map needs a Merge on its value type, an option on its payload, and a struct without its own impl Merge on every field, recursively through nested structs and the struct's type arguments (a struct reached again through itself adds no condition). Otherwise lvar_new, lvar T and Map.merge require change (W-CRDT-1) with the path to the first field that has none. Sets and lists merge by union, which needs only equality, so their element type needs no Merge.
  • C.11.6 Prefix scan. xs.pscan(f, e) and xs.pscan_incl(f, e) take a list of T, f: (T, T) -> T and e: T (W-TY-1 otherwise) and return a list of the same length. Element i of pscan combines xs[0..i] and element i of pscan_incl combines xs[0..=i]; pscan gives e at index 0, the empty prefix, and the empty list scans to the empty list. Evaluation is on a fixed tree (the up-sweep and down-sweep of Blelloch) of C.8: the range [lo, hi) splits at lo + p, with p the largest power of two below hi - lo (host::tree_split). The up-sweep stores the combination of each node's range, left operand before right. The down-sweep gives each node an offset: none at the root; the parent's offset to the left child; to the right child the left child's sum, combined after the parent's offset when there is one. Element i of pscan is the offset of leaf i, or e when it has none; element i of pscan_incl is xs[i] combined after that offset. The tree depends on n alone, so every run and every target applies f to the same operands in the same bracketing and order, and the result is bit-identical for an f that is itself deterministic on each target, floats included. Law: if f is associative, every bracketing of a prefix has the same value, so element i equals the left fold of its prefix. No identity law is needed: e is never combined, it only stands for the empty prefix. If f is not associative (float addition) the result is still fixed, but can differ from the left fold, as for a reduction on the fixed tree (C.8, T18). Work: fewer than 2n applications of f for pscan and fewer than 3n for pscan_incl; depth O(log n). The reference (conc.rs) and the runtimes of every emitter (rt.rs, rt.py, rt.js, rt.scala) use the same split.
  • C.11.8 LVars. lvar T requires T: Merge (W-CRDT-1). An LVar holds a value, the optional top of lvar_new(bottom, top), and a frozen bit. put(d) sets the value v to v ⊔ d with the program's Merge; it is trap("lvar conflict") when the result is the top, and trap("lvar put after freeze") when the LVar is frozen and the result differs from v (a put that changes nothing is allowed). freeze() sets the bit and returns the exact value. wait(Q) returns the t in Q with t ⊔ v = v, in the same Merge order as put, and blocks until there is one. The threshold tests charge no fuel and no budget, so the cost of a wait does not depend on how often a schedule rechecks it. A Q with more than one element must be pairwise incompatible: distinct elements join to the top. Every wait checks this before it reads the value and is otherwise trap("lvar thresholds are not pairwise incompatible"); the check does not read the value, so its outcome does not depend on the schedule. A trap is a defined result, so δ stays total. W-LVAR-1: inside the branches of one par, or the body of a for ... par, a freeze while some branch may put, where a call to a function or method that puts to (or freezes) an LVar it did not create counts as a put (or a freeze). An LVar a branch creates with lvar_new and does not rebind is its own and does not count. The rule does not match the name of a put with the name of a freeze, so an alias, a parameter or a helper cannot hide a freeze. W-LVAR-2: an empty threshold list, or a list with two elements that are, or on some input can be, one below the other in the program's Merge (conc::lvar_gate). This is decided at admission when every element takes finitely many values: a constant, or if c then a else b over such, with every combination checked, since two thresholds where one is below the other are compatible for any top. A parameter whose declared type is finite (a kind of nullary variants, or bool) and which the body never rebinds ranges over every value of its type, so it is decided too; since every value of such a type is at or above its bottom, a list with such a parameter and another element requires change whenever the bottom is below that element. Where an element is not finite in this sense (a parameter of an unbounded type, a computed value), incompatibility depends on the input, and the check every wait makes against the top, with its trap, is the defined behaviour. Model: T29q, T29s, T29a; the rule table conc::LVAR_RULES ties each rule and trap to its Lean declaration (see T29s).
  • C.11.8 convergence notes. The frozen bit, and the rule that only a put that would change a frozen LVar is an error, follow Kuper, Turon, Krishnaswami and Newton (POPL 2014, Sec. 3.3 and 4.2). Threshold sets and their incomp premise follow Kuper and Newton (FHPC 2013, Sec. 3.3). T29q has the shape of the POPL 2014 Theorem 1 for this fragment. Their proof goes through an Independence lemma and quasi-confluence; the one here uses an invariant (the value joined with the puts still to come is the join of all puts), which suffices because there is no allocation: T29s takes a store of many LVars as the product lattice over locations and proves the invariant per location, and T29a adds lvar_new as a step that allocates a location named by a deterministic counter (thread i's k-th allocation is (i, k)), so locations do not depend on the schedule and the POPL 2014 permutation of locations is not needed. Their library marks code that freezes as QuasiDet in its type. In RCE, the freezes that could race with a put instead require change (W-LVAR-1), so an admitted program is deterministic, and the frozen bit turns a race the rule misses into an error instead of a different answer. FHPC 2013 suggests validating user lattices with QuickCheck; the sample search here is that kind of test, and is used only to find counterexamples.
  • C.11.9 Structured spawn. spawn f(...) -> h gives a join handle. In a module a task function may spawn only inside scope; fn main is an implicit scope (W-SCOPE-1). A join handle cannot leave its scope (W-SCOPE-1).
  • C.11.10 Transactions. atomic applies all its actor sends or none (T30). W-ATOM-1: spawn, a receive, select or another wait inside atomic. W-ATOM-2: actors of one atomic on different nodes.
  • C.11.11 Placement and supervision. node N {A, B} places actors on a node. W-NODE-1: a placed name that is not an actor, or an actor placed twice. supervisor S strategy k with k one of one_for_one, one_for_all, rest_for_one (W-SUP-1); each child must be an actor (W-SUP-2), and a duplicate child requires change (W-NAME-2). Run-time meaning (normative). A supervisor declaration is one static supervisor; it supervises every actor whose type is one of its children, so the set an actor belongs to is fixed by the program, not by spawn order. When the step of a handler of such an actor is kept for its message (a trap or a fail), the run log records Kept(reason), then Restart(child, instance, reason, tick t, k), where instance is the actor's id (6.6) and k counts this child's restarts in the window below. The strategy then resets the region of the failed actor (one_for_one), of every actor of the supervisor's child types (one_for_all), or of those whose child is declared at or after the failed one (rest_for_one), to the actor's initializers. Intensity is measured in logical ticks, never wall time: with const RESTART_WINDOW: u64 = W only restarts at ticks t' with t - t' < W count, otherwise every restart of the run counts; more than the child's restart bound stops the supervisor with Stopped(supervisor S) and the run ends Stopped. Mailbox policy: a restarted actor keeps its mailbox, since Form law 3 drops no message; only the message that failed is consumed, and it is logged as kept. A handler that fails inside atomic (C.11.10) leaves every handler of the batch uncommitted (T30), and the failing actor is then supervised as above. Restart as input. Derivation. The state of a run is the fold of its log (T3). A restart changes actor state without a message, so it must be an entry of the log that the fold applies, or the state is not a function of the log. The decision is therefore an input of the run: at a crash the run records RestartIn{tick, sup, child, id, reset, stop} (RunResult.restarts), and a replay given these inputs (RunCfg.restarts) applies each logged decision at its crash without consulting the supervisor's policy. A log thus replays under the decisions it records even after the strategy, bound or RESTART_WINDOW in the source has changed (the resolver rule of Appendix D, applied to supervision). A replayed decision for another actor or supervisor than the one that crashed is replay diverged. Checked by spec/checker/tests/conc06b_run.rs (supervisor_restarts_then_stops, restart_is_an_input_replay_consumes: replay reproduces the log, logged decisions govern under a changed bound, an edited decision is applied as logged, a mismatched one diverges) and emit_run.rs actor_kept_outcomes_match (the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes take the same decisions as the reference, with and without a window) and restart_inputs_replay_on_every_target (each runtime prints its decisions with restart-log, replays a logged list given as restart TICK|SUP|CHILD|ID|STOP|RESET,... under a changed bound exactly as the reference does, and diverges on a mismatched decision). Stable ids and upgrades. Derivation. A logged decision names actors by id, and replay applies it to the actor with that id, so a log replays on an upgraded program exactly when the upgrade maps each logged id to the same instance. An id built from source text (a line, a count of unrelated creations) changes under edits that do not touch supervision, and T7 forbids identifiers in ids. What both an upgrade that keeps supervision and a renaming preserve is the position of an instance: its place in the supervisor tree and its order among its creating task's creations at that place. Ids are therefore those paths (6.6): i.j, creating task, ordinal for a supervised actor; -, task, ordinal for an unsupervised one; parent and ordinal for a task. Since ids are positional, a log is meaningful only against the tree it was recorded under, so the tree is the log's schema: version 1 of the restart log is a header restartlog v1 tree=S/c,... (every position by its declared supervisor and child names, in declaration order; RunResult.tree, conc::sup_tree) followed by the restartin lines. Migration rule (normative): a version 1 log replays on a program in which every recorded position still holds the same declared supervisor and child, that is the recorded supervisors are the program's first ones in order and each keeps its recorded children as its first ones in order; new children may follow a supervisor's recorded ones and new supervisors may follow the recorded ones, since neither moves a recorded position. Any other change (a position removed or renamed, a supervisor or child inserted before a recorded one, a reorder) is detected before the first step: the run stops with trap: upgrade removed supervisor position S/c or trap: upgrade reordered supervisor position S/c for the first recorded position that fails, and nothing is replayed (conc::tree_migrates, RunCfg.restart_tree). A log without a header is version 0: its decisions replay with each decision's position checked when it is taken, so a decision whose position is gone stops the run with the removed-position trap at that crash, and a decision for another actor is replay diverged; neither is ever applied to a different instance. A log whose tree does not migrate is converted by recording it again under the new program; no rule rewrites positional ids across a moved position, because the instance a moved position denotes is not determined by the log. Checked by conc06b_run.rs (restart_log_schema_migration_rule, actor_and_task_ids_survive_structure_preserving_edits) and emit_run.rs restart_replay_survives_upgrades_and_traps_on_tree_changes (a log recorded on one program replays on an upgrade that shifts every line and adds a function, an actor type and a supervisor; removal and reorder traps; the version 0 per-decision check; on the reference and on the Rust, Python, JavaScript and Scala runtimes, which print the header with restart-log and take it as restart-tree S/c,...). The run log of fn main is not D: actors run by rce run, not by the host of Appendix E (HC-6).
  • C.11.12 Real time. interrupt event E priority p with p an integer literal in 0..=255 (W-INTR-1). step ... deadline n with n a positive integer literal in ticks, and const TICK_NS: u64 = n when declared (W-RT-1). TICK_NS only relates logical ticks to a nominal duration for reporting; no construct reads a wall clock (6.3 N11).
  • C.11.4 Replicated state. replicated state R is a region whose log is shared by replicas; a replica that applied a prefix of the log holds the fold of that prefix (T31).

sections.title: C.12 Rules that are not draft 0.6
sections.html: The reference checker also raises three rules that belong to the 0.5 language and are now listed in section 7: W-MOD-3 (an import's name that clashes with a declaration or with another import's name), W-VIS-1 (use of a name private to its module, the form W-MOD-1 takes in link.rs) and W-TRAIT-3 (a type used with ==, < or a generic bound that does not implement the required trait).

sections.title: C.14 Emitters and running
sections.html: rce run runs programs on the reference evaluator (conc.rs). The program emitters (emit/conc06.rs) run the branches of a par with more than one branch at the same time where the target allows it (Rust and Python threads, JavaScript workers) and in source order in Scala; in every case the store, the outputs and the trap point are those of source order (C.4, T16), the branches' results and costs being merged in source order after they finish; a par whose branches wait on LVars is run by restart (a repeated attempt puts nothing new, since puts are joins and W-CRDT-1 makes every join idempotent), and budgets charge the same costs as the evaluator, so trap("budget") falls on the same operation on every target. Workgroups run lane after lane per phase. The 0.6b actor, session and node constructs follow the limits of 10.5.

sections.title: C.15 Releases
sections.html:
# rce-version: V is a release label (2.7): tolerated, ignored, not hashed. A release label names exactly one spec commit: the text of this document at that commit is the language of that release, there is one language in it, and no label selects among alternatives inside a text. The rule that decides what needs a new release: the meaning of a module (its outputs, states and outcomes, including where a budget traps) is determined by the text of its release, so a change that gives a valid program of an existing release a different meaning that the old text defined is a new release with a new label, never a silent change to the old text; a change that makes the implementations meet text that already defined the meaning, or that only touches artifacts outside a program's meaning, is an erratum and goes into the text that the next release names. A release is never edited after it is named, and a label is never reused for a different commit.

Costs. A standard library method call costs c_call + work(m, n, k) (C.6.4) wherever it is written and wherever it is executed from; linking modules changes no cost, since there is only one rule. Example: a function that holds with budget B and calls an imported function whose body sorts an 8-element list is charged 24 more than a call to a function with no body, in the reference evaluator and every runtime.

An example whose earlier event is kept required change under W-INT-1 before and now holds when its last step and final state are as it states; every example that held before holds with the same trace, so no valid program changes meaning

The first row is the one change since draft 0.6 that moved where a with budget block traps; it is what made the earlier text a different release. Every other row is an erratum, an extension or a change outside a program's meaning. Checked by spec/checker/tests/method_costs.rs (every method charges the table in the reference and every runtime), spec/checker/tests/call_site_cost.rs (the same cost in the reference evaluator and the Rust, Python and JavaScript emitters on a linked program) and spec/checker/tests/reserved_words.rs (the one reserved list).

sections.title: C.16 Indexed values
sections.html: The eight names of 5.16 are on the reserved list (2.4): a program may not declare struct Text or struct Html, which earlier drafts allowed, and that requirement is part of the release that first carried the list (C.15). C.lit(s) costs c_call, C.encode(t) costs c_call plus the size of t (the linear class of C.6.4) and .raw() costs c_call (the text is not copied), in the reference evaluator and every runtime; the indices are erased, so nothing else in C.6 changes (spec/checker/tests/indexed.rs).

sections.title: C.17 Appendix F
sections.html: Appendix F is part of the language. Under it, programs that earlier drafts accepted require change (unused values, shadowing, dropped results, flows to lower labels), and it changes the value of a &mut argument after a failed call, so it is a new release by the C.15 rule. It is specified and implemented in part: a construct of it that an implementation does not have requires change (W-RES-1, reserved, not implemented, F.12), and no cost of C.6 is defined for it beyond the costs F.10 names.

chapters.title: Appendix D. The engine profile: handler specs and fits (normative)
chapters.question: Which compiled node id does `deliverable D1` become? (for example role_R1)

sections.html:
This appendix defines the second input language of the engine: the handler spec, a line-oriented .rce file that rce check, rce compile, rce run, rce auto and rce form read (src/spec/parser.rs), and the JSON fit that says what each node of the compiled graph does (src/form/fit.rs). It is a profile tied to the language spec, not a second programming language: a handler spec declares a graph and its contracts; the behaviour of each node is a fit entry, and the compiled result is a Form P = (S, E, δ, D, λ) as in 6.1, with S, E and δ given by D.6. A file is a handler spec when its first non-blank, non-comment line starts with spec; otherwise it is a module of sections 2 to 10. Example:

spec "orders-form" v0.1.0
reason "Demo for the Form compiler" by "david"
currency max_age=24h

Implementation status. This appendix describes the engine profile. The code it names (src/spec/, src/form/) belongs to the engine crate, which is not in this repository. The reference checker in spec/checker has no src/spec or src/form, rce-spec-check does not read handler specs, and no file under spec/checker/src, spec/checker/tests, spec/checker/examples or spec/examples mentions a W-HS rule. So nothing in this appendix is checked by the tools published here; the rules below are a specification of the engine, and its tests are not published.

sections.title: D.1 Lexical rules
sections.html:
• The file is UTF-8 text read line by line. A line that is blank after trimming, or whose first non-space characters are # or //, is skipped.
  • A top-level line starts in column 0. A body line starts with a space or a tab and belongs to the nearest preceding top-level block. A blank line ends a body.
  • Tokens are separated by white space. A token that starts with " runs to the next " (no escapes); its value is the text between the quotes.
  • Durations: hours are N or Nh; milliseconds are Nms, Ns (seconds) or N. N is a decimal integer.

sections.title: D.3 Meaning of each declaration
sections.html:
• spec NAME VERSION: the name and version of the spec. The version is recorded in the compiled graph's metadata (spec_version) and in the Form IR (FormIr.version). The version is not yet checked.
  • reason WHY by AUTHOR: why an artifact exists. A top-level reason belongs to the spec; a body reason belongs to its block. A reason is recorded on the node or edge it explains and enters the log with every mutation that creates it. Reasons are data: they never change δ.
  • currency: when the spec's toolchain and dependencies were last verified (last_checked), the versions seen then, and the maximum age max_age in hours. Parsing is not a check: without last_checked the record is unchecked. rce currency FILE --mark records a check by writing last_checked back into the file. A record is stale when it was never checked or is older than max_age; the promotion gate records a stale spec, and blocks on it when the engine's enforce_currency policy is on (off by default).
  • objective, constraint, acceptance: requirements. Acceptance properties and their error budget are not inputs of δ: no step reads them. They decide whether a candidate passes the promotion gate, and so which δ is installed next (see the versioning of δ below).
  • deliverable D compiles to the node del_D (an executor and a sink), role R to role_R (kind executor, decision, escalation or source), dependency P to dep_P (a source). flow F from A to B compiles to the edge flow_F; escalation E from A to B timeout t to esc_E. An endpoint names a node id, a node name or a declared id; an unknown flow endpoint requires change (the compiler stops), an unknown escalation endpoint is a diagnostic.
  • change_control: who may approve changes to the spec, the minimum review period, and whether the spec is frozen. These bind the engine's promotion path (spec mutations are logged and need an approver). They are not inputs of δ; they govern which δ may be installed, and by whom.

δ is versioned. A promotion that passes the gate is committed as a RESOLVE entry of D (PromoteEscalation with a resolve stamp) that records the log height h of the entry, the version of δ at its node (raised by one at each RESOLVE for that node), and the sha256 digests of the installed HandlerSpec and of the fit evidence the gate accepted. The new handler governs every entry after h, and every entry before h was computed under the previous one. A tick is one step and no input can be committed inside it, so a step in flight when a RESOLVE is requested finishes under the δ it started with. The state after n entries is the fold of D under the δ in force at each height: s(i+1) = δ_v(i)(s(i), D(i)), where v(i) is the version set by the last RESOLVE before i. A fold applies each RESOLVE at the height it records and stops at one whose height, version or spec digest differs from the fold's; the fit digest is recorded and not refolded, since the fit evidence is not in D. The handler installed is the one the entry carries; only an opaque handler (no spec) runs as the live object, and every result it returns is in D (ExternalResult).

sections.title: D.4 Fits
sections.html:
A fit is a JSON object:

{ "handlers": { NODE: HandlerSpec | {"kind": "term", "term": TERM}
                       | {"kind": "recorded", "contract": C, "table": {SHA256: RESULT}} },
  "types":    { SOURCE_NODE: TYPE },
  "keys":     { SINK_NODE: [COLUMN, ...] },
  "reads":    { SINK_NODE: {"key": [FIELD, ...], "into": FIELD} },
  "joins":    { SINK_NODE: [ {"relation": REL, "key": [FIELD, ...], "into": FIELD,
                              "scan": BOOL}, ... ] } }

An object with any of the five fields above is a full fit, even when it holds only reads or joins; any other object is a bare map of handlers and is read as handlers alone. NODE is a compiled node id (role_R1, dep_DEP1, del_D1). types gives the input contract of a source; keys the key of a sink's relation (default: the input number seq and the index n within the step). A recorded entry is an oracle: a recorded input replays its result and an unseen one escalates as "oracle miss".

sections.title: D.5 Reads, joins and scans
sections.html:
Each is applied before the body of every rule that writes the sink, to the state at the event's entry (pre-state, as in 6.4), in this order: the read, then the joins in list order.

  • reads[S] = {key, into}: the row of S's own relation whose key is the payload fields key (in key-column order) is put into the input as field into, or null when there is none. The relation must exist and its key must have as many columns as key names.
  • joins[S], an entry without scan: the row of relation relation keyed by the payload fields key, or null, into field into. The relation must exist and its key arity must match.
  • an entry with "scan": true: every row of relation as an array, in canonical key order (code point order of the canonical JSON key); key is ignored.
  • A payload that is not a record is passed unchanged. Joined rows and scans are typed as JSON. Each read or join is covered by the rule's SHA-256 id, and a rule with a read or a join is not monotone (CALM, form/laws.rs). A joins entry for a sink no rule writes requires change.
  • Every target (reference δ, Rust, Python, JavaScript for XState and SCXML) applies them identically.

CALM tags (normative). Each rule's monotone tag is derived by form::laws::calm_reason, never declared, and laws::check reports that an IR whose tag differs requires change. A rule is monotone only when it has no resolve, no read, no join and no scan. The reasons, by derivation:

Rule hasTagWhy
none of the belowmonotoneits writes only add keys and grow counters
resolvenot monotoneit deletes escalation rows
readnot monotoneread-modify-write of its own sink
keyed joinnot monotonethe joined row may be null now and present later, or overwritten
scannot monotoneit observes the whole relation, so also what is absent

The tag is conservative (sound, not complete): a join against an insert-only relation would be monotone in principle, but the profile does not prove insert-only, so it is not claimed. A Form is coordination-free (laws::coordination_free) iff every rule is monotone. Because every read, join and scan sees the entry state, the post-state of an input event does not depend on the order in which rules for different sinks run; only the output order does, and that is fixed by content hash (law 2).

sections.title: D.6 The compiled Form
sections.html: Σc has one region per node, Ready | Escalated. Σd has the logical clock, an input count and the typed relations of the sinks plus escalation and error. E is IN_<source>, TICK and RESOLVE_<node>. An input event normalizes the payload (6.3 N1), checks the source's contract (a mismatch is a reject output and an error row, not a kept step) and runs the rules in content-hash order. A timeout is converted to ticks of a nominal 100 ms, rounded up; the clock is logical (6.3 N11). D is the canonical log of 6.1: entries {seq, event, prev_hash, state_hash, hash} chained by SHA-256. Every event is applied (no outcome field is needed), since a contract mismatch is an output, not a kept step. The numeric edges are those of 6.3, with one recorded difference: in this profile an integer above i64::MAX is "integer out of range" (D.10).

sections.title: D.7 Relation to the language
sections.html:
A handler spec and a module of sections 2 to 10 both denote a Form, but the profile has no expressions of its own: node behaviour comes only from fits. A fit term is a term of the Form IR (form/ir.rs), not an RCE expression. A function of a module is used as a fit through its lowering (rce index, spec/checker/src/brick_lower.rs): a function f(p1: T1, ..., pn: Tn) -> R lowers to the term t with t({"p1": v1, ..., "pn": vn}) = f(v1, ..., vn), values in the Form's JSON embedding (lists and tuples as arrays, structs as objects). A trap of f is an error of t at the node module.f. A function that calls others lowers to a Form IR format 2 program (spec/proposals/form-ir-2.md): each callee is a definition keyed by the SHA-256 of its term's canonical JSON, and a call is a ref to that key; a function that calls nothing lowers to a bare format 1 term.

Statements lower store-passing: each is a term from an environment record (the variables in scope and the control fields $done, $ret, $brk, $cnt) to the next one, skipped once the function has returned or the iteration has been left. let, var, assignment (also compound and to a list item), push and pop statements, if, while c bound n (the iteration count traps past n, after the condition holds, as in 6.7), loop, for x in e (a range or a list), break, continue, return anywhere and check lower. Expressions: literals, constants (their values, by the reference evaluator), arithmetic (+ as plus: integers add, texts and lists concatenate), bit operations (band, bor, bxor, shl, shr, bnot; a shift amount outside 0..64 is an error, as it traps), comparisons, and and or (as cond), if, list and tuple literals, [v; n], indexing (at: a text is read as its UTF-8 bytes, as in 6.3; a negative index traps), fields, struct construction, the methods len (size, bytes of a text), chars, tostr, toint, upper, lower, contains, startswith, endswith, split, join, casts to i64 and usize, shared borrows, copy, and calls of other lowerable functions (by ref). A function with &mut parameters lowers by state-passing: its term returns [result, final values of the &mut parameters in parameter order] (the result is null for a function without one), and a call of it, as a statement, a let or var initializer or the right side of =, writes those values back to the borrowed places; such a call inside a larger expression is not lowered. match lowers arm by arm (variants by their $v tag, some/none, literals, ranges, tuples, alternatives, guards; no arm traps), and a variant value is its fields with $v. A function with result T ! E lowers with its errors as values: fail e returns {"$err": e}, try x [else e] (as a let/var initializer, an assignment's right side, a statement or a return value) tests x with has(x, "$err") (none for an optional) and returns the error, and x catch |e| h tests the same and evaluates h; a call of such a function anywhere else is not lowered. A recursive group (a cycle of the call graph) lowers to one fix term of its members' bodies, a call inside it being rec of the callee's index; bound n is a counter of active calls passed by every rec, trapping past n as in 6.7. The evaluator bounds rec nesting at 20000 (the reference evaluator's nesting limit) and calls per evaluation at 50000000 (its fuel); past either is an error, and an input on which the reference evaluator meets its own limits gives no vector. Integers are i64 or usize (a usize variable that would become negative traps); floats, narrower integers and closures are not lowered. A generic function lowers to one term for every instance, since the IR is untyped over JSON. A term over 1 MiB of JSON, not counting its definitions, or a program nested over 1000 levels is not lowered (catalog readers parse past JSON libraries' usual 128 levels, with a stated bound). Every construct not lowered is recorded in the catalog with its line and construct, never approximated.

rce index vectors N records the reference evaluator's results on N generated inputs per brick; rce-brick-verify (src/form/brick.rs) evaluates each term on them and reports agreement. Agreement is tested on vectors (spec/checker/tests/brick.rs), not proved.

sections.title: D.8 Lift guarantees (normative)
sections.html:
A brownfield lift (rce scan DIR --form, brownfield/lift.rs) reads existing Rust, Python, TypeScript or Go into a Form schema. A lift gives exactly these guarantees, and no other is claimed:

  • L1 Labeled: every relation, region, event and transition carries a label that starts with "unproven"; a lifted element is never presented as checked.
  • L2 Fail closed: a guard the lift cannot read is opaque, and Lifted::step does not step through it, rather than choose a branch it cannot read.
  • L3 Generated code agrees with the lift: code emitted from a lifted machine (--emit-machine) steps as Lifted::step.
  • L4 Evidence, not proof: agreement of the lift with the original program is tested on seeded runs of the original; its level is tested (8). A lift is an input to a gate, never an authority: what it proposes is admitted only through the checker and the gate, like any other proposal.

sections.title: D.9 Rules (normative)
sections.html:
These are checked by crate::spec::rules (src/spec/rules.rs) in the engine crate (see the implementation status above), run by the engine's rce check, and each diagnostic names its rule.

  • W-HS-VER-1: the spec version is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH of decimal integers (an optional leading v is allowed).
  • W-HS-VER-2 (compatibility, between an old and a new revision of one spec, rce diff): the version must not decrease; a revision that removes or modifies a declaration must increase MAJOR, or MINOR when MAJOR is 0; a revision that only adds declarations must increase at least MINOR; a revision with no change may keep the version. Flows are declarations here: a flow whose endpoints change is modified.
  • W-HS-CUR-1: a max_age that is not a positive integer number of hours (N or Nh, N ≥ 1).
  • W-HS-CUR-2 (staleness): at check time now, the currency record is stale when it was never checked or now - last_checked exceeds max_age hours. A stale spec is not accepted by rce check --strict or by the promotion gate when the engine's enforce_currency policy is on; otherwise it is reported as a warning naming W-HS-CUR-2. This is the one rule of the appendix whose verdict depends on a time given as an input (see D.10).
  • W-HS-REASON-1: the spec, or a declaration that compiles to a node or an edge (deliverable, role, dependency, flow, escalation), has no reason line, or a reason whose text is empty or unspecified.
  • W-HS-DUR-1: a duration that is not a decimal integer with an allowed suffix (D.1).
  • W-HS-KW-1: an unknown body keyword or change_control word.

sections.title: D.10 Recorded differences and open items
sections.html:
• Integers in [2^63, 2^64) are u64 values, as in the language (6.3 N2): the u64 operators compute on them exactly, comparisons, sort, lmin, lmax, min and max order them exactly, and the f64 and f32 operators convert them to f64. The signed operators do not compute on them ("integer out of range"), which no well-typed program reaches, since a signed value is never at or above 2^63. A JSON integer beyond u64 is read as a float (form::num); no integer type of the language holds one.
  • W-HS-CUR-2 takes now. 10.1 item 1 says the subcommands of section 10 read no clock; the staleness check is outside them, but a verdict that depends on now is a function of its recorded inputs only if now is recorded with the verdict. Whether it must be is not decided.
  • The cost model of extraction (est_j) and the gate's certificate are outside this appendix, except the break-even receipt of D.11.
  • InstallHandler and RetireHandler also change δ at the height of their entry and carry the same RESOLVE stamp as a promotion: height, the next δ version at the node (versions count every install, promotion and retirement there), the digest of the installed spec (for a retirement, the digest of the stub, distinct from an opaque install) and a fit digest. A fold stops at one whose stamp does not match. Entries written before the stamp existed carry none and fold as before.

sections.title: D.11 Promotion break-even (receipt)
sections.html:
Each promotion record (promoted or not promoted) carries a break-even receipt break_even with three terms and n* = J_build / (J_model_path - J_handler), the number of inputs after which the promoted handler has paid back its build:

  • J_build: the est_j of the gear resolution that wrote the handler plus the coverage shadow run of the promotion path. Static checks (proof, kernel) are not priced and not included, so J_build and n* are lower bounds.
  • J_model_path: joules per input on the model path, the est_j of one gear resolution (the price the retirement rule uses for savings).
  • J_handler: joules per input of the handler, the shadow run's priced operations per sample plus one dispatch.

Each term is {j, basis} with basis one of est (a model of the work, including a model provider's own figure), reported (an OS or on-chip energy counter: RAPL, NVML, IOReport), measured (a wall or shunt meter on a named rail) or unpriced (no figure; j is null, never 0). The terms the engine fills today are est or unpriced: a gear receipt's est_j is an estimate by schema and is never relabeled from its free text. A figure without a basis is reported as invalid when a record is read, and the type that holds a term has no constructor from a bare number. n_star is {kind: unpriced} when any term is unpriced (it is never computed from the other terms or from a default), {kind: never} when J_model_path - J_handler <= 0, and otherwise {kind: value, n, inputs = ⌈n⌉}; its basis is the weakest of the three (unpriced < est < reported < measured). The promotion path's last step records the same figures as text. Implemented in src/runtime/break_even.rs, tested there and in the engine's promotion tests.

Readings: provenance, boundary and amortization (normative; P4, P5, P6 of the receipt field proposals of 13 Oct 2026). These rules apply to every term labeled reported or measured, in every receipt that holds one, and are checked where a term is built and where a record is read:

  1. A reading carries provenance = {sampler, counter, interval_s, idle_baseline_w, machine, boundary}: the four names non-empty, interval_s finite and > 0, idle_baseline_w finite and >= 0 (0 when no baseline was subtracted). boundary says what the joules include (package, package+dram, rail:VDD_GPU). A reading without a valid provenance is reported as invalid, and so is one with unknown fields. Derivation: the label reported or measured claims that something was read; a reading that cannot be reproduced or compared (which counter, over what interval, against which baseline, on which machine, inside which boundary) does not support that claim, so a term that lacks it is not a reading, and labeling it one would be unsound.
  2. A term labeled est or unpriced carries no provenance (nothing was read); one that does is reported as invalid.
  3. A reading carries amortization, one of {kind: per_call}, {kind: batch_mean, n >= 1}, {kind: per_solved_task}. An est term may carry one; the engine's own estimates omit it.
  4. Figures of different kinds are never added or subtracted: a sum of two terms whose amortization differs (absent counts as its own kind) is reported as invalid, and so is a break-even whose J_model_path and J_handler differ in kind (n* divides by their difference) or whose J_build is a mean (batch_mean or per_solved_task; J_build is a one-off total). Derivation: a batch mean added to a per-call figure, or a per-task figure subtracted from a per-input one, is arithmetic on different units; no result of it is a figure of either kind.
  5. A sum of two readings keeps the weaker label only when both come from the same sampler, counter, machine and boundary (the intervals add); otherwise it is reported as invalid. A sum with an est term is est with no provenance (unpriced < est < reported < measured, as for n*).
  6. A stored break-even receipt is re-derived from its terms when read; a stored n* that disagrees with them is reported as invalid.

The est wire form is unchanged ({"j": 2.5, "basis": "est"}), so no stored receipt changes meaning; no receipt in the repository holds a reading today. Implemented by Term, Provenance and Amortization in src/runtime/break_even.rs (no constructor makes a reading without provenance and amortization), tested there (p4_*, p6_*).

The receipt is a measurement record. It is not an input to δ, to any check, or to the decision to promote, so it does not change the meaning of any program or handler spec in any language version (C.15: receipts are version-independent).

chapters.title: Appendix E. The host contract (normative)
chapters.question: Which fcntl command is the append barrier on macOS? (for example F_SETFL)

sections.html:
This appendix states what a host must do to run an RCE program. A host is everything outside δ and λ: the code that admits events, appends the log D (6.1), runs λ's outputs as effects, answers foreign calls and talks to devices. The language defines meaning; the host is conforming when every run it performs is the fold of its own log (T3) and the log it leaves on storage can be replayed with every adapter disconnected (T37). The appendix applies to every version (C.15): it constrains hosts and the format of D, and it gives no valid program a different meaning.

Figure (informative). The five primitives, adapters, the single admitter (HC-1), typed results (HC-3) and replay with adapters disconnected (HC-8, T37). Source: docs/figures.

The rules were derived from a survey of operating systems, embedded kernels, browsers, language runtimes, replay systems, storage engines and compute fabrics. A primitive is in the contract only when (a) every surveyed target can supply it and (b) its result is a pure function of logged data or is itself logged. What fails (b), because it depends on timing, ordering, hardware or another process, enters as an event, as 5.15 already requires. Every target supplies: pure computation on bytes with integer operations and binary64 round-to-nearest-even, append-only storage, SHA-256 as pure code, one input queue and one output queue, and a monotonic counter read only by the admitter. Everything else is an adapter.

sections.title: E.1 Terms
sections.html:
• Admitter. The one component that orders inputs into E and appends entries to D.
  • Adapter. Host code that turns one outside source (a keyboard, a socket, a file, a clock, a GPU, a foreign library) into events, or one output request into an effect and a result event.
  • Host entry. An entry of D whose event type starts with host. (E.5). No RCE identifier contains a dot, so no program declares such an event, and δ is the identity on it: δ(s, e) = (s, []) and the entry's state_hash equals the previous entry's (or that of s₀ for the first). The fold law of 6.1 is unchanged.
  • Durable. An entry is durable when the barrier of E.3 for its storage returned success.
  • Delivery by declaration (HD-1 to HD-4). The host delivers each value as the module declares its event, matching fields by name, and what a declaration cannot take is kept: recorded in D by host.Kept with its reason, not delivered. The rules are stated in E.4c: HD-1 results, HD-2 HTTP, HD-3 received bytes, HD-4 host inputs. Sections before E.4c cite them as E.4c HD-n.

sections.title: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
sections.html:
• HC-1 One admitter per term. At any log height a program instance has exactly one admitter, the holder of the current term (E.2b). Every input reaches δ only after the admitter appended it to D, in D's order. The admitter is a role, not a machine: when it fails, another host takes the role for a higher term and continues the same D (E.2b). A host without replication holds term 0 for its lifetime, which is the single admitter of earlier versions.
  • HC-2 Only the admitter reads clocks. Wall time and monotonic time enter only as events (Tick(n), host.WallTime when an adapter supplies it, and the result of a WallClock request, HC-32). Time inside the language is logical (6.3 N11, C.11.12).
  • HC-3 Typed output requests. Each effect requested by λ (a write, a send, a draw, a foreign call) has exactly one result event: delivered, failed, timed out or unreachable. A result is delivered as the module declares its event, and a result the module declares no event for is recorded in D (E.4c, HD-1). A race inside the adapter (for example a file checked and then opened) is resolved by the adapter; the program sees one atomic outcome. The answer of a model runtime (F.5.6) is delivered only on an event the program declares extern "model" event, and the host fills no capability for it (HC-5); a program that declares none receives no model text.
  • HC-4 Foreign code. Foreign code runs only through 5.11, with its arguments copied or borrowed for the call only, under fuel, and its result or trap logged as Foreign(f, arguments, result). An isolated component boundary (a WebAssembly component per call) is the recommended adapter; it does not change the rule.
  • HC-5 Capabilities. Authority comes only from capabilities minted by logged events (5.16 Cap[A] in a version 0.8 module). The host holds no ambient authority on the program's behalf. This is the sandbox, and its contract is independent of any OS: the checker admits only programs whose effects go through granted capabilities, and the deterministic host does not perform any effect without one, before any OS layer is involved. The same contract then has enforcement targets underneath the host, entered at start as strictly as the target allows: WASM (the module imports only the granted host functions), bare metal (no OS; the engine is the only host and capabilities are the whole I/O surface), Linux (Landlock and seccomp), macOS (Seatbelt, sandbox_init), Windows (AppContainer, to do) and other OSes (FreeBSD Capsicum cap_enter, OpenBSD pledge/unveil, iOS, Android: to do). The contract is planned to conform to OpenIE's Sandbox v0.1 standard (https://sandbox.transaction.science: S0-S7 tiers, §5 Grants, §6 energy and §7 attestation receipts) and to JCP v0.3 (https://jcp.transaction.science); see REMAINING-PLAN W1h-std. The program loses nothing, since 5.15 gives it no ambient authority.
  • HC-5a The printed target is the installed target. The line a host prints when it enters an OS target is generated from the rules it installed, so it names each restriction at the granularity the target enforces and never one the target did not install. The reference (sandbox.rs) lists every address an adapter may use with how it is used: connected to (net, peer), bound after the target is entered (net, and a http address whose bind is still being retried), or bound before (http, chan), whose listener is then only accepted on. It makes the rules and the line from that one list. On macOS the Seatbelt profile denies all network use, then allows binding and inbound connections on the port of each listening grant and outbound connections to the port of each connecting grant, at localhost for a loopback address and at any address otherwise, because Seatbelt names no other address; it allows the system name resolver only when a grant names a host by name. The line says that these rules cover TCP and UDP and that the net adapter checks the exact address. On Linux, with Landlock ABI 4 or later, TCP bind is allowed only on the ports of listening grants and connect only on the ports of connecting grants, at any address on those ports, and the line says "by port"; a listener bound before entering needs no rule; below ABI 4 the line says that Landlock does not restrict the network. seccomp does not permit new IP sockets unless some grant is connected to or bound after entering, so with http alone neither the host nor a PTY child can open a socket; otherwise no layer restricts UDP, and the line says so. Landlock also handles reading a file and listing a directory: they are allowed only under the log directory, /dev, the granted roots (fs, blob, media, wasm) and, under names and only then, the files /etc/passwd and /etc/group (HC-33), and the line names them. Landlock has no right for lstat or readlink, so it restricts neither, and the line says so; seccomp denies none of lstat, readlink or getdents, so the requests of HC-30 and HC-31 run under DIR. Under pty, whose programs read the whole system, and with a grant that names a host by name, whose resolver reads the system's configuration after entering, reads are not handled, and the line says which of the two is the reason. The channel adapters start their threads after the target is entered, so Landlock covers them as well. The Seatbelt rules follow Apple's profile language and are still to be confirmed on a macOS machine; the two tests that do so run only there.
  • HC-6 Tick scheduler. Concurrency runs under the tick semantics of 6.8. The host runs fn main (tasks, actors, supervisors; C.5, C.13) with its scheduler as a live task whose every transition is an entry of D. host.MainStart {links, max_ticks, seed} starts the task; host.MainInput {a, b, partition, tick} logs an input to it (a link change), and host.MainInput {event, tick} feeds it a program event (canonical event JSON): at that tick the scheduler logs Input(..) and delivers the event to every live actor whose type has an on handler for it, in actor-id order, or logs Unhandled(..) when there is none (an input event has no addressee, so its receivers are the program's handlers of it, as for the steps on E of a Form; Host::main_event, conc::RunCfg.events, tests/host_sched.rs program_events_feed_the_live_task_and_replay, tests/conc06b_run.rs program_events_feed_the_running_task; the emitted runtimes take the same inputs as event TICK|Name|f=v,..., a field's value given by its declared type as a decimal integer, true/false or text, and log Input(..) and Unhandled(..) with actor-log; a malformed event is an input error, exit status 2, not a program trap; tests/emit_run.rs program_events_agree_on_every_target on the Rust, Python, JavaScript and Scala runtimes); host.Step {cause, i, node, tick, what} logs one scheduler step, including the arm the environment chose at each select nondet; host.MainEnd {choices, outcome, ticks} ends it. Program inputs to δ may be admitted between any two of these entries. While the task is live its state (the start entry, the inputs logged so far, the number of steps logged and a hash chain over them) is part of the state D folds to, and the state_hash of every entry covers it, so the state after each entry is the fold of D up to that entry and a host rebuilt from any prefix continues the same run. Replay re-runs the scheduler on the logged inputs and stops at an entry unless the step it logs is the next step the scheduler takes and the end agrees in outcome and choices (T21). An input whose tick is not after the last logged step is not admitted: it is not logged, and an input is also not admitted if re-running on it would change a step already in D, so an input never rewrites the past. No snapshot is taken while a task is live. A host may execute tasks in parallel only when the result equals the tick semantics (T1, T21). Reference: Host::main_begin, main_input, main_event, main_step, main_end, and run_main for a run whose inputs are all known at the start. Derivation: law 1 of E.2c makes each nondeterministic choice of the run an entry of D, and the requirement that state be the fold of D at every entry, not only between runs, makes the task's progress part of that state. The task's inputs are link changes, program events and the environment's choices, each an entry of D under the same causality rule. The emitted runtimes do not take program events (G14).
  • HC-7 Numerics and limits. The host reproduces 6.3 bit for bit and enforces fuel, SIZE_LIMIT and VALUE_LIMIT (6.7, N9) as the reference does, on every run.
  • HC-7a Fuel per input. A host is event driven, so fuel is charged per admitted input: each input (one application of δ, including constructing its event) starts with the full fuel of 6.7, and no budget is shared across inputs. Every input has its own bound and a session never starves however long it runs. The reference trace (rce trace), the host and replay all reset fuel per input, so a kept step for fuel is a function of that input and the state before it, and D is the same on each.
  • HC-8 Replay. A host offers a replay mode that reads D, disconnects every adapter and re-derives every state hash. Replay reads no clock, file, network, device or environment (T37).
  • HC-9 Priority admission. Interrupt sources carry a priority in 0..255 (T25, C.11.12). Inputs admitted together are ordered by priority, highest first. Inputs with a source and sequence number are ordered by the window key of HC-15. Inputs given together without source identity (admit_simultaneous) are ordered by priority, then by the bytes of their canonical event JSON, so the order is a function of the set of inputs and not of the order the caller passed them in. Either way the order chosen is D's order. A real-time bound holds only on a kernel with a priority scheduler; a general-purpose OS gives none.

sections.title: E.2a Canonical admission (HC-15 to HC-17)
sections.html:
The order of D must not depend on when inputs arrive. Arrival timing may decide only which window an input lands in, and the window boundary is defined by logical time, never by a wall clock.

  • HC-15 Windows. Every input carries its source id (text), a per-source sequence number (1, 2, ... with no reuse) and the logical tick its source stamped on it. When the module declares event Tick(n: u64), a window closes when a Tick(n) input not yet in D is offered: window k gets upto = n, holds every offered input with tick at most upto that is not already in D, and the Tick(n) is its last input. The boundary is therefore a logged fact, never a wall clock and never a choice of the caller. An input whose tick is at or below the upto of the last window in D is late: it is admitted in the next window and its host.Input carries "late":true, so whether an input was late is decided by D. A host whose module declares no Tick closes windows by close_window(upto) from its own logical time. Apart from the closing Tick, the order inside a window is the total key (priority descending, source id ascending, sequence ascending).
