So two admitters given the same window contents append the same entries in the same order whatever the arrival order, and two hosts given the same inputs per window produce byte-identical D.
  • HC-16 Exactly once. The dedupe key is (source, seq). A (source, seq) already in D, or offered twice, is a duplicate and is not appended again. Two copies of one (source, seq) with different payloads are ordered by their event bytes, and the lower one is admitted, so the choice does not depend on arrival. An input after a gap in its source's sequence is held for a later window, so each source is admitted in its own order and nothing is skipped. A source retransmits until acked, and the admitter acks an input only after the barrier (HS-2) that covers its window succeeded. A crash before the ack leads to a retransmission, which HC-16 turns into a duplicate when the input did reach D. Exactly once covers only inputs that carry a source and sequence number. A typed input (HC-10b: a line of rce host run or serve) and an HTTP request (HC-24) carry none, so a client's retry of one is a new input, and a program that must apply a retried request once keeps its own key in its state. A duplicate is acked, and the window that finds it holds no outcome for it, so the client that retried learns that its input is in D but not how its step ended; it reads that from D.
  • HC-17 Window entries. Closing a window appends host.Window {count, id, term, upto}, then, before each admitted input, host.Input {late (only when true), seq, source, window}. The dedupe state is the fold of these entries: on open and on replay the admitter rebuilds, per source, the highest seq in D. A host.Input counts only when the program entry it announces follows it, so a cut between the two (HS-4) admits nothing. These are host entries: δ never reads them and they leave the state hash unchanged.

sections.title: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
sections.html:
A host may keep D on a replicated log so that losing the admitter's machine neither stops the program for good nor forks D. The reference implementation is spec/checker/src/raft.rs (Raft log replication behind a Transport trait, with a loopback switch and a TCP transport, and RaftStore, the E.3 Store of a host on the leader). spec/checker/src/repl.rs is a smaller model of the same rules on whole logs.

  • HC-18 Interface. A replicated log offers the host the Store of E.3 with two additions: elect(term), which succeeds only with grants from a quorum of replicas, each of which then promises not to accept an append from a lower term, and returns the most up-to-date log among the granting quorum, ordered by (term of the last write, length); and an append at a term that a replica accepts only while it has promised no higher term. The barrier succeeds only when a quorum accepted every entry up to it, so a durable entry (HS-2) is a committed entry.
  • HC-19 Term fence in D. A host that won elect(t) folds the log it received (HS-4 verification of the whole chain, then HC-8), then appends host.Term {leader, term} and makes it durable before admitting any input. t must exceed every term already in D. Every host.Window carries the term. The new admitter's adapters are fresh, so it appends host.Restarted after host.Term (HC-22), and a request emitted under an older term with no result in D gets one result, failed with interrupted (HC-3). The term in D is the fence token: an entry of D was appended by the holder of the most recent host.Term before it.
  • HC-18a Transport. Replication follows Raft's AppendEntries and RequestVote: an append carries (prev_idx, prev_term) and a follower does not accept it unless its log has an entry at prev_idx with that term (log matching), deletes a conflicting suffix and appends what is missing. The current term and the vote are written to stable storage before a candidate asks for votes, before a vote is granted, and before an append is acknowledged. A vote goes only to a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date by (last term, last index). The leader advances the commit index only over entries of its own term held by a quorum. A follower that needs entries the leader has compacted receives the leader's snapshot (an HS-5 snapshot of the state at that index) and keeps any suffix of its own log that matches it. The transport may lose, delay, duplicate or reorder messages. Timeouts are counted in logical ticks, so a loopback run is a function of its seed. Snapshots travel in chunks of bounded size, each carrying its byte offset; a follower accepts a chunk only at the offset it expects, acknowledges the next offset it needs, and installs the snapshot only when the final chunk arrives, so loss, duplication and reordering of chunks cannot install a partial state. Membership changes use joint consensus: the leader appends a configuration entry C_old,new; a node uses the latest configuration in its log whether or not it is committed; while C_old,new is in force, elections and commitment need a majority of C_old and a majority of C_new; once C_old,new commits the leader appends C_new, and a leader that is not in C_new steps down once C_new commits. Derivation: safety rests on any two quorums intersecting (Quorum.lean, quorum_intersect). Switching directly from C_old to C_new admits a majority of each that share no node, hence two leaders in one term; requiring both majorities during the transition keeps every pair of deciding quorums intersecting. Between hosts the transport runs over TCP inside mutual TLS with pinned ed25519 keys: a frame is accepted only if the peer id it claims matches the key that authenticated the connection, so a node without a pinned key cannot vote or append.
  • HC-20 Deposed admitter. An admitter whose barrier is not granted because a higher term was granted has had its role taken. By HS-3 it appends nothing further and acks nothing, so its unacked inputs are retransmitted to the new admitter and HC-16 removes those that did commit. Committed entries are never removed: the new admitter's log contains every entry a quorum had accepted, so D after a failover extends D before it.

Safety of HC-18 to HC-20 does not depend on clocks. A leader lease, which would let the admitter serve reads without a quorum round, relies on bounded clock skew and is not part of the contract.

Convergence notes. Calvin (Thomson et al., SIGMOD 2012) also fixes the order of inputs before executing them: it "divides time into 10-millisecond epochs", each sequencer compiles the requests of an epoch into a batch, and schedulers interleave "(in a deterministic, round-robin manner) all sequencers' batches for that epoch". Its epochs are wall clock intervals; E.2a's windows are logical, and its merge key orders by priority, source and sequence where Calvin interleaves by sequencer. Calvin also states that "single-node sequencers ... represent potential single points of failure", the concern HC-18 to HC-20 address. FoundationDB (Zhou et al., SIGMOD 2021) keeps a singleton Sequencer that "assigns read and commit versions"; the Coordinators "form a disk Paxos group" and select a ClusterController, which recruits singletons that "are re-recruited if they fail or crash". Its transaction processing "is divided into epochs, where each epoch represents a generation of the transaction management system with its unique Sequencer process", and a recovering Sequencer "locks the coordinated states to prevent another Sequencer process from recovering at the same time". RCE's terms play the role of those generations, recorded in D as host.Term. Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, USENIX ATC 2014, extended version) gives the properties HC-18 relies on: "Election Safety: at most one leader can be elected in a given term"; "If a server receives a request with a stale term number, it rejects the request"; and "Leader Completeness: if a log entry is committed in a given term, then that entry will be present in the logs of the leaders for all higher-numbered terms". Raft notes that a heartbeat lease "would rely on timing for safety (it assumes bounded clock skew)", which is why E.2b leaves leases out. Raft's Figure 2 lists currentTerm, votedFor and log[] as "Persistent state on all servers: (Updated on stable storage before responding to RPCs)", which is the order HC-18a requires. On membership, Raft states that "Agreement (for elections and entry commitment) requires separate majorities from both the old and new configurations" and that "a server always uses the latest configuration in its log, regardless of whether the entry is committed"; HC-18a follows both. Raft's rule that servers disregard RequestVote while they believe a current leader exists, which limits disruption by removed servers, is a liveness measure and is not implemented.

sections.title: E.2c Derivation from laws (informative)
sections.html:
E.2a to E.2b and HC-6, HC-12 are derived from the following laws rather than from the code that existed when they were written. Each law is stated, then the design it forces.

  1. Deterministic state machines agree when their logs agree. Raft: "Each log contains the same commands in the same order, so each state machine processes the same sequence of commands. Since the state machines are deterministic, each computes the same state and the same sequence of outputs." So every nondeterministic choice that can affect a result must be an entry of D: the order of inputs (HC-15), the scheduler's choices and the environment seed of a fn main run (HC-6), and placement decisions (HC-12). Replay re-derives each one and stops where a derivation differs from D, so D is checked, not trusted.
  2. Safety must not depend on timing; liveness must. Raft: "safety must not depend on timing ... However, availability ... must inevitably depend on timing." The law behind it is Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (JACM 1985), Theorem 1: "No consensus protocol is totally correct in spite of one fault", in a model where processes "do not have access to synchronized clocks, so algorithms based on time-outs, for example, cannot be used". Their conclusion asks for "more refined models of distributed computing that better reflect realistic assumptions about processor and communication timings". Raft's election timeout is such an assumption, and it is the only place E.2b uses one. So terms, votes and fences decide safety (HC-18 to HC-20), timeouts count logical ticks and decide only when an election starts (HC-18a), window boundaries are logged ticks (HC-15), and leader leases, which would make safety depend on bounded clock skew, are excluded.
  3. Exactly once is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent dedupe. Raft: "clients ... assign unique serial numbers to every command. Then, the state machine tracks the latest serial number processed for each client". So sources retransmit until acked and the admitter dedupes by (source, seq), with the dedupe state folded from D so that it survives failover (HC-16, HC-17). No transport is trusted to deliver once.
  4. End-to-end argument. A guarantee that only the endpoints can check belongs at the endpoints. Durability and exactly-once are checked where D is committed: the admitter acks only after a quorum commit (HC-16, HC-18), and the transport may lose, duplicate or reorder (HC-18a).
  5. Under a partition, consistency or availability (CAP); otherwise, latency or consistency (PACELC). RCE chooses consistency: a minority side cannot commit, so it cannot admit (HC-20). Without a partition each window costs one quorum round; windows batch inputs to amortise it, the same trade Calvin makes with its epochs.
  6. Floating-point addition is not associative. A parallel reduction reproduces the sequential bits only if it evaluates one fixed tree. So placement may change cost and never bits (HC-12, HC-13, T18), and a fabric enters only after a probe equal to the reference.

sections.title: E.3 Storage: durable append (HS-1 to HS-5)
sections.html:
• HS-1 D is the base truth. A host stores one primary artefact: D. Snapshots and indexes are caches derived from it (HS-4, E.6).
  • HS-2 Durable append. An entry is durable only after the barrier for its storage succeeded. The admitter reports no output of a step as durable before the step's entry is durable.
StorageAppend barrierNew file or rename barrier
Linuxwrite then fdatasync (or fsync) on the segmentfsync of the directory after create or rename
macOS, iOSfcntl(F_FULLFSYNC); plain fsync is not a barrier, since the drive may reorder and delay writesF_FULLFSYNC on the directory
WindowsFILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING, or FlushFileBuffersMoveFileEx with MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH
FreeBSD, other POSIXfsync on the segmentfsync of the directory
WASI, browser, no file systemnonethe host declares volatile in host.StorageCaps (E.5); no entry is reported durable

A host that cannot meet its row declares volatile. A setting that weakens a barrier (SQLite synchronous=OFF, RocksDB sync=false, LMDB MDB_NOSYNC) is not a conforming D store.

  • HS-3 A failed barrier is fatal. After a failed barrier the file system may already have discarded the failed pages and marked them clean, so a retry can report success for data that is lost. The admitter therefore stops: it admits nothing more, retries nothing, emits host.StorageFault to the outside when it still can, and the next start recovers by HS-4. It never retries and continues (T39).
  • HS-4 Verify on open. On open, the host checks the chain of D from the genesis hash (64 zeros): each entry's prev_hash is the previous entry's hash and its hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of {event, prev_hash, seq, state_hash} with the event in its positional form (6.1), which the host rebuilds from the stored event and the module; a host.* entry is hashed as stored. D is cut after the longest prefix that verifies, and the host logs host.Truncated with the number of entries dropped. A torn tail after a crash, a corrupted entry and a misdirected write are detected, never folded into state (T38). Replay of the kept prefix then re-derives each state_hash (HC-8); a mismatch is a host fault (HS-3).
  • HS-5 Snapshots are caches. A snapshot is (seq, state_hash, bytes), the bytes being the positional form of the state (6.1). It is used only when the hash of its bytes equals the state_hash of D at seq and the bytes decode, guided by the declared field types in declaration order, to a state that re-encodes to the same bytes; otherwise it is discarded. Loading one changes no meaning.

sections.title: E.4 Inputs are events (HC-10, HC-10a, HC-10b)
sections.html:
HC-10. Every value that enters a run is an event or a logged answer in D. This includes key, pointer, resize and focus input; Tick and host.WallTime; every file, network, PTY, audio and GPU readback result; foreign results and traps; select nondet choices; Delivered, TimedOut and Unreachable; capability minting; lifecycle (suspend, resume, process kill); random bytes; and the host entries of E.5. An input that is not in D does not exist for the program.

  • HC-10a Bytes are delivered exactly. An adapter that receives bytes from outside delivers exactly the bytes it received, in order, as a List[i64] whose elements are in 0..255 (the byte type of core.bytes), and D records them as a list of integers (6.1). No text holds every byte sequence, and a read may end inside a UTF-8 character, so a host does not decode received bytes unless the module takes them as text (E.4c HD-3): the program decodes them (text.utf8), and a body that is not UTF-8 is a value the program can answer rather than a trap. One delivery holds at most SIZE_LIMIT (N9) bytes, so the delivered value can always be built. The data of NetRecvDone (HC-23) and the body of HttpRequest (HC-24) follow this rule. Declared as text, either is delivered by E.4c HD-3: as text when it is UTF-8, never split inside a character, and kept in D as bytes when it is not.
  • HC-10b Typed inputs are inputs. An input read from the input stream (a line on stdin of rce host serve, the events of rce host run) is admitted whatever event of the module it names, an event the host delivers itself included: StepKept, Restarted, Synced, WallTime, HttpRequest, HttpMalformed, or a result KDone of a struct K the module declares, that is, every event of the module that some host delivers, whatever adapters this run is granted, so the mark is a function of the module and D. Before such an input the admitter appends host.Typed {seq}, seq being the typed input's own seq, so D records which of these inputs were typed and which the host delivered. A typed input is an ordinary input: it answers no request (HC-3), a typed StepKept starts no descent (HC-21), and the kept outcome of its step is delivered as for any other input. Replay reads the mark: the input at seq is folded as typed, and a host.Typed that the input does not follow (the host stopped between the two appends) records an input that was never admitted, which is not completed on open. Replay treats as a host fault a StepKept or Restarted that is neither the delivery after host.StepKept or host.Restarted, typed, nor announced by host.Input (E.2a). An input given by its name and arguments (Host::admit_event) is typed in the same way; the inputs of a window carry host.Input instead. Reference: Host::admit, host::How.

sections.title: E.4a Kept steps and restarts (HC-21, HC-22)
sections.html:
A kept step and a restart of the host are facts of the run. A program that is not told of them waits for an effect the kept step would have requested, or for a socket that belonged to a process that is gone, so both enter D and reach the program as inputs.

  • HC-21 A kept step is an input. When the step for an input is kept (T8), the admitter appends the input with the state unchanged, then host.StepKept {cause, seq}, where seq is the kept entry's seq and cause is fail (a declared error left the step), fuel, size (SIZE_LIMIT), value (VALUE_LIMIT), depth (the evaluation depth of 6.7) or trap (any other trap of 6.3 or 6.7). When the module declares event StepKept, the admitter then delivers StepKept with the same payload, as the module declares it (E.4c, HD-4), as an ordinary input with the full fuel of HC-7a, and appends host.Bind for it at start. Delivery is bounded. A step descends from a delivered StepKept when it is that delivery, or when it is the result of a request made by a step that descends from it (so the results of the StepKept step's requests, the results of the requests those steps make, and so on); a typed StepKept (HC-10b) is an ordinary input and descends from nothing. A kept step that descends from a delivered StepKept is recorded in D as host.StepKept and is not delivered again as a StepKept. Each input whose step is kept therefore leads to at most one delivered StepKept, and a StepKept step whose effects in turn lead to kept steps ends after its results are recorded. Replay derives the same descent from D, matching each result to the first request queued with its kind and req. The cause names no declaration, so D stays name-free (T7); the kept step's text, which can name a declared error, is not in D, and replay re-derives it. Replay requires each kept entry to be followed by the matching host.StepKept and, when StepKept is declared, by the entries its delivery appends (the delivered StepKept, or host.Kept), and treats a D in which one is missing, extra or different as a host fault. A D that ends before them, because the host stopped in between, is completed on open, and by a new admitter before its host.Term (HC-19), before anything else is appended; no snapshot (HS-5) is taken while D owes them. rce host replay and the validation after every run report the number of kept entries, and replay prints the cause and text of each. Reference: Host::kept, interp::Cause.
  • HC-22 A restart is an input, and ids are never reused. Adapter resources (sockets, terminals, media tracks) belong to one host process. A host that opens a D holding entries appends, after the entries that open it (HS-4, E.5), host.Restarted {below}, below being that entry's own seq. Every adapter that issues resource ids then issues them from below upward, so an id issued before the restart never names a resource of the new process; when the module declares event Restarted the admitter delivers it with the same payload, as the module declares it (E.4c, HD-4); and only then does every request outstanding in D get its one result, failed with interrupted (HC-3). The requests the Restarted step makes are performed, not interrupted. A host that takes the admitter role does the same after its host.Term (HC-19). Replay treats as a host fault a host.Restarted whose below is not its own seq, or one not followed by the entries the delivery of Restarted appends when it is declared. A host loop started on an existing D continues Tick(n) from the last n in D, so tick numbers keep rising across restarts. Reference: Host::restarted, Adapter::restart.

sections.title: E.4b The net adapter and the HTTP event host (HC-23 to HC-26)
sections.html:
• HC-23 The net adapter. net HOST:PORT, given once per address, grants TCP as effects. Authority is the granted addresses, compared by their exact text (HC-5); a request that names an address not granted, or an id the adapter did not issue, fails. Each request has one result (HC-3):

    RequestData of the resultFails with
    NetConnect(req, addr)the id of the connectiontimed_out after NET_CONNECT_MS, or the error
    NetListen(req, addr)the id of the listenerthe bind error
    NetAccept(req, id)the id of a new connectionnone when no connection is waiting
    NetSend(req, id, data)the number of bytes handed to the connectionclosed, send buffer full, byte outside 0..255
    NetRecv(req, id, max)the bytes received so far, at most max, possibly none (HC-10a); taken as text, up to 3 more to complete a character (E.4c HD-3)eof when the peer closed and nothing is left, closed, the read error
    NetClose(req, id)0; err lists the bytes of a character carried for a read that did not come (E.4c HD-3)no socket N

    data is text, sent as its UTF-8, or a List[i64] of 0..255. A send hands the bytes to the connection's own writer and returns at once, so no request waits for a peer except NetConnect, which waits at most NET_CONNECT_MS (5,000 ms), and NetRecv and NetAccept never wait. The writer fails the connection when its peer takes no byte for NET_WRITE_MS (30,000 ms) while bytes wait; later requests on it fail with closed, and a send that would leave more than NET_QUEUE_MAX (1,000,000) bytes waiting fails with send buffer full. NetClose closes once the bytes handed over are written. max defaults to 65,536 and is capped at SIZE_LIMIT. These values decide only which result a request gets, and the result is in D. Ids are never reused within D (HC-22). A program that serves HTTP on this adapter frames bytes itself and polls with Tick, one connection at a time (spec/checker/tests/host/notes_net.rce); the HTTP event host below serves the same program without polling.

  • HC-24 HTTP requests are inputs. rce host serve http HOST:PORT FILE D (one address, under serve only) binds the address before the OS target is entered (HC-5a) and appends host.HttpListen {addr and the limits of HC-25}, or {addr, error} when the bind failed; a failed bind is retried every second, and the bind that succeeds appends host.HttpListen with the limits. Connections are served concurrently, at most CONNS_MAX (256) at once. The host frames each request (HC-25) and admits it as one input HttpRequest(id, method, target, version, names, values, body): the method, the target and the version (for example HTTP/1.1) as sent, the field names as written and their values without surrounding spaces and tabs, in order, and the body as the bytes left after its framing is removed (HC-10a); trailer fields are checked and not delivered. A request that breaks the syntax, a limit or a deadline after its first byte is one input HttpMalformed(id, status, why), with the status of HC-25 and the reason. A connection that closes before a request is complete, or stays idle for IDLE_MS before the first byte of one, adds nothing to D. The id is the seq of the entry that delivers the input (its own entry, or, when host.Kept records it first under E.4c HD-2, the entry after that one), so StepKept(seq) (HC-21) names the request. The requests of one connection are admitted one at a time, each after the response to the previous one, so responses keep the order of the requests (RFC 9112 9.3.2); Expect: 100-continue from HTTP/1.1 on, with a body to come, gets the interim response HTTP/1.1 100 Continue once the head is accepted (HC-26). At start the host appends host.Bind for HttpRequest and HttpMalformed, when declared. Replay reads requests from D and never parses (HC-8). These are the host's values: to a module declared with exactly them they are delivered unchanged, and to any other declaration as E.4c HD-2 says (the body of HttpRespond may be text or List[i64]):

    RCE
    event HttpRequest(id: u64, method: text, target: text, version: text, names: List[text], values: List[text], body: List[i64])
event HttpMalformed(id: u64, status: u64, why: text)
event HttpRespondDone(req: u64, status: text, data: u64?, err: text)

struct HttpRespond
    req: u64
    status: u64
    names: List[text]
    values: List[text]
    body: text

    The host loop reads one queue (stdin lines, HTTP inputs, and SIGTERM and SIGINT, which one thread waits for) and admits in rounds of up to 64 inputs, with one barrier per round. Each time it performs queued requests, on open (HC-22) too, it performs at most DRAIN_MAX (64) of them; the rest are performed in the next round, which starts at once, so a stop and other inputs are read between drains even while results keep requesting effects. An effect waits for a barrier only when the entry that requested it is not yet durable (HS-2), and a barrier that would only confirm the previous confirmation is not taken, so a host with nothing to admit appends nothing. Lines are read as bytes. A stdin line that is not events of the module (it is not UTF-8, does not parse, names no event of the module, or one of its events cannot be built) is held whole: none of its events is appended, and it is delivered as Input(data), data being the bytes of the line with its line end, built into the declared type like any delivery (E.4c): as List[i64], or as text when they are UTF-8 (E.4c HD-3). With no Input declared, or one the line cannot be built into, host.Kept records the line in D, as text when it is UTF-8 and as its bytes otherwise; rce host run holds its lines the same way. Only a storage fault (HS-3) stops the loop. With http the end of stdin does not end the loop; SIGTERM or SIGINT stops accepting connections, waits at most STOP_MS (5,000 ms) for the open requests, takes the final barrier and validates the run (HC-8). PTY children start with no signal blocked.

  • HC-25 Framing, limits and deadlines. The syntax is RFC 9112 with the strict choices of net.http: lines end in CRLF; the request line is a method of tchar characters (RFC 9110 5.6.2), a visible-ASCII target and HTTP/ with a digit, a dot and a digit, after at most 16 empty lines; field names are of tchar characters too, and a field line does not continue an earlier one (obsolete line folding); a request has at most one Host field, and exactly one from HTTP/1.1 on (RFC 9112 3.2); a request has Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length, not both; Transfer-Encoding ends in chunked and names it once; the values listed in Content-Length agree. A request that breaks one of these (a bare CR or LF, a folded line, both framings, and so on) is delivered and recorded as HttpMalformed with status 400. The host's parser and net.http.parse_message(b, true, false, false) agree on every vector of stdlib/tests/net/http_checks.rce and on 10,000 seeded mutations of them. Only the host gives 505 for a version other than 1.x, 501 for a transfer coding before chunked, and applies these limits and deadlines:

    NameValuePast it
    LINE_MAX8,192 bytes of request line414
    HEAD_MAX65,536 bytes of head431
    FIELDS_MAX100 field lines431
    BODY_MAX1,000,000 bytes of body (SIZE_LIMIT); a chunked body's encoding at most BODY_MAX + HEAD_MAX413
    HEAD_MS10,000 ms from the first byte to the end of the head408
    BODY_MS30,000 ms from the end of the head to the end of the body408
    IDLE_MS5,000 ms between requeststhe connection closes, nothing is appended
    RESPOND_MS60,000 ms for the program's responsethe connection closes; a later HttpRespond fails with no request N
    WRITE_MS30,000 ms to write one responsethe connection closes

    Any other error of syntax is 400. The values are engine constants (HC-14) and host.HttpListen records them, so D says under which limits its requests were admitted. A deadline decides only whether a request is admitted and when a connection closes, never what an admitted request holds. A connection closes once its HttpMalformed is answered, and once the host has answered a request itself (E.4c HD-2).

  • HC-26 Responses are a function of D. The program answers with the effect HttpRespond(req, status, names, values, body). Its result HttpRespondDone is delivered with, as data, the length in bytes of the response the host made and handed to the request's connection, which writes it after the result is logged; a write that then fails (the client closed, or WRITE_MS passed) closes the connection and is not reported, so delivered means handed to the connection, not received by the client. The host checks a response before it writes anything: status 200 to 599, field names of tchar characters, values of printable ASCII (space to ~) or tab, as many values as names, no Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding (the host writes the framing), Connection only as close, and no body for 204 and 304. A response that fails a check fails the effect with the reason and leaves the request open, so the program can answer it again; a req that is not open fails with no request N. The host writes HTTP/1.1, the status and its reason phrase (RFC 9110 15; empty for a status it does not list), the program's fields in order, Content-Length (not for 204 and 304), Connection: close when the connection closes after this response and the program did not write it, an empty line and the body (none for HEAD). The connection closes after the response when the request asked for it (from HTTP/1.1 on, Connection: close; for HTTP/1.0, a Connection field without keep-alive, or none), when the program wrote Connection: close, after an HttpMalformed, and after a response the host makes itself (E.4c HD-2). The method, the version and the fields that decide this are in D, in the host's whole value of the request: its entry, or the host.Kept that records it first when the module takes less of it (E.4c). So every byte of a response, and whether the connection closes after it, is a function of D: replay re-derives every HttpRespond request (host::replay_outputs); host::http_inputs reads, for each HTTP input of D, from that whole value and the module, whether it was HEAD, whether the connection closes, and the status of a response the host makes itself, as the live host decided them (a typed input, HC-10b, is not an HTTP input); and http::response_bytes makes from these the bytes the client received. The interim HTTP/1.1 100 Continue of HC-24 is transport, not output of the program: it is written when the head is accepted, before the body arrives, for a request that may never enter D (its client may close, or its body time out), and it is the one thing the host writes that is not a function of D.

sections.title: E.4c Delivery by declaration (HD-1 to HD-4)
sections.html:
A host starts on any module the checker admits. It compares each event it delivers, and each request struct of a kind it performs, with the module's declarations, and delivers each value as the module declares it, matching fields by name. Determinism is kept by recording in D what the host delivered and what it did not, not by restricting what a module may declare.

  • Delivery. The host's value of a delivery is a set of named fields: {req, status, data, err} for a result (HC-3), the payload of host.StepKept, host.Restarted, host.Synced and host.WallTime (E.5), {n} for the frame tick Tick (HC-2; none when Tick declares no field), {data} for a line held as Input (HC-24), and the fields of HC-24 for an HTTP input. A declared field takes the host's field of the same name when its value converts exactly to the declared type: an integer within the range of the declared integer type, a number to f64, a boolean, text to text, a list element by element, a value to T? as some, a type alias as the type it names, and received bytes to text only by HD-3. An optional field takes none when the host has no value for it. The host's fields the event does not declare are not delivered. A delivery cannot be built when a declared field that is not optional has no value, or when a value has no exact conversion.

  • Recording. Before a delivery that is not the host's whole value, and in place of one that cannot be built or whose event the module does not declare, the admitter appends host.Kept {event, why}: event is the host's whole value as {payload, type}, and why says what was not delivered and why. When the host entry just before the delivery holds the whole value (host.StepKept, host.Restarted, host.Synced, host.WallTime), host.Kept is appended only for a delivery that cannot be built, and an event the module does not declare is not delivered, as before. Replay plans each delivery again from the module and the value that host.Kept or the host entry holds, requires the same reason and the same delivery after it, and treats a D that differs as a host fault; a D that ends between host.Kept and its delivery is completed on open (HC-21). What the host delivers is therefore a function of D (T37). Reference: Host::build, Host::plan.

  • Notice. At start the host prints one line for each declaration that is not exactly the host's value, naming it and saying what the host will deliver and record (Host::delivery_notes). The run continues.

  • HD-1 Results. Each request struct of a kind the host performs is bound, whatever its result event declares. The result KDone, K being the kind, is delivered as the module declares KDone. A result whose data has no exact conversion to the declared data type is delivered as failed, with the reason in err (HC-3), and host.Kept keeps the data. A result whose req is not delivered as an integer (for example req: u64?) is recorded by host.Kept before it: replay matches a result with no such record to its request by that integer, and one with the record by the req the record holds, so each request has its one result however KDone declares req (HC-3, HC-21). When the module declares no KDone, the effect is still performed and its result is recorded in D as host.Kept, not delivered; the result answers its request, so a restart does not interrupt it (HC-22).

  • HD-2 HTTP. http serves any module. HttpRequest, HttpMalformed and the result HttpRespondDone are matched by field name like any delivery, the body by HD-3, and the request HttpRespond is read by field name: names, values and body are empty when the struct does not declare them, and a status that is not an integer from 200 to 599 fails the effect (HC-26). A request that cannot be delivered as HttpRequest, because the module does not declare it or this request cannot be built for the declaration, is recorded in D as host.Kept and delivered as HttpMalformed {id, status, why} when that can be built, why naming the reason. Its status is 415 Unsupported Media Type when the body is not UTF-8 and the module takes it as text (RFC 9110 15.5.16 allows the format problem to be found by inspecting the content directly), and 501 Not Implemented otherwise: RFC 9110 15.6.2 gives 501 when the server does not support the functionality the request needs, which is the case of a module that takes no requests or none of this form, and unlike 500 it reports a lasting property of the server rather than an unexpected condition, and unlike 503 it is not temporary. The program can answer an input delivered with its id, the seq of the entry that delivers it, as an integer, when the module declares struct HttpRespond with req and status of integer types. Any other input (one not delivered, one delivered without its id, or any input of a module whose HttpRespond cannot name a request and a status) the host answers itself once the batch is durable (HS-2), with the host's status of it: 501 for a request delivered as HttpRequest, the status above for one that is not, and the status of HC-25 for a malformed request, whatever HttpMalformed declares; with no fields and no body, and it closes the connection after it. The start notice says when a module's declarations leave every request to the host. Who answers, and with what status, is read from the host's whole value of the input and the module (host::http_inputs), so every request is in D and every byte the host writes is a function of D (HC-26).

  • HD-3 Received bytes. Received bytes (the data of NetRecvDone, the body of HttpRequest) are delivered exactly as List[i64] (HC-10a). Declared as text (through an alias or ?), they are delivered as text when they are UTF-8. A stream read never splits a character: when the module takes the data of NetRecvDone as text, a read that would end inside a character reads up to 3 bytes past max to complete it, a character whose bytes have not arrived is carried to the next read on that connection, and what was carried is delivered as it is at the end of the stream, with the bytes read before an error, and before the failure of the connection; a NetClose of a connection that still carries bytes lists them in its err. Bytes that are not UTF-8 are delivered as a failed result with err naming the offset of the first byte that is not, or as HttpMalformed 415 (HD-2), and host.Kept records the bytes in D, so nothing received is lost.

  • HD-4 Host inputs. StepKept (HC-21), Restarted (HC-22), Synced, WallTime, Presented (HC-29) and the frame tick Tick (HC-2) are matched by field name like any delivery. Declared as StepKept(seq: u64), a kept step is delivered with its seq, and the host.StepKept before it holds the cause. Declared with a field the host has no value for, StepKept is never delivered, and each host.StepKept is followed by host.Kept with the reason. Delivery stays bounded (HC-21) whatever the declaration. Tick takes the count in its field n, or no count when it declares no field; a Tick no count can be built into is not delivered, which the host loop says once at start, and a count that no longer converts (Tick(n: u8) past 255) is recorded once as host.Kept, after which no tick is delivered, since no later count converts either.

rce check does not make these comparisons, because what a host delivers depends on the adapters it is granted.

sections.title: E.4d The program that wrote D (HC-27)
sections.html: • HC-27 A log is bound to the program that wrote it. Beside the log D the host keeps D.program, the module hash of the program (F.5.3: the SHA-256 of its canonical unparse, so layout and comments are not part of it). rce host run and rce host serve write it when it is absent, which binds a new log and adopts a log written before this rule. A program whose module hash differs from D.program requires change on that log: the host names both hashes and opens nothing, so D is unchanged. rce host replay checks D.program when it is present. A log replays to the state its program derived only with that program, so a changed program starts a new log; for a change that rce change classifies as an erratum (10.11), the operator may write the new hash to D.program, and that act is the record of the decision. The module hash covers the program's own text, not the library modules it uses, which the checker's build pins (F.5.3).

sections.title: E.4e What the host reports to its terminal (HC-28)
sections.html: • HC-28 The host reports its status, and the report is not an effect. rce host run and rce host serve write their status to stderr as records of OSC 7501 (an operating system command sequence), the Program Status Protocol that libghostty-vt parses and Herdr (herdr.dev) shows: ESC ] 7501 ; state=S:app=rce:title=T:msg=M ESC \, where T is the module name and M a short line of text, each in standard base64 with padding. S is idle once the host has opened D and waits for input, working while it admits an input from outside and steps the program, idle again once the entries are appended to D, done when the host stops cleanly (at the end of the input, and for rce host serve also on SIGTERM, SIGINT or an emitted Exit, HC-24), and error when it stops on a failure or on a program that requires change. The idle message gives the number of entries of D and the first 12 hex digits of the state hash. A round of the host loop that holds only a frame tick (HD-4), the host's own clock, writes no record. A record is written only when S changes. The host never reports blocked, since it asks no person anything. Records are written only when stderr is a terminal; RCE_STATUS=on writes them whatever stderr is, and RCE_STATUS=off writes none. A report is not in D, no program reads it, and replay and the state hash do not depend on it, so D is the same byte for byte with reports and without them. When the host loop ends, rce host run and rce host serve also write one plain line to stderr, whatever stderr is: durable N entries=M state_hash H, the durable mark (HS-2, none before the first barrier), the number of entries of D and the state hash. Standard output carries only the program's output: the Display bytes under serve, and under run the listing of the admitted entries and the final state.

sections.title: E.4f Frames and their confirmations (HC-29)
sections.html:
• HC-29 Frames are derived from D, and a confirmation is an input. A view tree is a value of ui.view.View (stdlib/lib/ui/view.rce): a flat arena of nodes with tags, keys, attributes, texts and child lists, node 0 its root. A frame is a view tree that a step emits as Frame(view), an output struct Frame the module declares with a field view of type View, as it emits Display(data); the frame's seq is the seq of the entry whose step emitted it. Its view_digest and frame_digest are those ui.view defines: BLAKE3 of the deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949, 4.2.1) of the tree, and BLAKE3 of the frame record ["rce.ui.frame/1", seq, view_digest]. An emitted Frame whose view is not a tree (each node reached from node 0 once, with parent links that agree) is not a frame: the host says so on stderr, and replay derives the same. A renderer is code outside the program that shows frames to a person.

    What is in D. The inputs, as for every program (HC-10), and nothing for a frame: a frame is an output of δ for its entry, so the frames of a session, their digests and their order are a function of D, and rce host replay frames FILE D re-derives every one with every adapter disconnected (HC-8). What is not in D. The frames, their digests, the diff operations between them and their ui.rules findings, all derived; and what a renderer draws, when it draws it, and what a platform accessibility interface reports, none of which a program reads.

    For ui.rules, the step word of a frame is its field ev: text when Frame declares one, else start for the first frame of D, tick when its entry is a Tick, and the event type of its entry otherwise; its time is its field ms: i64 when declared, else 0 for the first frame and 16 ms (the frame period of HC-14) for each Tick entry since the previous frame. Both are a function of D.

    Under frames FILE, rce host run and rce host serve append one line per frame to FILE, after the entries of its batch are appended (HC-1), so a renderer is never shown a frame that D does not hold. A line is canonical JSON with keys sorted: ev, frame_digest, input (the entry's event type), ms, ops (the operations view.diff gives from the previous frame's view, in the order it gives them; null for the first frame of D), seq, view (the seven lists of the view tree) and view_digest. rce host replay frames FILE D prints the same lines, byte for byte, each followed by its ui.rules findings, then the report of every frame as one trace (rules.findings, rules.report), so the rules are checked on exactly the frames a session showed.

    A renderer's confirmation that it presented a frame is an input. Under presented FILE, rce host serve reads lines SEQ FRAME_DIGEST that a renderer appends to FILE. For one that names a frame derived from D (that seq and that frame digest), the admitter appends host.Presented {digest, seq}, then delivers Presented(seq, digest) as the module declares it (E.4c, HD-4). A confirmation that names no such frame is refused: the host says so on stderr and appends nothing. Replay treats a host.Presented that names no frame derived from the entries before it as a host fault. So a program counts a frame as shown, not only emitted, by its step on Presented, and that count is a function of D.

    A host takes and uses no snapshot (HS-5) of a module that declares Frame: its frames derive from every entry of D (the first frame's word, the ticks since the previous frame, the frames a confirmation can name), so it is always folded from the start of D.

    Decision on open question Q4 of spec/proposals/human-interface.md (2026-11-01). A confirmation enters D as a host-named input, and does not stay outside D as HC-28's status does. That a person was shown a frame is a fact from outside the program on which a program may act (an alarm counted as annunciated only once shown, ISA-18.2), and HC-10 gives such a fact no other way in; a status report changes nothing that a program reads. The confirmation names which frame was presented, not how it looked: pixels and the timing of presentation stay outside D. Reference: spec/checker/src/frame.rs, Host::presented.

sections.title: E.4g Directories, entries, the zone and account names (HC-30 to HC-33)
sections.html:
A listing such as ls -l (programs/systems/ls.rce) reads a directory's names, each entry's own record and link text, the owner and group names and the local time of each modification time. Each is a request with one result event (HC-3), so each is in D (HC-10) and replay re-derives the listing from D alone (HC-8).

  • HC-30 Directory names are bytes. FileList(req, path) under fs DIR answers the names of the directory, without . and .., each as its exact bytes (HC-10a), in byte order. A module that takes them as List[List[i64]] receives two names that differ only in bytes that are not UTF-8 as two names. One that takes them as List[text] receives them by E.4c HD-3: as text when every name is UTF-8, and otherwise the result is delivered as failed, naming the element and the offset, and host.Kept keeps the bytes in D. A request's path is text or bytes, so a name that is not UTF-8 can be named again. A Display(data) whose data is a List[i64] with every element in 0..255 is written to stdout as those bytes, so such a name is printed as it is. Reference: adapters::FileAdapter, host::BYTES_LIST_FIELDS.
  • HC-31 lstat and readlink do not follow the entry. FileLstat(req, path) answers the lstat(2) record {mode, nlink, uid, gid, size, mtime, mtime_ns, blocks} of the entry the path names (mtime in seconds since the Unix epoch, mtime_ns the nanoseconds past them, blocks in 512-byte units), and FileReadlink(req, path) the text of a symbolic link as its exact bytes, unchanged. Neither follows a final symbolic link. The root check of HC-5 applies to the path that is read, not to where a link points: the directory that holds the entry, resolved with every link in it followed, must be under DIR, and a path whose last part is . or .. names a directory itself, which must be under DIR. A link whose target leaves DIR is therefore an entry of DIR: its record and its text are delivered, and reading the text does not follow it. FileRead, FileWrite, FileAppend and FileList follow links and refuse a path that resolves outside DIR, as before. Reference: FileAdapter::resolve_entry.
  • HC-32 The clock and the zone's offset are answers. WallClock(req) answers the wall clock in nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. LocalOffset(req, at) answers the offset east of UTC, in seconds, of the host's time zone at at seconds since the epoch, by the zone's rules (localtime(3): the zone of TZ, else /etc/localtime), which the host reads once at start, before it enters the OS target of HC-5. The offset is a request and not a field of host.WallTime, because a listing needs the offset at each modification time, and a zone's offset changes with summer time. Neither request needs a grant: like random bytes (HC-10), each answer is an input and gives no authority over any resource. When the module binds LocalOffset, the admitter appends host.Zone {file, sha256, tz} at start: the value of TZ (null when it is not set), the zone file the C library reads for it (empty for a POSIX rule such as EST5EDT,M3.2.0,M11.1.0, which names no file) and that file's SHA-256, so D says which rules gave its offsets. Replay reads every answer from D, and no clock or zone file. Reference: adapters::WallClockAdapter, adapters::LocalOffsetAdapter, Host::zone.
  • HC-33 Account names need the names grant. UserName(req, id) and GroupName(req, id) answer the name of a user or group id as its exact bytes: the first field of the first line of /etc/passwd or /etc/group (the files source of the Name Service Switch) whose third field is the id, or failed when no line has it. They are performed only under names, a mode word of rce host run and rce host serve (PC-3; it takes no value, since the two files are fixed), because the databases are files outside every granted root and name the people of the machine, and HC-5 gives the host no ambient authority. Without names no adapter answers them, and the OS target of HC-5a does not allow reading the two files. The adapter reads the files and does not call getpwuid(3), whose other sources (NIS, LDAP, systemd) may answer from the network or from another process, which no file grant bounds. Reference: adapters::NameAdapter.

sections.title: E.5 Host entries
sections.html:
A host entry is {type: host.<Name>, payload}. Its payload is canonical JSON. The host entries are:

TypePayloadWhen
host.StorageCapsbarrier (E.3 row name, or volatile)at open
host.Truncateddropped (u64)at open, when HS-4 cut D

sections.title: E.6 Fabrics and placement (HC-11 to HC-14)
sections.html:
• HC-11 Fabric discovery as events. At start and on hot-plug the host appends host.FabricCaps: ISA flags, each GPU adapter's features and float controls (rounding mode, denormal preservation, signed zero, inf and NaN preservation per width), NPU receipts, memory topology and which counters can be read. Replay reads the same record, so every decision taken from it is a function of D.
  • HC-12 Automatic placement. The engine places each lane-wise array operation, for … par body and reduction itself, from the cost table of C.6.4 extended with per-fabric overhead and throughput (time = overhead + work / throughput), whose calibration results are host.Calibrated entries. A program needs no annotation. with device (5.13) and device kernels stay hints that never change meaning. Placement is a function of the host entries of D, so it is the same on replay (T37): the host logs each decision as host.Placed and replay re-derives it and stops where the derivation differs from D. A fabric is a candidate for a class only after a host.Exact probe equal to the CPU reference (HC-13). Reference executor (Host::place_sum, place_lanes, place_par): the classes are sum.f64, lanes.f64.<op> for the lane-wise binary64 operations add, sub, mul, div, neg and sqrt, and par.<class> for a for … par body over 0..n combined by a given operation. On cpu and cpu.threads lanes are split into contiguous chunks across threads, which cannot change a lane's result because lanes do not read each other, and every combination, sums included, is evaluated as the fixed tree of C.8 (host::tree_split: the left subtree takes the largest power of two below the length), whose shape is a function of the length alone, so the bits are the same for any thread count and any combine, associative or not. Host::probe_fabric runs the probe vector (signed zeros, subnormal results, infinities, NaN, and sums of every length up to 64 with cancellation) on the fabric and on the CPU reference and logs host.Exact with both digests. A placement onto a fabric without an executor is not performed and is not logged; replay re-derives placements from D and needs no executor. Derivation: law 6 of E.2c fixes the tree; law 1 makes the choice of fabric an entry of D; HC-13 makes a fabric trusted only by evidence in D. Platform fabrics (informative interface). A GPU through wgpu, or an NPU, enters by implementing FabricExec {id, lanes(op, a, b), sum(xs)} and Host::register_fabric. The contract: each lane is the correctly rounded binary64 result of the named operation, with no contraction into fused multiply-add and no flushing of subnormals, and sum evaluates exactly the fixed tree of C.8. A device without binary64, or one that cannot meet the contract, fails its probe and is never placed. A run-time error from a placed fabric falls back to the CPU reference, which has the same bits. for … par bodies are host closures and run only on cpu or cpu.threads; placing them on a device needs the body compiled to a kernel, which belongs to the platform worker together with the wgpu implementation of this interface. The tick scheduler's for … par (conc.rs) and the four runtimes combine with the same host::tree_split, so a reduction gives the same bits whether the scheduler or the placement executor runs it (host_place.rs forpar_reference_and_placement_share_the_tree).
  • HC-13 Bit-exactness gate. A fabric computes a value that reaches state only for an operation on its logged exact list: integer operations; IEEE add, sub, mul, div and sqrt with round-to-nearest-even, no contraction and no flush to zero; and reductions in the fixed tree of T18. An operation enters the list by a probe whose digest equals the CPU reference digest, logged as host.Exact. Everything else (transcendentals, vendor BLAS, f16, NPU, any WGSL float operation, whose rounding WGSL does not specify) is either output only (λ sinks) or verified: recomputed on the reference, or checked against a logged digest per device.
  • HC-14 No performance flags. No user-visible setting chooses performance. The engine derives the build profile (optimization, link time optimization, codegen units, target ISA from host.FabricCaps), the allocator and collection policy and the I/O backend. A knob is admissible only when it cannot change meaning (decision 38; 10.1). Fast math, floating contraction, excess precision and hash-seed randomization do not exist under the contract. Capabilities whose use changes no result are on by default; input capabilities (hardware random numbers, clocks, energy and thermal counters) are events; those that change bits are gated by HC-13.

Figure (informative). Survey measurements behind E.6: cost of strict IEEE mode on GPU kernels and a calibrated dispatch model. Source: docs/figures.

sections.title: E.7 The fabric record
sections.html: host.FabricCaps has the payload {cpu, gpus, npus, memory, counters}. cpu lists ISA feature names; each GPU and NPU entry has an id, an API name and the float controls as booleans; memory lists nodes with their size in bytes; counters names the readable energy and performance counters. Field order is canonical (6.1). A host that cannot query a field writes null for it; placement then treats that fabric as absent.

sections.title: E.8 RCEdb: storage and queries written in RCE
sections.html:
The database of an RCE system is written in RCE. The host supplies only durable append (E.3) and sync result events (host.Synced, delivered by a binding); it supplies no query engine, index or cache whose behaviour reaches δ.

Figure (informative). D is the one primary artefact; indexes are deterministic folds written in RCE (example 55); queries read them in a defined order. Source: docs/figures.

  • HS-6 Bindings. At start the host appends one host.Bind per result kind it delivers, naming an event the program declares (for example host.Synced to event Synced(upto: u64)). The program's checker types the bound event as any other; a payload that does not fit does not apply at admission: the state is kept (5.1).
  • HS-7 Indexes are projections. An index is a pure function of a prefix of D and the index definition, rebuilt by folding D and checked by a digest per seq. Its structure (B-tree, LSM, hash) is a placement choice with no effect on meaning, so a foreign store (SQLite, RocksDB, LMDB) may hold an index, and its durability settings do not matter for correctness: a lost index is refolded from D.
  • HS-8 Queries. A query is an RCE term over state using keyed reads, keyed joins and scans in canonical key order (6.1, D.5). Results are in canonical order, never unspecified. A query states in its type whether it is a set or a bag. Float aggregation uses the fixed tree of T18. Recursive queries are not in D.5.
  • HS-9 Time travel. The state as of seq is the fold of D up to seq (T3), so any past state is queryable with no storage beyond snapshots.

Example 55 (examples/55_rcedb.rce) is a keyed store in RCE: puts are state writes, a scan sorts the keys (keys() then sort()) so its order is canonical, and a bound Synced event moves the durable mark.

E.8.1 The graph index (design refinement)

Figure E.1. The base record is D, a hash-chained log and so a linear graph. The primary index is a typed property graph folded from a prefix of D by RCE code. Queries are typed RCE values evaluated against that graph. Source: docs/figures.

The base record does not change: it is the hash-chained log of E.3, and every other structure is a projection of it (HS-7). Three consequences follow from rules that are already normative, and so they hold for any index shape, the graph index included:

  • As of is a fold of a prefix. The state as of entry k is the fold of δ over the first k entries (HS-9, T37), so an "as of" query is the same query over a shorter prefix. There is no second time model to keep in step.
  • Results have one order. A query result is an RCE value, so it has the canonical order of 7.1 (HS-8, and the 6.7 erratum for maps). No result order is left to the engine.
  • Queries terminate. A query is an RCE function, so T2 and W-REC-1 apply: a query that the checker cannot show terminates requires change; it is not run with a timeout.

The rest of the refinement is proposed, not normative. It is listed in E.11 as G-1 to G-6 so that it can be adopted, changed or rejected on its own.

sections.title: E.9 Existing ecosystems
sections.html: Code in other languages and engines stays reachable as foreign calls (5.11, HC-4): a SQL engine, a numerical library, an operating system service or a model runtime is called from fn main or a task function, and its result is logged. Its order, its timing and its numerics are therefore recorded and replayed, never re-executed (T32). Text sent to a foreign SQL, HTML, URL or JSON sink is Text[C] (5.16), so no query or markup is built from data.

sections.title: E.10 Theorems and conformance
sections.html:
• T37 Host replay. For every adapter oracle, replaying D with every adapter disconnected gives the live run's state after every entry, host entries leave the state unchanged, and two runs that logged the same host entries make the same placements.

  • T38 Verify on open. The verified prefix of a log is a prefix of it, is a valid chain, equals the log when the log is valid, and a valid log followed by any entry that does not link is cut back to the valid log.

  • T39 Fatal barrier. After a failed barrier the admitter appends nothing, whatever arrives, and the log of an admitter still running is exactly the entries it was given: a failed barrier is never followed by further appends.

  • T40 Canonical windows. The entries of a window are a function of its inputs: any permutation of a window's inputs gives the same entries, so D is independent of arrival order within every window of a sequence of windows, and sorting a window loses and adds no input. Proved on a model where an input has an injective key (the HC-15 key with the event bytes) and dedupe keeps one copy of each key.

  • T41 Prefix across terms. A replica that promised a higher term leaves its log unchanged on an append from a lower one, and every committed prefix is a prefix of D after any number of term changes. This is T38 and T39 under leader change. Quorum intersection, Election Safety (one leader per term, from the durable single vote) and Leader Completeness are proved for every reachable state of a whole-log protocol model whose steps are elections under the vote rule, leader appends, fenced writes and commits, from the initial state and with no further hypotheses. The proof is strong induction on terms: a leader of a term above t shares a voter with the commit quorum, the vote rule makes its starting log at least as up to date as that voter's, so it either holds the committed prefix directly or was started from the log of an earlier term above t, which holds it by induction. Election Safety is derived in the same model, from the durable vote and quorum intersection, rather than assumed. Verdi (Woos et al., CPP 2016) reports a Coq proof of state machine safety for Raft in "530 lines of code and 50,000 lines of proof"; RCE's proof is smaller and covers the whole-log model only.

Lean: RCE/Host.lean (T37 to T39), RCE/Quorum.lean (T41: quorum_intersect, election_safety, elect_fresh, commit_seed, leader_completeness, committed_in_later_replicas, proved for every reachable state of the protocol model with no further hypotheses; only Lean's standard axioms), RCE/Admit.lean (T40, T41: window_perm, log_permwise, window_complete, fenced_append_unchanged, committed_prefix_preserved). The link from Lean to the host: RCE/AdmitVectors.lean extracts 40 vectors from window (lake env lean --run), and tests/lean_admit.rs requires the checked-in vectors to equal that output and host.rs to produce the same window order for each vector's arrival order. Conformance: spec/checker/tests/host_contract.rs checks every example log against HS-4 (intact, torn tail, a flipped byte, a swapped pair), HC-8 and T37 (each example log re-folded with host entries interleaved, every state hash equal, every host entry's state hash equal to its predecessor's), HC-12 (placement from host entries only), HS-6 to HS-9 on example 55, and that every rule of this appendix is cited by a test.

sections.title: E.11 Proposed rules (not normative)
sections.html:
The rules in this section are proposed. They come from a survey of other languages (LESSONS.md in the language-structure study) and are recorded here so that they can be reviewed against this appendix. None of them is part of the host contract yet: a conformant host need not meet them, and no test enforces them. Each one is adopted, changed or rejected by a later draft. Where a proposal restates a rule that already holds (for example 6.3 numerics or T1 determinism), it says so.

Numerics.

  • N-1 (adopted as 6.3 N3, F1 to F9). Float operations are IEEE 754 binary64 or binary32, round to nearest even. No fused multiply-add unless the program writes one. No NaN reaches a value (F4, F5). Transcendental functions are correctly rounded RCE code in the math module or absent (F9).
  • N-8 (adopted as 6.3 N3 F2). A float expression has exactly one evaluation: one rounding per operator, in source order. Contraction, reassociation and algebraic rewrites are not valid compilations, and a float rewrite is never admitted by the rewrite prover.
  • N-9 (proposed). Every reduction is a left fold unless the program names a different fixed tree. A parallel schedule chosen by placement (HC-12) must reproduce the bits of the named tree. Thread count, fabric and batch size are never inputs to a numeric result.

Ticks and causality.

  • K-1 (proposed). The step index is the only built-in time. Physical time enters only as a logged input (host.WallTime, HC-2).
  • K-2 (proposed). Within a step each output field has exactly one defining expression, and evaluation order follows dependencies, not text order.
  • K-3 (proposed). The dependency graph inside a step is acyclic; feedback flows only through the prior state S. The check is conservative: some valid programs are rejected.
  • K-4 (proposed). Values sampled at different rates combine only through explicit sample and hold operators checked at compile time. There is no implicit buffering.
  • K-5 (proposed). Each compiled step has a worst-case cost bound computed statically and reported by the toolchain, per fabric.
  • K-6 (proposed). Every derived value in a step is computable by forward propagation from inputs and state. A step that is accepted only by guessing a fixpoint is rejected.
  • K-7 (proposed). Parallel sub-steps share only read-only state and broadcast values; writes are local to the sub-step.
  • K-8 (proposed). A merge of simultaneous writes uses a combiner from a checked library of commutative and associative operators, or one with a machine-checked proof. Float addition is not admitted.
  • K-9 (proposed). Cancellation and suspension of a sub-step are language constructs with defined strong and weak semantics at tick boundaries, and are logged. The draft must say which clock a delayed read uses under suspension.

Effects.

  • E-x (proposed). The effects emitted in one step are totally ordered by a deterministic rule, and the order is recorded in the log. No effect order is left unspecified. Relation: HC-1 already orders admission; this extends the order to outputs inside one step.

Spec conformance.

  • S-1 (proposed). The reference interpreter is normative. Prose is derived from it, and a disagreement is a spec bug resolved in favor of a versioned reference. (LESSONS.md uses S-1 twice; this is the conformance rule. The other, "no behavior depends on caching, interning, allocation or scheduling", is already implied by T1 and HC-8.) The 6.7 map order was such a disagreement, settled for the text: the reference now iterates maps in canonical key order (erratum, C.15).
  • S-2 (proposed). Every spec rule has machine-checkable conformance cases, and a runtime is conformant only if it passes all of them with bit-identical logs. E.10 follows this for the host rules.
  • S-3 (proposed). The spec has no implementation-defined or unspecified clauses. Every case has one defined result or is a compile-time error.
  • S-4 (proposed). Errors are values with a defined order of checking; which error a step yields is deterministic and logged.

Hashes.

  • C-3 (proposed). The hash function, canonical serialization and byte order are fixed in the spec and versioned, so hashes are bit-identical across conformant runtimes. Relation: the D log already fixes SHA-256 over canonical JSON (E.3); the proposal adds a version tag to that choice.

Verification.

  • V-6 (proposed). A release build replays a conformance and regression log on two independently built runtimes (for example the reference evaluator and an emitted target), and any divergence blocks the release.

Tensor unification of primitives.

Figure (informative, proposed). Tensor unification of primitives. Source: figures/src/infographics/make_tensor.py; PNG.

  • TU-1 (proposed). Every primitive value is an n-dimensional tensor Tensor[elem, shape], where elem is one of the primitive element types of 5.1 and shape is a list of non-negative dimensions. A scalar is the rank 0 tensor Tensor[elem, []]. Relation: generalizes the primitive types of 5.1; a version 0.5 to 0.8 program keeps its meaning because each of its scalars is read as rank 0.
  • TU-2 (proposed). The shape is part of the type and is checked statically. An operation whose operand shapes do not agree (for example a matrix product of [m, k] and [j, n] with k not equal to j) is a checker error, never a run-time trap. Dimensions are literals or names bound in the signature; a shape that cannot be determined statically requires change. Relation: a new W-rule in 9 when adopted.
  • TU-3 (proposed). A record whose fields all have one element type and one shape may be read as a tensor over a named axis ({x: f64, y: f64} as Tensor[f64, [axis: {x, y}]]). Field names index that axis. A record with mixed field types stays a record.
  • TU-4 (proposed). Every reduction over an axis follows N-9: a left fold over the axis in index order unless the program names a different fixed tree. The shape and the named tree, never the thread count or fabric, determine the bits.
  • TU-5 (proposed). Text, maps, graphs and sum types remain separate canonical values. They are ragged and are never padded or densified into tensors; a tensor element is never one of them.
  • TU-6 (proposed). Placement (HC-12) keys the fabric cost table by (pure operation, element type, shape). Choosing a fabric changes cost only; HC-7 and N-9 fix the result bits.

Convergence sources. Each source was read as noted; claims rest only on the passages cited.

  • BQN specification, types (read in full): "An array is a rectangular collection of data. It is defined by a shape, which is a list of non-negative integer lengths, and a ravel" whose length is the product of the shape; non-arrays are atoms. This is the shape-plus-ravel model of TU-1. APL, BQN's ancestor, was not read for this proposal.
  • Paszke et al., "Getting to the Point: Index Sets and Parallelism-Preserving Autodiff for Pointful Array Programming" (Dex), arXiv:2104.05372 (full text scanned, hits reviewed): arrays have types n=>a indexed by typed index sets (IndexSet n), so the index domain of an array is part of its type. This is the basis of TU-2 and of TU-3's named axes.
  • Henriksen et al., "Futhark: Purely Functional GPU-Programming with Nested Parallelism and In-Place Array Updates", PLDI 2017 (full text scanned, hits reviewed): "All arrays must be regular, meaning that, all rows of an array must have the same shape"; where shape cannot be verified statically, Futhark inserts dynamic checks. TU-2 takes the regularity rule and requires change instead of checking dynamically; TU-5 keeps irregular data out of tensors.
  • Julia manual, "Multi-dimensional Arrays" (read in full): "The base array type in Julia is the abstract type AbstractArray{T,N}. It is parameterized by the number of dimensions N and the element type T." Julia puts element type and rank in the type but checks sizes at run time; TU-2 goes further by putting the shape in the type.

RCEdb graph index (E.8.1). These refine HS-6 to HS-9. Convergence sources are listed after the rules; they are observations of convergent design, not proof that the rules are right.

  • G-1 (proposed). The primary index of RCEdb is a typed property graph projected from the log: nodes and edges have declared RCE types (a label is a type, a property is a field), and the projection is ordinary RCE code, a fold of δ over a log prefix (HS-7).
  • G-2 (proposed). Every node and edge carries the id of the event that created it, and the id of the event that retracted it if any. Provenance is a field of the value, so it is checked, hashed and replayed like any other field.
  • G-3 (proposed). A query is a graph pattern written as a typed RCE value (node patterns, edge patterns, quantified paths, predicates as RCE functions), never as a string. Ill-typed patterns require change (the checker reports them); there is no query text to inject into (5.16). The pattern vocabulary is the read-only GQL fragment that MGQL mechanizes (node and edge atoms in five directions, label expressions with &, |, ! and %, property maps, quantifiers *, +, ?, {i}, {i,j}, pattern lists joined on shared variables), so that each RCE pattern has a stated GQL reading. A variable declared inside a quantifier has a list type outside it, and a variable under ? is nullable.
  • G-4 (proposed). A query states in its type whether it returns a set or a bag of rows, and the result is in canonical order (7.1). Bag is the default, as in GQL, where a match yields one row per homomorphism; a set result, distinct aggregates and distinct composite operators are opt-in. All composite operators in one composite query are the same operator with the same qualifier (GQL SR:3 of ISO section 14.2, as cited by MGQL).
  • G-5 (proposed). The checker proves that every query terminates in one of two ways: each unbounded path quantifier is bounded by a declared length (bound n, 6.7) or by a restrictor that makes the match set finite (no repeated edge, no repeated node; under no repeated edge the repetition count of any quantifier is at most the edge count of the graph), or the query is recursive and is evaluated as a stratified fixpoint (negation and aggregation only over lower strata), which terminates because the graph is finite.
  • G-6 (proposed). Tables and documents are special cases of the graph projection: a table is a node type with scalar fields and no edges, a document is a tree of nodes reached by containment edges. They are projections of the same log, not separate stores.

Convergence sources (read-ledger pass 8 of the language-structure survey, and the MGQL entry of the RCEdb GQL notes; the ISO text itself was not read, it is paywalled, and ISO section numbers below are as cited by GPML and MGQL):

  • GQL, ISO/IEC 39075:2024, published 12 April 2024, is the ISO standard query language for property graphs (G-1). Its pattern-matching part (GPML, Deutsch et al., arXiv 2112.06217, section 5) states that "GPML queries must demonstrably terminate", and requires every unbounded quantifier to sit inside a restrictor (TRAIL, ACYCLIC, SIMPLE) or a selector (G-5).
  • MGQL (Thimmaiah, Lin and Gligoric, PACMPL 10 OOPSLA2, article 327, 2026, doi 10.1145/3839459) is a small-step operational semantics and type system for a read-only GQL fragment, mechanized in Lean 4 (about 23,600 lines, no sorry), with a deterministic interpreter and a checked type checker. It is grounded in ISO/IEC 39075 section by section. It works under bag semantics (G-4), fixes the TRAIL path mode and DIFFERENT EDGES match mode because they make matching terminate, caps unbounded quantifiers at the graph's edge count (G-5), types graph elements by the graph they belong to and refines them by graph schemas (G-1), and gives quantified-path variables list types (G-3). It does not cover ORDER BY, selectors such as ANY SHORTEST, other path modes, or updates, and its validation is six LDBC SNB queries against golden results, not a comparison with shipping engines.
  • Cypher (Francis et al., SIGMOD 2018) defines MATCH over tables that are bags of records, and departs from homomorphism matching by not repeating a relationship in one match, which keeps the match set finite (G-4, G-5). openCypher is the open specification of that language.
  • Datalog and Soufflé (P-SOU, D-SOUR in pass 3): negation must be stratifiable, and evaluation is a fixpoint that ends when no new facts appear (G-5).
  • Datomic stores "a set of immutable atomic facts called datoms", each a five-tuple that includes the transaction that asserted or retracted it, and an as-of view keeps only the datoms true at a transaction (G-2, E.8.1). XTDB keeps the full system-time history of every entity so that a past version stays queryable (E.8.1).

Where RCE differs from these sources: GQL and Cypher queries are strings and their result order is unspecified without ORDER BY; RCE patterns are typed values with one canonical order. GQL selectors such as ANY SHORTEST may pick one of several equal paths; under G-4 a selector that picks among ties must pick by canonical order.

chapters.title: Appendix F. Draft 0.9 (normative; implemented in part, see F.12)

sections.html:
Appendix F specifies the language's security, hygiene and contract rules. It applies the proposals of the 2025+ language survey (spec/LANGUAGE-REVIEW.md records the earlier review) and of the security study, after a full read of their sources. Each rule here is derived from a stated principle or an existing theorem, and the derivation is given next to the rule; none is taken from a source language for its own sake. The decisions are recorded in 9.7 and 9.8.

Status of this appendix. It is a specification, implemented in part by the reference checker, and it applies to every module: no declaration selects it (2.7). F.12 lists, rule by rule, what the reference checker enforces and what it does not. A construct of this appendix that the checker does not implement is reserved, not implemented (W-RES-1): it requires change, is never read as an ordinary name and never silently ignored; a rule of this appendix that is not a construct and is not implemented is listed in F.12 as not enforced. The Lean files, the emitters and the tree-sitter port do not implement all of Appendix F (an emitter does not yet print a module that needs a rule it does not implement, F.4.4). Every theorem it adds (T42 to T56, section 8) is stated; T48, T51 and T53 are proved of models (RCE/Discharged.lean), and the other twelve are unproved; no proof is claimed of the implementation.

Release label. Earlier working notes called this list "draft 0.6", then "version 0.9". It is part of the one language of this text. By the C.15 rule a release that carries it is a new release, not an erratum or extension of an earlier one: under it, programs that earlier text accepted require change (F.3, F.4), and it gives &mut arguments a different value after a failed call (F.4.4). A release label names exactly one spec commit (C.15).

Principles used for derivation. (a) Least privilege: authority is a value that is passed, never ambient (5.15). (b) Soundness: a rule that the checker enforces must be enough for the theorem that relies on it. (c) Determinism: the same program and log give the same result on every target (T1, T3). (d) Totality: every evaluation ends (T2, T4). (e) One meaning per construct, and no meaning that depends on position, tool, platform or flag. A proposal that breaks (b), (c) or (d) is excluded (F.2), whatever its benefit.

Reserved words. These ten words are on the reserved list of 2.4 (except directly after .):

requires  ensures   decreases ghost     ct
declassify endorse  release   label     law

and the type names World, Template, Shell, Prompt, Header and mathint, which no module may declare (W-NAME-2), as in 5.16. They are reserved in every module; a word whose construct this checker does not have requires change: W-RES-1 (F.12).

sections.title: F.1 How an item is applied
sections.html: Each item has: the construct, its rules (named W-rules), its cost under C.6, the theorem it relies on, and the assurance level of 8 (checked, tested or stated). Tiers are dependency order: an item uses only constructs of its own tier or an earlier one. Grammar changes are written here in the notation of 01-notation.md and are not yet merged into the checked grammar of section 3; when they are, rce-spec-check must report 0 conflicts before this appendix loses the word "specified, not yet implemented".

sections.title: F.2 Non-goals (excluded because each breaks a theorem)
sections.html:
