1. Effect handlers (resumable or multi-shot). A handler that resumes a computation makes the meaning of a state change depend on where the handler is declared and how many times it resumes. That breaks T2 (the bound B_P is computed from the call graph, and a resumed computation re-enters it) and T3 (the log would need the continuation, not the events). The effect system stays the context table of 5.2, and failure stays a value (F.4.4).
  2. Switchable contracts. A contract that is enforced in one build and ignored in another gives one program two meanings, which section 1 and decision 38 rule out (there is no build profile that changes meaning). Contracts (F.6.2) are always enforced.
  3. Mutable aliasing across par, and any relaxation of W-PAR-1. W-PAR-1 exists so that every interleaving gives the source-order result (T16). Two branches that may write what the other reads have more than one result. Branch footprints stay disjoint on writes.
  4. Runtime reflection. A program that can inspect its own declarations, names or types at run time observes what T7 says it cannot: the program's names. Compile-time code is pure and cannot reflect either (F.8). Legitimate uses are met by closed derive of built-in traits (5.9) and by tool steps that emit ordinary source.
  5. Other excluded constructs: size parameters read off values, pointers, alloc, bitcast, uninitialized memory, shared mutable pointers, unsafe, operator overloading of order operators, inheritance and runtime casts, defer and other implicit scope-end code, await, live variables, coroutine iterators, loop-else, generator expressions and set or map comprehensions (the list comprehension of section 3 stays: it is the one spelling of map and filter over a bounded source, and C.6 costs it), glob imports, conditional compilation, build features, Python interop and any foreign call outside the World rule (F.4.1). Each either lets a value depend on something other than the program and its log (T1, T3, T7), lets two names alias mutable state (T6, T16), or adds a second spelling for a construct that already has one (principle e). The reasons are per item in F.8.

sections.title: F.3 Tier 0: repair and hygiene
sections.html:
F.3.1 Stale text (P11). Items of the specification that did not match the specification itself or the implementations are corrected in this draft and listed in 9.7: decisions 8, 11, 12, 21 and 29, the Copy list of 5.5 (it now includes f32), 2.7 (the release label), and the status paragraph of the overview. These are errata (C.15 rule).

F.3.2 Unused values (P8). In every module:

  • W-UNUSED-1: a let, var, parameter, pattern binding or use name that is never read requires change. The wildcard _ and any name beginning with _ are exempt as the one spelling for "deliberately unused"; a name beginning with _ that is read also requires change (so the spelling means one thing).
  • W-UNUSED-2: a match arm that cannot be reached (W-MATCH-2 already) and an if, elif, while or guard whose condition is a comptime constant (9.8, Q17) require change.
  • W-DROP-1: an expression statement whose value is not () requires change, except a call whose result type is declared (). (Under 5.2, discarding an error union already requires change; this extends it to every non-unit value.) To drop on purpose, bind to _: let _ = f(x).
  • W-ASSIGN-1: an assignment whose value is overwritten before any read on every path requires change (an unused store).

Derivation: principle (e) and the S8 hygiene rule below; a value that is computed and discarded has no observable effect (O4, no destructors), so it is dead code or a mistake, and requiring change in it costs no expressiveness. Examples and the fuzz generator must be written clean before the rules are enabled (F.11).

F.3.3 Lexical hygiene (S8). In every module:

  • W-LEX-4: a source text containing a bidirectional control character (U+202A to U+202E, U+2066 to U+2069), a zero-width or invisible format character (U+200B to U+200F, U+2060, U+FEFF after the first position) or a Unicode scalar value that is not assigned in the pinned Unicode version (6.3 N7) inside a string or comment requires change. A string that needs one of these writes it with \u{...}. Identifiers are ASCII (2.3), so look-alike names cannot occur. The reference checker also reports as requiring change, in a string or comment, the C0 and C1 controls other than the line feed, the other invisible or blank-looking format characters (U+00AD, U+034F, U+061C, U+115F, U+1160, U+17B4, U+17B5, U+180E, U+2061 to U+2064, U+3164, U+FFA0, U+FFF9 to U+FFFB), the tag block (U+E0000 to U+E007F) and Unicode noncharacters; for "unassigned" it reports planes 4 to 13 and the noncharacters only, because no general-category table is vendored (F.12).
  • W-NAME-3: shadowing. A declaration whose name is visible in any enclosing scope of the same function (a local, a parameter, a field of the state region, a module-level name or an imported name) requires change, and the report names both sites. Under W-NAME-2, only shadowing of a parameter, field or module-level name required change; this extends it to every enclosing local.
  • Enum variants are always written qualified by their type (Color.Red), so a pattern name never means a variant by accident (this closes the case that W-PAT-1 handles by requiring change).
  • The tokenizer takes the longest token at each position, and no token depends on context. This is a requirement on the lexer of 2.3 that the reference lexer must be checked against (F.11).

Derivation: T1 and principle (e): the meaning of a token or a name must not change with a tool, a font or a position.

F.3.4 Arithmetic and floats (restated, normative). These are already the meaning of 6.3 and are restated so that Appendix F is complete: + - * on fixed-width integers trap on overflow; division by zero and an out-of-range shift trap; wrapping, saturating and checked forms are named methods (5.15); integers have the same width on every target; one float operation is one IEEE 754 operation with one rounding (no contraction of a*b+c, no extended precision); a float that would be NaN or infinite traps (decision 51), so f64 == and the total order of 6.3 agree and Eq and Ord hold for f64. New here: a bounded integer type is distinct from its base (a refined type, 5.1) and an operation whose result leaves the range traps, never wraps; division and remainder name their rounding as methods div_floor, div_trunc, div_euclid and div_exact (the last traps on a nonzero remainder), with the Euclidean law a == (a / b) * b + a % b and 0 <= a % b < |b| for div_euclid; conversions between int and float are named methods with a stated rounding and trap on non-finite or non-representable input; no hidden big integers (mathint exists only in ghost code, F.6.3). Obligation: the two classes of == and < on -0 and +0 must be shown to agree with the total order of 6.3 (check C-F1, F.11).

sections.title: F.4 Tier 1: base mechanisms
sections.html:
F.4.1 World capability (P7). World is an opaque type. A World value is attested by the host for the event that starts a command or task, exactly as a Cap[A] is (5.16), and it is subject to the rules of W-CAP-1: it appears only as the type of a parameter or event payload field, never stored, sent or captured. It is passed by borrow, &World, so a callee cannot keep it. Rules:

  • W-WORLD-1: an extern declaration (5.11) has &World as its first parameter; a call to a foreign function passes a &World that the caller itself holds; fn main and task functions may declare a &World parameter, and no other context may (a pure function, a step or a handler holds none, as 5.2 already forbids the call). A foreign function declared without it is W-WORLD-1.
  • Time, randomness, files, network and the environment have no primitive (5.15). They are inputs: an event carrying the value (for time, an event the host supplies with the time as payload) or a foreign result that is logged (5.11). A call that is restored and retried (F.4.4) sees the same logged inputs.
  • Randomness is a generator value passed explicitly with an explicit seed in an event, never a global generator. Sleeping and terminal output are foreign operations through &World.
  • A program that must run indefinitely is not written with a loop; it is a total step function from (state, input) to (state, output) driven by the host, as 6.1 and Appendix E already define. while true still requires change under the loop bound of 6.7.

Derivation: least privilege (a): a foreign call is authority, so it must be held by value; determinism (c): every input is an event or a logged result, so T32 (replay) covers the whole boundary. main(w: World) -> World with the world threaded back was not adopted: the log already sequences foreign effects (T32), so threading adds nothing for determinism, and a returned capability could be stored. Cost: &World is erased at run time (an index like the types of 5.16), so δ, the log and the emitters are unchanged. Theorem: T32 extended to every foreign call (stated, unproved, T53).

F.4.2 Information-flow labels (S1). A type may carry a label set: τ @ {A, B}, where each name is declared label A. A label set is ordered by inclusion (⊑); the empty set is public; the join of two sets is their union. A value of label L may flow only to a place of label L' with L ⊑ L'. Secret[τ] (5.16) is τ @ {secret} with a built-in label secret; W-SEC-1 becomes a case of the rules below, and its equality release (== between two secrets) stays the one release without an explicit release. Rules:

  • W-IFC-1: a flow to a place of lower label (an assignment, a call argument, a return, a field, an emit field, a send) requires change. An emit field and a channel have the public label unless declared @ {...}.
  • W-IFC-2: implicit flows. The label of the control context (the join of the labels of the conditions of every enclosing if, match, while, for and guard) joins into every value assigned and every emit or send made in it. A loop bound whose label is not public requires change (the number of iterations is observable).
  • W-IFC-3: provenance. A label name records the input it came from (the event field or foreign result that introduced it); the diagnostic of a flow that requires change names the origin and the sink. Provenance is a property of the checker's report, not of the value, so it never changes a run.
  • W-IFC-4: kept-outcome channel. A trap or fail is itself observable (the kept outcome and its text are an output, 6.1). So a trap site whose deciding operands (a divisor, an index, an operand of an overflowing operation, a size) or whose control context have a non-public label requires change unless the operation is a checked form that returns Option, whose label is the join of its operands. The kept-outcome text of a trap or fail carries the join of the labels of the operands that decide it; a fail payload with a non-public label requires change if the function can return it to a public context.
  • W-IFC-5: robust declassification. release e (the only way to lower a label) is allowed only in a function that holds a Cap[A] (5.16) whose authority struct names the label, and only when the control context and the operands that decide whether to release have trusted integrity. Integrity is a second set, {untrusted}, carried the same way: event payload fields are untrusted unless declared otherwise, and endorse e (requires a Cap[A] that names it) is the only way to make a value trusted. A release decided by untrusted data requires change, so an attacker cannot steer what is released.
  • match, function calls (the result takes the join of the arguments and the control context), the ? operator, and the derived Eq, Ord, Hash and Show of 5.9 are label aware: each result carries the join of the labels it read. A generic function is checked per instantiation (monomorphized, 5.9).
  • Ghost values (F.6.3) carry no label because they are never observable.

Derivation: soundness (b) for T36, which proves noninterference only for secret equality bits; the general statement needs labels, implicit flows, the kept-outcome channel (W-IFC-4: otherwise a trap on a secret index leaks the index) and robust declassification (W-IFC-5: otherwise the declassification decision is itself an attacker-controlled channel). Cost: labels are erased at run time. Theorems: T42 noninterference, T43 robust declassification (stated, unproved).

F.4.3 Definition hashes and rce api-diff (P10). Every item (function, type, kind, trait, event, error, constant, state region) has a definition hash: SHA-256 of the canonical encoding (6.1) of its name-free form (6.6) together with the version, the signature, every contract (F.6.2), decreases measure, ghost clause, label annotation and the definition hashes of the items it names. A mutually recursive group is hashed as one unit. Tool metadata, formatting, comments and the order of declarations in a file are not hashed (Q3). Module membership is an explicit manifest list covered by the module hash (F.5.3); a module's name is an alias.

rce api-diff OLD NEW compares two module sets by exported definition and prints one row per change from this closed table:

ChangeClass
an export is addedcompatible
a body changes under an unchanged signature, contracts and measurecompatible
a requires is weakened, or an ensures is strengthenedcompatible
a requires is strengthened, or an ensures is weakenedbreaking
a parameter changes from borrow to consume or &mut, or the reversebreaking
a record field or an enum variant is addedbreaking (a pattern may now be incomplete)
an export is removed or renamed, or its kind changesbreaking
a parameter type, the result type or the shape of a type changes in any other waybreaking
a closure-taking parameter changes from borrowing to escapingbreaking

Callers rely only on a callee's contracts; an opaque function promises only its contract, and a transparent function (one whose ensures fully determines its result) may be inlined by the checker for proof. Derivation: T7 extended from event names to items (the hash must not depend on names), and determinism (c): a build is a function of hashes. The tool is a pure function of its two inputs. Theorem: T50 (stated, unproved).

F.4.4 Transactional calls (P1). A call that returns by fail leaves every &mut argument and every owned local of the callee's caller as they were at the call. (The earlier rule wrote them back on every outcome; it is retired, 6.2, and T33 now states the restore.) Rules:

  • The restore applies only if every effect since entry is undoable. The undoable effects are: writes to owned values (locals, &mut arguments, the state fields of the region of a step) and emit into the step's pending output (discarded with the event on a trap, 6.4). Channel send and receive, spawn, foreign calls, World operations and host entries are not undoable.
  • W-TX-1: a function body in which a non-undoable effect can happen before a fail on some path (a path from a non-undoable effect to a fail, or to a call of a function that may fail) requires change. So a function that performs I/O does not also fail after it; it returns a Result value (F.8) the caller examines. (Q1.)
  • A trap is unchanged: the whole event does not apply and the state is as before the event (T8). A kept step inside par restores the whole par (C.4); a contract failure in par reports the lowest-numbered failing branch.
  • A consumed linear value (5.12) is consumed whether or not the call fails; consuming a linear handle is not an undoable effect (Q11), so a function that consumes a linear value and then may fail is W-TX-1.
  • Labels (F.4.2): after a restore, the only information in the outcome is that the call failed and the fail payload, which W-IFC-4 already labels.

Derivation: atomicity (T8) extended from events to calls; the static rule makes the restore total with no handler stack, so there is nothing to nest (user-defined handler nesting is excluded, F.2). Cost: the emitters already copy &mut arguments out (T34); a call that may fail copies them in instead, charged as the existing copy-out. Theorem: T47 (stated, unproved).

sections.title: F.5 Tier 2: items that use Tier 1
sections.html:
F.5.1 Capability-only effects (S2). 5.16 gives Cap[A] and Guarded[τ, A]; this appendix adds the file-system and revocation rules on top of the same mechanism. No new ambient authority exists: the process has no current directory, no environment and no global default.

  • W-CAP-3: a foreign function (5.11) that reads or writes a path takes a Cap[DirRead] or Cap[DirWrite] parameter after its &World. DirRead and DirWrite are declared authority structs with a root: text field. The host checks at the call that the path is under root after normalizing it (the normalization is part of the capability's contract, stated in the manifest, F.5.3); the capability's value is logged with the call (5.11), so replay does not re-check it.
  • Attenuation only narrows: c.narrow(sub) returns a Cap[A] whose root is a path extension of c's. There is no operation that widens. A closure that captures a Cap[A], &World or any value of a non-public label requires change (W-CAP-1 extended; F.8, closures): authority held by a closure must be visible in its capture list.
  • W-CAP-4 (caretaker): a Cap[A] that is handed to another component is handed as a caretaker, a handle the granter keeps and can revoke with a logged event host.revoke(id). A revoke is an entry of the log like any other, so whether a use is before or after a revoke is a function of the log order and replay is exact (T3).
  • W-CAP-5: a use of a revoked caretaker keeps the state, with the fixed record {kind: "capability", reason: "revoked", id: ...}; revoking twice is a no-op entry; a revoked caretaker is never valid again (there is no un-revoke).
  • A bound on permission is not a bound on authority: a component with a Cap[DirRead] can pass what it read to any component it can call. The checker bounds which calls it can make (labels, F.4.2), not what a held capability may do with data it has already read. The spec states this limit so that no reader takes narrow for confinement.

Derivation: least privilege (a) and soundness (b): 5.16's Guarded rule is correct only if capabilities cannot be forged, widened or stored; revocation is added as a log entry because any other form (a mutable flag) would be a second state that T1 does not cover. Theorem: T51 (stated, unproved).

F.5.2 Typed output for shell, prompt and structured text (S3). The contexts of 5.16 (Html, Url, Sql, Json) gain two more, Shell and Prompt, with the same mechanism (Text[C], W-CTX-1, made only by C.lit, C.encode and C.t"..." of F.6.1).

  • Shell: a command is not a string. Shell.cmd(program, args) takes a string literal program and a List[Text[ShellArg]]; ShellArg.encode(t) makes one argument from any text, and the host runs the program with exactly that argument vector, with no shell parsing. There is no Shell text a program can assemble into a command line.
  • Prompt: a prompt for a model is Prompt.t"... {x} ..." in which the literal segments are instructions and each field is encoded by Prompt.encode, which wraps the field as a quoted data block with a delimiter chosen so that the field text cannot contain it (the delimiter is derived from the SHA-256 of the field, so it is deterministic). The type records that the data inside the block is untrusted; under W-IFC-5, a release that a model's output decides then requires change. A model runtime is a foreign sink of context Prompt (E.9), so its text parameters are &Text[Prompt] (W-CTX-2, F.5.6).
  • Parsing input is strict and has one meaning: duplicate keys, trailing bytes and rebinding are parse errors (Json input); a missing field has no default; a value of a refined type is made only by its validating constructor (R.check, F.6.2), so deserialization cannot create a value outside its predicate; migrations between versions of a persisted record are explicit versioned functions, never implicit defaults.
  • Text operations name their unit: len_bytes and len_chars (code points); there is no unqualified len on text. Equality is exact code point equality; normalization is an explicit function at input boundaries. The emitter does not print identifiers that cannot be represented in a target, and never transliterates them.

Derivation: soundness (b) for T36, which covers four encoders; the same proof shape (every structural metacharacter comes from a literal) extends to the two new contexts. Theorem: T44 (stated, unproved).

F.5.3 Hash-pinned supply chain (S5). A program is built from a manifest, a canonical JSON file (6.1) with one spelling per key; unknown keys, features, build flags, globs and inheritance require change. The manifest lists every module (the explicit membership of F.4.3) with its SHA-256, and every dependency by hash. Rules:

  • W-PIN-1: a module whose hash differs from its manifest entry, a dependency that is not pinned by hash, an import that is a glob or relative path, and an import cycle (W-MOD-2) require change. Imports are an unordered set; adding an export is always compatible. There is no resolver: the manifest is the whole answer.
  • The built-in standard library (4.1) is one dependency, stdlib, pinned by the SHA-256 of the canonical text of the library's own manifest, which pins each of its modules. A stdlib pin that differs from the library the tool carries, a stdlib pin while that library differs from its own manifest, and a dependency named after a module or a namespace of the library (such as enc, data or text) require change (W-PIN-1), so a program names by hash exactly the library it was checked against.
  • A published definition is immutable: a hash names one text forever. A correction is a new definition with a new hash. Withdrawal is a signed advisory, a canonical JSON object {kind: "advisory", hash, reason, issued_by, seq} signed with Ed25519 (RFC 8032, deterministic) over its SHA-256 (Q5). An advisory never changes what a hash means, only whether a tool warns on it.
  • Compile-time file reads are listed in the manifest and hashed (they are pinned imports, not I/O, 5.10).
  • A build records the SLSA level 1 provenance: source hash, compiler hash, manifest hash and artifact hash, as one log entry. An artifact is a cache keyed by the hash of source plus language version; no result may depend on whether the cache was used.
  • The formatter is canonical and its version is pinned in the manifest; a definition's hash is taken over the parsed canonical form, so formatting never changes a hash.

Derivation: determinism (c): a build is a function of its pinned inputs. Theorem: T54 (stated, unproved); it assumes SHA-256 is collision resistant, which is an assumption, not a theorem of this document.

F.5.4 Constant-time functions (S4). ct fn declares a function whose control flow and memory access do not depend on a secret.

  • W-CTFN-1: in a ct fn, a value whose label contains secret (F.4.2) may not decide an if, match or and/or operand, an index, a loop bound, a shift amount, a divisor, or the argument of a call to a function that is not itself ct. The branchless ct_choose(c, a, b) and the bitwise and arithmetic operators on fixed-width integers (with the usual trap rules) are allowed. Operations that can trap on a secret already require change under W-IFC-4.
  • In RCE, secret branching requires change; it is not compiled away (a compiler that rewrites secret branches into selects changes the cost model silently).
  • W-CTFN-2: an emitter whose target cannot give constant-time guarantees (Python, JavaScript) does not print a ct fn; it gives the fixed message "ct fn is not emitted for this target"; the reference evaluator runs it with its ordinary semantics, since time is not observable there. Whether a target does give the guarantee is stated per target in 10.5, not assumed.
  • ct is compile-time information only; it does not change a value.

Derivation: S1 plus the observation that timing is a channel a label cannot see; the rule closes it by making the program, not the compiler, secret independent. Theorem: T45 (stated, unproved): for two runs that differ only in secret-labelled inputs the sequence of branch and index decisions is equal. The theorem is about the program's control flow, not about a processor.

F.5.5 Declared budgets (S6). A foreign function declared model in the manifest (a call whose cost is chosen by the outside, such as a model inference) may be called only inside a with budget B block (C.5).

  • W-BUD-1: a call to a model foreign function outside with budget requires change. The budget is charged at one rule granularity per call (C.6): an emitter counts the same units as the evaluator, so trap("budget") falls on the same operation on every target (10.5).
  • When a loop or recursion carries decreases (F.6.4) and the bound it implies is below the budget, W-BUD-1 does not require a run-time counter for it; the budget remains the limit, so the counter is an optimization and never a semantic change.
  • A budget exhausted is a trap (the state is kept, T8), not a retry.

Derivation: totality (d): a call whose cost the program cannot bound must be bounded by the program's own budget. Theorem: T52 (stated, unproved). Implementation cost is the largest of the tier: every emitter must count at one granularity (10.5).

F.5.6 The model boundary (S3, S6). A model runtime is foreign code (5.11, HC-4) whose input is a prompt and whose output is text an attacker may have steered. Both directions use mechanisms that already exist: the context Prompt of F.5.2 on the way in, the untrusted integrity tag of F.4.2 and the capabilities of 5.16 on the way out.

  • W-CTX-2: every text parameter of an extern "model" fn has the type &Text[Prompt]; &text, &[scalar] and &mut [scalar] require change there, and the other parameters are bool, an integer or f64 (5.11). A Text[Prompt] is made only by Prompt.lit of a literal, Prompt.encode and + of two of them (W-CTX-1), so the instruction text of every request comes from the program and all data sits in encoded blocks. An argument labeled untrusted (F.4.2) requires change unless it is passed as the &Text[Prompt] parameter. At run time a Text[Prompt] is its text, so the call convention of 5.11 is unchanged.
  • W-CTX-3: a model call is not control dependent on untrusted data, and no argument was steered by it outside a Prompt.encode block. Requires change: a call in a control context labeled untrusted (an if, match, while, for or and/or decided by such a value); a call after a return, break, continue, fail or ? taken under such a condition in the same function, and, for a loop, every call in its body; a Text[Prompt] argument whose untrusted part did not come only from Prompt.encode (for example one chosen by an untrusted branch). With W-CTX-2, untrusted data reaches a model only inside a block made by Prompt.encode: it decides neither which instructions are sent nor whether a request is made, unless a step that holds the capability of label untrusted by A endorses it first (W-IFC-5). Like W-IFC-2 the rule is termination insensitive: a trap or exhausted fuel ends the run, and the end is logged (C.5). It runs in the label analysis, so only in a module that writes a label (F.12).
  • extern "model" event Name(fields) declares the event on which the host delivers a model runtime's answers (HC-3). It is an event in every other respect (5.1, δ, examples, the Form); the declaration adds no keyword.
  • W-IFC-7: a field of an extern "model" event and the result of an extern "model" fn are untrusted: a label set written on one must name untrusted, so T @ {} cannot endorse a model answer by declaration. An extern "model" event has no field whose type contains Cap or Guarded. Only the ABI model declares an event (W-FFI-1).

Consequences, with no further rule: a step on a model event holds no capability, so it cannot write Guarded state (W-CAP-2), cannot endorse (W-IFC-5) and cannot release; a release decided by a model answer, directly or after the answer was stored, requires change (W-IFC-5); the answer reaches a privileged decision only after a step on another event, which carries the capability, endorses it. Writes and outputs that the program did not declare privileged (unguarded state, unlabeled output) stay open to a model answer, as they are to every other event: privilege is what the program declares.

Derivation: E.9 sends text to every foreign sink as Text[C], and a model is the foreign sink whose context is Prompt (W-CTX-2). HC-10 makes a foreign result an input, and F.4.2 makes an input untrusted; W-IFC-7 removes the one declaration (@ {}) that would let a model answer skip that. HC-5 mints authority only from logged events of a grant, and a model is not a grant, so its event carries no Cap. Which event a host adapter fills is a host fact (E.1), and the checker sees only the program, so the mark is in the program and the host is bound to it by HC-3; neither half alone suffices, as for HC-5. Residual risk, stated: encoding delimits data, it cannot make a model ignore it, so prompt injection is defined (the program states which text is instruction and which is data) and the model's reaction stays untrusted. A host passes the scalar arguments of a model call as typed values, never spliced into the prompt text. Theorem: T44 for the request; no new theorem.

F.5.7 Header text (S3). A mail or HTTP header is a line protocol: a CR or LF inside a header value ends the header and starts another (CWE-93, CWE-113). The context Header gives header text the mechanism of F.5.2 (Text[Header], W-CTX-1, made only by Header.lit and Header.encode and + of two of them, never carried by an event payload).

  • Header.lit takes one string literal with no CR and no LF (W-CTX-1).
  • Header.encode(t) is t when it contains no CR and no LF, and traps otherwise; a trap is the defined outcome (C.5), so a header value is always one line. In a labeled control context the trap is observable and W-IFC-4 applies, as for every operation that can trap.

Derivation: E.9 sends text to every foreign sink as Text[C]; a header is such a sink, and its one metacharacter is the line end. An encoding that rewrites CR or LF would change the value a reader sees, so instead a literal with them requires change and Header.encode traps on them. Folding, encoded words (RFC 2047) and header names are outside the context: the program writes the name as a literal.

sections.title: F.6 Tier 3: independent language features
sections.html:
F.6.1 Template text t"..." (P6). A template literal has fixed segments and named fields: t"Hello, {name}! You have {n} messages.". Its type is Template[τ] for the record τ of its fields (here {name: text, n: i64}), and it is not text.

  • Fields are {name} or {a.b}: an identifier or a field path, never an expression, and no nested quotes (Q22). A brace not followed by a valid field requires change ({{ and }} write literal braces); an empty field requires change.
  • W-TPL-1: a Template plus text, or a template used as text, requires change. A template is made into text only by a renderer: C.t"..." for a context C (F.5.2) renders each field through C.encode; text.t"..." renders each field through tostr, and a field type that is not text must implement Show (5.9; Q18). There is no implicit locale and no implicit display.
  • Equality of two templates is structural: same fixed segments, same field names.

Derivation: one meaning per construct (e) and T36 (the typed renderer is the only place text and structure meet). Cost: a render charges the linear class of C.6.4 on the total size. Theorem: T44 (the typed render preserves the literal-only structure).

F.6.2 Contracts: requires and ensures (P2). A function may carry clauses after its signature:

fn withdraw(acct: &mut Account, amount: u64) -> u64
    requires amount > 0
    requires amount <= acct.balance
    ensures result == amount
    ...
  • Each clause is a pure, total bool expression (a refined-type predicate fragment extended to any pure function call; and, or, not; no implication operator, not a or b is the spelling, Q35). result names the return value in ensures and is a reserved name there. old does not exist; to refer to an entry value, bind it with ghost let (F.6.3) before the first statement, which a clause may name.
  • Contracts are always enforced: requires is checked on entry and ensures on every return. A violation is one defined kept outcome (a trap that keeps the state for the call's event) with the fixed record {kind: "contract", clause: "requires" | "ensures", function: <definition hash>, index: <clause number in written order>}. No source span (it would make output depend on whitespace, Q28). No unspecified behaviour exists, so C++26's "ignore" and "observe" semantics are not adopted (F.2, item 2).
  • A contract with no satisfying value is an error: under W-CON-1 a function requires change when its requires clauses are, in the decidable fragment of W-REF-1, false for every argument. Outside that fragment nothing is decided statically (Q33); the enforcement makes every call of such a function trap, keeping the state, and never succeed vacuously.
  • The checker may assume a callee's ensures after the call and must prove the callee's requires before it where the fragment decides it, and otherwise the call is checked at run time by the enforcement. Contracts are never inferred and are covered by the definition hash (F.4.3).
  • A refined type type R = τ where p (5.1) has the total function R.check(v: τ) -> R? that returns some exactly when p holds (Q15). There is no witness clause and no implicit conversion from τ to R.
  • A type with an invariant is opaque outside its module: construction only by the validating constructor; fields are not exported.
  • A function value (a closure or fn value) has no contracts here, and a function with requires becomes a value only wrapped to return Option or Result (F.8).

Derivation: soundness (b), P2: a callee's meaning is its contract; an enforced check is the cheapest rule that keeps every theorem (the check is an ordinary guard, so δ stays total and T8 gives the rollback). Cost: one comparison per clause, charged as C.6.4 operators. Theorem: T46 (stated, unproved).

F.6.3 ghost (P3). ghost let x = e, ghost fn and ghost parameters exist only for contracts and measures.

  • W-GHOST-1: a ghost value may not flow into a non-ghost place, into an emit, a send, a branch condition of real code, a loop bound or an index. Ghost code is erased before evaluation, emission and hashing of the run (it is hashed in the definition, F.4.3). Ghost code is total (F.6.4) and pure.
  • mathint, the mathematical integer, exists only in ghost code and in contracts (Q31). It is unbounded and has no runtime representation. Quantifiers, forall over a finite range or collection, are allowed in ghost expressions only; an unbounded quantifier requires change (it cannot be evaluated, and enforced contracts must be).
  • Ghost values carry no label (F.4.2) and nothing is auto-initialized.

Derivation: noninterference (b): ghost data are not observable, so they may not steer observable data. Theorem: T49 (stated, unproved): erasing ghost code does not change δ or λ.

F.6.4 decreases (P4). A recursive group (6.7) and a loop may carry decreases m1, m2, ..., a lexicographic tuple of measures.

  • Each measure is a natural number (u64 or mathint nonnegative), finite data under the structural order of sums and records, or a tuple of these. Anything else requires change (W-DEC-1).
  • W-DEC-1: every call to a function of the same group, from any path, passes a tuple strictly smaller in the lexicographic order than the caller's entry tuple. A group's measure is one tuple for the whole group (Q2); a tail call does not waive the check.
  • decreases is required for a recursive group that the structural rules or the layered summed measures of 6.7 do not already admit; where they admit it the clause is optional, and a written measure is checked and hashed. It never replaces the loop bound and the run-time LOOP_LIMIT: both hold (so T2's bound is unchanged and the proof of 6.7 stays valid).
  • There is no unbounded loop: loops iterate a finite collection, a bounded range or a while with decreases and the loop bound of 6.7. Range bounds are evaluated left then right, both always. first is a search that returns Option.
  • Strict positivity holds without a rule: a recursive kind mentions itself only as a direct field, because a fn type cannot occur inside a data type (W-TY-2) (Q23).

Derivation: totality (d), T2 and T4. Theorem: T48 (stated, unproved).

F.6.5 if let (P5). The statement is written in the block form of every other statement of this language (blocks are indentation, 3.7):

if let P = e and c1 and c2
    A
else
    B

where P is a pattern of 5.3, e and each c are comparison expressions (CmpExpr, so an and or or inside needs parentheses), and A and B are blocks. It means the match with the arm P if c1 and c2 (the clauses c are evaluated left to right, only after P matched) running A, and a wildcard arm running B; e is evaluated once. Bindings of P are in scope in the c and in A only, and the borrow of the scrutinee ends with the match, so B does not hold it (a B that changes the place e read is allowed). The condition is a bool always (no truthiness); a failed pattern or a false c goes to B; without else the failed case does nothing, and A then has type (). There is no elif after an if let. A condition has no side effects to roll back, because expressions in conditions are pure (W-EFF-1 context rules, 5.2). W-IFLET-1: an operand c that is not a comparison requires change, and a binding unused in A is W-UNUSED-1. An irrefutable pattern leaves the wildcard arm unreachable, which requires change under W-MATCH-2. The spelling of the first draft, if let P = e then A else B with a chain and let P2 = e2, is not the grammar of this language and is withdrawn: a chain with a second let is specified for a later draft and is reserved, not implemented (W-RES-1).

Derivation: determinism (c); one construct style (e): the other statements take blocks, not then. if let is sugar over match, so no theorem changes (T10 holds because the grammar delta of F.13 is LALR(1), F.11). Not an assurance claim beyond that.

F.6.6 Trait laws (P9). A trait may declare law name(p: τ, ...): e, a pure total bool expression over the trait's methods. impl need not repeat it. Conformance is explicit, declared where the type or the trait is defined (the orphan rule of 5.9), all or nothing, with no duck typing and no partial conformance; conflicting default methods require change (W-TRAIT-1, W-TRAIT-2 extended). A generic function is bounded by traits only, with one instance per trait and type, no variance and no subtyping.

  • W-LAW-1: admission (6.9) evaluates every law of every impl on a fixed, deterministic sample: the values of the impl type that appear in examples and checks of the program, the boundary values of its fields (zero, one, the extremes of the range, empty, a singleton), and their pairs and triples up to 64 tuples in canonical order. A law that fails on any requires change.
  • This is a test, not a proof. The law is not assumed by any theorem; an implementation may not use a law to rewrite code. Assurance level: tested.

Derivation: soundness (b): promising a law that is never checked is a hole; promising only that it was sampled is true. Theorem: none (stated as tested).

sections.title: F.7 Tier 4: tooling contract (no language or emitter change)
sections.html:
F.7.1 The editor and agent broker (S7). A broker is a tool process that mediates an assistant's use of a user's files, secrets, network and processes. The lethal trifecta is the combination, in one session, of (1) access to private data, (2) exposure to content an attacker can write, and (3) a way to send data out. The broker contract:

  • TRIFECTA-1: the broker tracks the three properties per session as grants. A session holds at most two without an explicit user grant event for the third. A grant is a logged event (T3), so what a session could do is a function of its log.
  • TRIFECTA-2: content from outside the user's own workspace is untrusted (F.4.2). A tool call whose arguments carry untrusted data may not use a capability that is not already granted to untrusted data, and a broker never resolves ambiguity silently: it shows the call and waits for an event.
  • TRIFECTA-3: outbound sends carry the label join of everything the session has read; the broker does not perform a send whose label is not below the destination's, as W-IFC-1 does for programs.
  • W-TRI-1 (static): a program that has private and untrusted inputs and an external sink with no release path that satisfies W-IFC-5 requires change; the rule is a consequence of W-IFC-1 and is stated so the broker and the checker agree. The checker enforces it by W-IFC-1 (a labeled value reaching an emit, a send, a foreign argument or a public store) and W-IFC-5 (a release needs a held capability and a trusted deciding context), with no separate check: a separate check would also require change in programs in which the private value never reaches the sink, which W-IFC-1 admits. A model answer is an untrusted input by W-IFC-7 (F.5.6).
  • No program observes timing or hidden tool state: rce tools never expose a clock or an address to a program, proof automation reports its cost and keeps budgets, and an automation that uses a solver records a certificate or an audited axiom.

The broker invariant follows by induction on grants (T55, stated, unproved). Residual risks are stated, not hidden: the user can grant all three, a tool outside the broker is outside the contract, and a model's output is treated as untrusted data, never as an instruction the checker can verify.

sections.title: F.8 Further rules (derived, grouped)
sections.html:
Each row states a rule of this appendix and its derivation; "already" means the text of the cited section already gives that meaning and this appendix only states it where a reader would look.

TopicRuleDerivation
ClosuresClosures capture immutable values by copy or move, with an explicit capture list; no captured var; a closure that borrows must not escape (5.6); a capture of &World, Cap or a non-public label requires change (F.5.1)T6, T16, least privilege
TypesNo subtyping, no any, no implicit conversion, no cross-type equality, no implicit join of unlike if branches or array elements; generics are invariantT6, T7
Enums and matchClosed sums; exhaustive (W-MATCH-1); duplicate and unreachable arms require change (W-MATCH-2); variants qualifiedT1
CallsOne function per name in a scope (W-NAME-2), no overloading, no default parameters, arguments evaluated in written order; argument labels (decision 18) are checked: a wrong label is W-TY-1, so a label is documentation the checker verifies (Q16)T1
parArms are expressions; at least two; return, break and ? written directly in an arm require change (Q4); a kept step in any arm restores the whole par (C.4); a right side that writes what the place reads is a conflicting borrow; W-PAR-1 is unchangedT16
AssignmentPlace operands first, left to right, then the right sideT1
ImportsAcyclic; no glob; unordered set; explicit exports, nothing public by defaultT1
CommentsOnly # line comments exist (Q34); they never nest and nothing inside a string starts oneT1
LiteralsOne spelling per literal: a single _ between digits is the only separator (2.5) (Q36); no 1. or .5; one string form; char is a Unicode scalar valueT1
OperatorsComparison operators are non-associative: a chain is a syntax error (R3 of section 3), no chain sugar (Q8); mixing bitwise, shift, arithmetic and and/or in one expression is defined by the precedence of section 3 (decision 13), so no parenthesization rule exists; and and or short-circuit, apply to bool and return boolT1, contracts need the left operand as a hypothesis for the right
Order operators< is a total order on ordered types only; subset, prefix and merge are named methodsT1
ContainersSome/None are explicit, never false; no tuple coercion; duplicate map-literal keys require change; map and set iteration in canonical Ord order, and equality is order independent because the representation is canonical (Q6, Q19); no weak referencesT1, T6
Indexingxs[i] requires change unless the checker proves i < len(xs); get(xs, i) returns Option; slices are as in 6.3 N8; ranges keep their two spellings, .. and ..= (Q7)totality
ClassesThere are none: no inheritance, no virtual dispatch, no runtime casts, no identity equality, no field defaults; constructors are ordinary pure functionsT6, T7, T16
ErrorsFailure is a Result value with a closed enum of error kinds; no raise, try ... finally, with; the kept outcome is not a value and has no type (Q24)T1, F.4.4
Numeric namesNamed conversions with stated rounding; non-finite input traps; NaN does not exist (Q9)T1
Pointers and memoryNone; recursive data are kind with Box (5.1); vectors have no layout promise (Q29)T6, T16
Reflection and deriveNone at run time or compile time; derive is the closed built-in set of 5.9, user-defined derive is not offered (Q20); a type whose field lacks the trait cannot derive it (W-TRAIT-3)T7
Compile-time codePure, total, no declaration injection, no dependence on its call point, no platform conditionals, no assume (a comptime assert over symbolic values requires change); types are not values; value parameters only in the array-length fragment (Q10)T1, T7
Linear valuesCapability and resource handles are consumed exactly once by named functions (5.12); a type parameter is instantiated only by non-linear types; no implicit Discard (Q26)T12
Numeric typesBounded integers are distinct types; out-of-range traps (F.3.4)T14
Function valuesTotal pure fn types only; a partial function is wrapped to return Option or ResultT2
IterationExplicit finite folds and step functions; no coroutine iterators except iter (5.14)T15
ProgramsA reactive program is a total step function driven by the host (Q32); an interpreter and a compiler must agree, and the conformance suite compares themT1, T9
ForeignA foreign boundary is declared in the manifest with its full signature and library hash and is a World operation (Q30); raw pointers, C struct layouts and path-searched libraries require change; Python interop requires changeT6, T32, T54
ToolingNo flag changes meaning; build artifacts are caches; the audit report is a committed file and the checker compares against it; tests run in canonical order; plugins report only; emitter names are injective and never collide with a target's reserved wordsT1
Release gateLean proofs are built with lake build, no sorry, only the standard axioms (8); theorem statements are frozen in a module and compared; the Lean model is the reference semantics and every backend is tested against itT9
DiagnosticsA diagnostic names the true rule, or says only that the text requires change; version-unstable text is never a program valueT7
PersistencePersistent storage only through World with validating constructorsT32

sections.title: F.9 Theorem obligations (stated, unproved)
sections.html:
These rows are copied into section 8 with status stated, unproved. None has a Lean statement, a checker test or a counterexample search yet.

Statement
T42Noninterference with labels: two runs whose inputs agree on every public-label field give equal public outputs, including the kept outcome, for every accepted program (F.4.2)
T43Robust declassification: a release is reached only on a path whose control context and deciding operands are trusted (F.4.2)
T44Typed output: every structural metacharacter of a rendered Text[C] or Template of any context of 5.16 and F.5.2 comes from a literal segment (F.5.2, F.6.1)
T45Constant time: two runs of a ct fn that differ only in secret-labelled inputs take the same sequence of branch, index and loop decisions (F.5.4)
T46Contract enforcement: if a call returns, its requires held at entry and its ensures held at the return; otherwise the step of the call's event keeps the state, with the fixed record (F.6.2)
T47Transactional calls: a call that returns by fail leaves the caller's &mut arguments and locals equal to their values at the call (F.4.4)
T48Termination by written measure: an accepted recursive group or loop with a decreases tuple ends (F.6.4)
T49Ghost erasure: erasing ghost code does not change δ, λ or the log (F.6.3)
T50Definition hash: two definitions with equal hash have equal meaning; a change that rce api-diff marks compatible does not change the result of any accepted caller for inputs satisfying its requires (F.4.3)
T51Revocation: no capability use after a host.revoke entry for its caretaker in the log is admitted (F.5.1)
T52Budgets: a program with a budget does at most the budget's units of work before trap("budget"), at the same operation on every target (F.5.5)
T53World replay: T32 for every foreign call through a World and every logged input (F.4.1)
T54Supply chain integrity: under SHA-256 collision resistance, an accepted build's modules are exactly the manifest's (F.5.3)
T55Broker invariant: by induction on grant events, no session holds all three trifecta properties without an explicit grant event (F.7)
T56Relaxed sequential borrows: the limited relaxation of 5.6 studied from group borrowing (a reference is invalidated only below steps that are not independent of it) preserves T6; the lemma is not proved and the relaxation is not adopted (5.6)

Not adopted until proved. The relaxed sequential borrow rule studied from Valen's group-borrowing design is sound in a limited form, and T56 is its obligation. 5.6 is unchanged here. Relaxing W-PAR-1 is not sound and is excluded (F.2, item 3).

sections.title: F.10 Cost, emitters and compatibility
sections.html:
• Labels, World, ghost code, contracts' proofs and indices are erased before evaluation; only enforced contract clauses, R.check, encoders (F.5.2), ct_choose and the restore of F.4.4 cost anything at run time, each charged as the C.6.4 operator or linear class named in its rule.
  • An emitter that cannot implement a rule exactly does not print the program; it gives a fixed message and never approximates (10.5); the targets for ct fn are stated in F.5.4.
  • Compatibility: there is one language, so no module is read under older rules. An older program can require change under F.3.2, F.3.3, F.4.2, F.5.1 and F.4.4; it is never silently re-read. The one-time migration of the standard library to these rules is recorded in the ledger of the change (renamed names, len_bytes).

sections.title: F.11 Checks before this appendix is implemented
sections.html:
1. Merge the grammar delta (keywords, t"...", clauses, if let, ct fn, ghost, release) into section 3 and require 0 LALR(1) conflicts, with the tree-sitter port agreeing (T10).
  2. Implement each W-rule of this appendix with accept and requires-change examples (the implemented ones are in spec/examples-0.9/, one file that requires change per rule, checked by tests/v09_examples.rs; the rest are listed in F.12); the fuzz generator must produce programs clean of F.3.2.
  3. C-F1: show that == and < on f64 -0 and +0 agree with the total order of 6.3 (F.3.4); C-F2: check the reference lexer against the longest-token and context-free rules (F.3.3).
  4. State T42 to T56 in Lean models and prove them in order of use; until a row of section 8 names a Lean declaration, its status stays stated, unproved.
  5. Run the conformance suite across evaluator and emitters for these programs, including budget sweeps across trap points (F.5.5).

sections.title: F.12 Implementation status of the reference checker
sections.html:
Implemented and tested (spec/checker/src/v09.rs, apidiff.rs; examples in spec/examples-0.9/; rce v09-status prints this list):

  • Under W-RES-1, the reserved words declassify and law and the type names Template and mathint require change (their constructs are not implemented), except directly after .; the # rce-version: label is ignored (2.7).

  • W-LEX-4 (F.3.3) as stated there, with the extra classes listed there.

  • W-UNUSED-1 (F.3.2), including the _ spelling and a read of a _ name; W-UNUSED-2 for a literal boolean condition; W-DROP-1 (in the type checker); W-ASSIGN-1 for an overwrite later in the same block; W-NAME-3 (shadowing of any enclosing local, parameter, state field or module-level name).

  • W-WORLD-1 (F.4.1): &World is held only by fn main, task functions and externs, is the first parameter of every extern, is passed whole and by name, and is never stored, returned, sent or captured. The checker erases it before evaluation, so the Form, the log and every emitter are unchanged.

  • Definition hashes, rce hash and rce api-diff OLD NEW (F.4.3), without contracts, measures, ghost clauses or labels, which do not exist yet.

  • W-TX-1 and the restore of &mut arguments on fail (F.4.4) in the reference evaluator. A catched call is not a fail point of its caller. The emitters and the Lean elaboration do not translate a module with a function that can fail after taking a &mut argument.

  • Information-flow labels (F.4.2, S1): T @ {A, B} label sets on declared types (parameters, returns, fields, let, var), label NAME [by AUTH] declarations (W-IFC-6 for an undeclared label), label propagation with the control-flow label (implicit flows), W-IFC-1 (a labeled value reaches a public sink: emit, send, a store into a public place, a call result), W-IFC-2 (a labeled value decides a loop count), W-IFC-4 (an operation that can trap, and a fail, whose deciding operand or control context is labeled), W-IFC-5 (release needs the held Cap[AUTH] and a trusted deciding context, and endorse needs label untrusted by AUTH and the held capability; event payloads are untrusted unless declared @ {}), with the source of each label named in the message and a per-instantiation check of calls. Under W-NAME-2, label, release and endorse used as names require change. The checker erases the labels, release and endorse before evaluation and emission, so a labeled program runs as the unlabeled one. declassify stays reserved, not implemented. The grammar delta is F.13; the Rust LALR(1) tables (0 conflicts), the tree-sitter grammar and its scanner, parser.c and the wasm are regenerated from it.

  • S2 directory capabilities (F.5.1): W-CAP-3 (a foreign function with a path or *_path parameter takes a Cap[DirRead] or Cap[DirWrite] after its &World; DirRead and DirWrite are declared structs with root: text; c.narrow(sub) is typed Cap[A] and requires change unless sub is, when a literal, a relative path with no . or .. segment); there is no operation that widens. A closure that captures a &World or a capability, by declared type, is W-CAP-1. A capability is () at run time, so the checker erases the directory capabilities of a foreign call like the world, and narrow evaluates to (). The caretaker semantics of W-CAP-4 and W-CAP-5 are implemented as a pure function of the log (caretaker.rs: admit, keep the state with the fixed record {id, kind: "capability", reason: "revoked"}, revoke twice is a no-op, no un-revoke), with unit tests. The call host.revoke(id) needs the host log, which the reference checker does not have, so it is reserved, not implemented (W-RES-1).

  • S3 typed output (F.5.2, F.5.7): the contexts ShellArg, Prompt and Header (with lit and encode; the Prompt delimiter is data- and the SHA-256 of the field, re-hashed until the field does not contain it; Header.encode traps on CR and LF) and Shell, made only by Shell.cmd(program, args) with a literal program and List[Text[ShellArg]] arguments, whose value is the canonical JSON {"args": [...], "program": ...} (an argument vector, never a command line). len_bytes and len_chars exist and len on text is W-LEN-1. Strict parsing, versioned migrations and the refined-type constructor R.check are not implemented. The templates Prompt.t"..." of F.6.1 are not implemented either (see below).

  • S6 model foreign functions (F.5.5): extern "model" fn declares one, and a call outside with budget requires change (W-BUD-1). The model boundary (F.5.6): W-CTX-2 (the parameter types, in the checker; an untrusted argument outside the &Text[Prompt] parameter, in the label analysis, so only in a module that writes a label), W-CTX-3 (label analysis, ifc.rs), extern "model" event and W-IFC-7 (tier2.rs). W-TRI-1 is enforced by W-IFC-1 and W-IFC-5 (F.7.1). The host clause of HC-3 for model answers has no adapter in the reference host yet. The budget counting is the one of C.5 and C.6, unchanged. No rule of Appendix F bounds allocation, so none is implemented; the arena capacity of 5.7 is the existing bound. The emitters translate Prompt and Header (lit is the literal, encode the function above, + concatenation; every target agrees with the reference evaluator, tests/emit.rs), so a program that calls a model is emitted. Neither the emitters nor the Lean elaboration translate narrow, Shell, ShellArg, len_bytes or len_chars, and the Lean elaboration does not translate Prompt or Header: they do not translate a module that uses one (W-RES-1).

  • S4 ct fn (F.5.4): ct is a keyword (a stray use is W-NAME-2). Under W-CTFN-1, a secret-labeled value (F.4.2) inside a ct fn requires change when it decides an if or match, an and or or operand, an index, a loop or for bound, a shift amount, a divisor, or an argument of a call to a function that is not a ct fn (a foreign function included); it is checked per call instantiation like the labels. ct_choose(c, a, b) evaluates both values and chooses one. W-CTFN-2: no emitter prints, and the Lean elaboration does not translate, a module with a ct fn ("ct fn is not emitted for this target"): 10.5 states no constant-time guarantee for any target, so none is assumed. The reference evaluator runs it with ordinary semantics; ct changes no value.

  • S5 hash-pinned manifest (F.5.3, rce manifest-check, manifest.rs): the manifest is canonical JSON with the keys dependencies (list of {name, sha256}), formatter, language (the release label "0.9", the hash domain of F.4.3), modules (list of {module, path, sha256}) and optional reads (list of {path, sha256}, the compile-time file reads); one final line feed is ignored and any other non-canonical spelling requires change. The hash of a module is the SHA-256 of its canonical unparse, so formatting never changes it. Under W-PIN-1, an unknown key, a module whose hash differs from its entry, a dependency not pinned by 64 lowercase hex digits, a path that is a glob, absolute or has a . or .. segment, an import that is neither a listed module nor a pinned dependency, and an import cycle (W-MOD-2) require change. A signed advisory is {advisory: {kind: "advisory", hash, reason, issued_by, seq}, signature} with the Ed25519 signature (RFC 8032, via ring) over the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the advisory object, by the key trusted for issued_by (given on the command line, key ISSUER HEXPUBKEY); seq of one issuer must increase. The lockfile's unsafe list is the pinned module and dependency hashes that carry a verified advisory; the tool prints them as UNSAFE and the manifest still checks (an advisory never changes what a hash means). SLSA provenance records, the build cache rule and the key distribution of advisories are not implemented. T54 stays unproved and assumes SHA-256 is collision resistant.

  • P2 contracts and P3 ghost (F.6.2, F.6.3, tier3.rs): requires E and ensures E are statements (ContractStmt) written before the first statement of a fn body, after any ghost let; a clause elsewhere requires change (W-CON-2). Clauses are enforced always: the checker lowers the fn to guards, requires first in written order, then the kept ghost lets, then the body in which every return (and the tail value) first binds result and runs the ensures guards. A violated guard traps with the text {"clause":"requires"|"ensures","function":"<definition hash>","index":N, "kind":"contract"} (keys in that sorted order, no spaces), where N counts all the clauses of the fn in written order from 0 and the hash is the definition hash of the fn as written (F.4.3: for a top-level fn the rce hash value, for a method the SHA-256 of its canonical text under the same prefix). There is no source span. Under W-CON-1, requires clauses that are false in the fragment of literal comparisons, and and the integer bounds of one name (x > 5 and x < 3) require change; under W-CON-2, result in requires, a binding named result in a fn with ensures, and a channel receive in a clause require change. ghost let and ghost fn: under W-GHOST-1, a ghost name in code that runs requires change; ghost code that no clause names (transitively) is erased, the rest is evaluated because an enforced clause needs it. The emitters do not print a module with a contract (W-RES-1). Not implemented: ghost parameters (W-RES-1), mathint and quantifiers, R.check, opaque types with invariants, assuming a callee's ensures and proving its requires statically (a call is checked by the enforcement), contracts on function values. T46 and T49 stay unproved.

  • P4 decreases (F.6.4): decreases m1, m2, ... is a leading statement of a fn body (ContractStmt). W-DEC-1 decides this fragment: each measure is an expression linear in the unsigned integer parameters (u8 to u128) of the fn, and every call to a fn of the same recursive group (the strongly connected component of the call graph among top-level fns, a fn that calls itself included) passes a tuple that is strictly smaller in the lexicographic order: the first position where the entry tuple and the callee's measure with the arguments substituted differ by a constant difference, and the positions before it are equal. A member of a group without a decreases, a different arity, a signed or non-linear measure and an argument outside the fragment require change. A measure has no run-time meaning (the recursion bound of 6.7 and the loop limit still hold) and is in the definition hash. A while may carry a measure as the first statement of its body (the loop form of W-DEC-1): each part is linear in the unsigned integer parameters and in the var names with a written unsigned type, each bound once in the fn; the top-level assignments of the body (x = e, x += e, x -= e, e linear) give the measure at the end of the body in terms of the entry values, and that tuple must be strictly smaller in the lexicographic order (a constant difference at the first position where the two differ). A measure name assigned anywhere else in the body, borrowed mutably, or a continue in the body, is outside the fragment and requires change: W-DEC-1; a decreases on a for or loop, or anywhere else than the start of a fn body or of a while body, is reserved, not implemented (W-RES-1). The loop measure is erased before evaluation and emission, and bound and LOOP_LIMIT still hold. The checker does not prove that a measure stays a natural number (the function form does not either). Not implemented: structural measures over data, mathint measures, calls of methods or through function values (not followed). A call is judged on its own, not on the branch it is in. T48 stays unproved.

  • P5 if let (F.6.5, block form): IfLetStmt of F.13, carried in the parser as match on @iflet(e) with the guard of the and comparisons and a wildcard arm (pass when there is no else); the formatter writes the if let back. W-IFLET-1 and the checks of match apply. A chain with a second let is reserved, not implemented.

  • P6 templates (F.6.1): TEMPLATE is a token (F.13). Only the two rendered forms are implemented: text.t"..." and C.t"..." for Html, Url, Sql, Json, ShellArg and Prompt. The parser expands them at once to the concatenation they mean (text: literal segments and f.tostr() of each field; a context: C.lit of each segment and C.encode of each field, joined with +), so the fields are ordinary reads and the context's typing (W-CTX-1) decides what a field may be. Fields are an identifier or a field path; {{ and }} are literal braces; an empty field, an expression, a stray brace and an unclosed field require change (W-TPL-2); so does a renderer that is neither text nor a context (W-TPL-1). A template that is not rendered at once is the Template[τ] value of F.6.1, which requires change as reserved, not implemented (W-RES-1), so W-TPL-1's text-plus-template cases cannot arise yet. The formatter writes the expansion, not the template (the meaning, and so the hash of the expansion, is the same). T44 stays unproved.

Not implemented (each is reserved, not implemented, or the closed list in crate::v09::UNIMPLEMENTED says that it is not enforced):

  • trait laws (P9, F.6.6): law inside a trait is reserved, not implemented; W-LAW-1 for trait laws needs a sample of impl values and an evaluator of a law over them, and neither exists, so no trait law is ever run or assumed (the laws of 6.11, over the reachable states of a program, are implemented);
  • declassify (F.4.2): always requires change; release with a held capability is the one way a labeled value leaves its label;
  • ghost parameters, mathint and quantifiers; R.check and opaque types with invariants; Template[t] as a value; structural measures over data and loop measures on for and loop; a chain and let in if let;
  • the qualified spelling of variants (F.3.3) is not enforced; S7 (F.7) belongs to the IDE broker and not to this checker; the allocation bound of S6 has no statement in F.5.5 to implement; provenance records, the build cache and the advisory key distribution of S5.

Why each still requires change (state of 18 October 2026). Each is a decision, so each has its reason here; none of them is left requiring change for lack of attention.

  • ct fn in the emitters and the Lean elaboration: W-CTFN-2 prescribes that the Python and JavaScript emitters do not print a ct fn, and the Rust and Scala emitters do not print one for the same reason. The property is that two runs that differ only in secrets take the same branch, index and loop decisions (T45); a translation that keeps the decisions equal says nothing about the timing the target's compiler or runtime then produces, and T45 is unproved. The reference evaluator runs the function.
  • Contracts in the emitters: a requires or ensures that fails keeps the state, with the fixed record (F.6.2, T46). The emitters translate the erased Form and have no outcome for a kept step distinct from a trap, so an emitted program could not report the record; adding one to four emitters and to the conformance adapters is a change of the emitter protocol, not a local translation.
  • Template values and Prompt.t"..." (F.6.1): the typed-output property (T44) is about the structural characters of the rendered text, so an emitter's escaping would have to be proved or tested per context and per target; no escaping function is specified for the four targets, and the formatter and the hash use the expansion, so a template that is not expanded cannot be hashed.
  • ghost parameters, mathint and quantifiers, R.check and opaque types with invariants: each needs an erasure that keeps δ, λ and the log (T49) and, for the proof obligations, a decision procedure or an SMT back end that F.6 does not name; without one a program that uses them would be accepted without the check that gives it a meaning.
  • Structural measures over data and loop measures on for and loop (F.6.4): termination (T48) is proved only of the model of a strictly decreasing natural-number measure; a measure over data needs the well-founded order of the data type, which F.6.4 does not define.
  • declassify (F.4.2): release with a held capability is the one way a labeled value leaves its label; a second way would need its own authority rule, and T43 (robust declassification) is unproved.
  • host.revoke (F.5.1): the call writes to the host log, which the reference checker does not have; the pure caretaker fold is implemented and tested, and T51 is proved of the log model only.
  • law in a trait (P9, F.6.6): W-LAW-1 for trait laws needs a sample of impl values and an evaluator of a law over them.

Read receipt. How many words does F, "Reserved words", add to the reserved list of 2.4? (a number)

sections.title: F.13 Grammar
sections.html:
These productions extend section 3 and Appendix C.2 for the constructs of this appendix that the reference checker implements (the label sets, label declarations, release and endorse of F.4.2, ct fn of F.5.4, extern "model" event of F.5.6, and the contract clauses, ghost let ghost fn and decreases of F.6.2 to F.6.4, if let of F.6.5, and the template renderers of F.6.1). A rule below with the name of an earlier rule replaces it; the others are new. The machine check of 3.12 builds the LALR(1) tables of section 3 with C.2 and then this section applied (lalr::book_grammar_09), lexing with label, release, endorse, ct, requires, ensures, decreases and ghost reserved and by contextual, and fails on any conflict. It runs that machine over spec/examples-0.9/ok. TEMPLATE is the token t written directly before a STRING (no space, and t not the end of a longer name); the checker accepts it only after a dot. The tree-sitter port (tree-sitter/grammar.js) carries the same productions. The constructs of F.5 to F.7 that are still reserved, not implemented (F.12) have no production yet.

Plain text of this block
Item         = UseDecl | IntentDecl | ExampleDecl | CheckDecl | LawDecl
             | [ "pub" ] ( ConstDecl | TypeDecl | StructDecl | KindDecl
                         | TraitDecl | FnDecl | ActorDecl | ProtocolDecl )
             | StateDecl | EventDecl | ErrorDecl | StepDecl | ImplDecl
             | ExternDecl | NodeDecl | SupervisorDecl | LabelDecl .
LabelDecl    = "label" NAME [ "by" NAME ] NEWLINE .
ExternDecl   = "extern" STRING ( FnSig | "event" NAME [ Payload ] ) NEWLINE .
FnDecl       = [ "ct" | "ghost" ] FnSig ( Block | "=" Expr NEWLINE ) .
Stmt         = SimpleStmt | LetStmt | VarStmt | IfStmt | WhileStmt | LoopStmt
             | ForStmt | MatchStmt | ReturnStmt | BreakStmt | ContinueStmt
             | EmitStmt | FailStmt | SpawnStmt | SelectStmt | ArenaStmt
             | DeviceStmt | YieldStmt | ComptimeStmt | CheckDecl | PassStmt
             | ParStmt | BudgetStmt | DeadlineStmt | GroupStmt | BarrierStmt
             | ScopeStmt | AtomicStmt | ContractStmt | GhostLet | IfLetStmt .
IfLetStmt    = "if" "let" Pattern "=" CmpExpr { "and" CmpExpr } Block [ "else" Block ] .
Postfix      = Primary
             | Postfix "(" [ Args ] ")"
             | Postfix "[" Expr { "," Expr } "]"
             | Postfix "[" [ Expr ] ":" [ Expr ] "]"
             | Postfix "." ( NAME | INT | TEMPLATE ) .
ContractStmt = ( "requires" | "ensures" ) Expr NEWLINE
             | "decreases" Expr { "," Expr } NEWLINE .
GhostLet     = "ghost" LetStmt .
RegionType   = BaseType [ "@" ( NAME | LabelSet ) ] .
LabelSet     = "{" [ NAME { "," NAME } ] "}" .
UnaryExpr    = ( "-" | "~" | "&" [ "mut" ] | "<-" | "comptime" | "release" | "endorse" ) UnaryExpr
             | Postfix .

This file says how an AI agent shows that it has read the whole RCE spec, rather than claiming to. The spec is split into chapter files small enough to read whole. Each chapter ends with a footer holding the SHA-256 of its body and has one read-receipt question whose answer appears only in that chapter.

What the agent must do

  1. Read every file spec/book/NN-*.md listed in INDEX.md, in full, in order. Skimming, searching or reading a summary does not count.
  2. For each chapter, copy the hash from its last line (<!-- body-sha256: ... -->) and answer its Read receipt question from the chapter's text. Answers are short: a word, a name, a rule or a number.
  3. Report the result as JSON, one entry per chapter:
{"files": {
  "00-overview.md": {"sha256": "<64 hex digits>", "answer": "<answer>"},
  "01-notation.md": {"sha256": "...", "answer": "..."}
}}
  1. Say plainly which files were not read, if any. Never fill in a hash or an answer for a file that was not read.

How it is checked

rce-book verify receipt.json (in spec/checker: cargo run --release --bin rce-book -- verify receipt.json) recomputes each chapter's hash from the file on disk and compares each answer with a salted SHA-256 stored in receipts.json (the answers themselves are not stored anywhere). It prints PASS or FAIL per chapter and VERIFIED only when every chapter passes. Answers are compared after trimming, lower-casing and collapsing spaces.

A hash alone proves only that the agent opened the file; the answer shows it read the part that holds it. A correct receipt is evidence of reading, not of understanding. The salts are public, so a determined agent could guess short answers by hashing words from a chapter; doing that still requires having the chapter's text.

Keeping it valid

When a chapter changes, run rce-book build: it rewrites the footers, INDEX.md and spec/RCE-SPEC.md. rce-spec-check fails if the book and the single file are out of sync. If a change removes the text that answers a chapter's question, change the question and its salted answer in receipts.json in the same commit.

    for x in evens(n)

items.name: 55_rcedb.rce
items.html:
spec/examples/55_rcedb.rce

Expected: accepted

module rcedb

intent "a keyed store written in RCE over the host's durable append (Appendix E.8): puts are state writes, a bound Synced event moves the durable mark, scans are in canonical key order"
    example Put(key: "b", val: "2"), Put(key: "a", val: "1"), Synced(upto: 1) -> durable == 1
    example Put(key: "k", val: "v"), Delete(key: "k") -> rows.len() == 0
    example Delete(key: "x") -> kept: Missing

state Db
    rows: Map[text, text] = {}
    writes: u64 = 0
    durable: u64 = 0

event Put(key: text, val: text)
event Delete(key: text)
event Synced(upto: u64)
event Scan(start: text)

error Missing(key: text)

struct Row
    key: text
    val: text

step Db on Put(key: k, val: v)
    rows[k] = v
    writes += 1
step Db on Delete(key: k)
    if not rows.contains(k)
        fail Missing(key: k)
    let _ = rows.remove(k)
    writes += 1
step Db on Synced(upto: n)
    if n > durable
        durable = n
step Db on Scan(start: f)
    var ks = rows.keys()
    ks.sort()
    for k in ks
        if k >= f
            let v = rows.get(k) catch ""
            emit Row(key: k.tostr(), val: v)

items.name: 57_float_vectors.rce
items.html:
spec/examples/57_float_vectors.rce

Expected: accepted

module floatvec

# Cross-target float vectors (6.3 N3). Every target must reproduce these bits:
# the trace hashes each state, so one differing bit changes the parity hash.
# Non-finite results (overflow, x / 0.0, sqrt of a negative) trap; examples
# cannot state a trap, so tests/float_rules.rs holds those vectors.
intent "IEEE 754 binary64 vectors that every target computes bit for bit"
    example MulSub(a: 0.1, b: 10.0, c: 1.0) -> 0.0
    example Add(a: 0.1, b: 0.2) -> 0.30000000000000004
    example Div(a: 1.0, b: 3.0) -> 0.3333333333333333
    example Sqrt(a: 2.0) -> 1.4142135623730951
    example Mul(a: 5e-324, b: 0.5) -> 0.0
    example Mul(a: 0.0, b: -1.0) -> -0.0
    example Mul(a: 5e-324, b: 3.0) -> 1.5e-323
    example Div(a: 2.2250738585072014e-308, b: 4503599627370496.0) -> 5e-324
    example Mul(a: 2.2250738585072014e-308, b: 0.5) -> 1.1125369292536007e-308
    example Add(a: 1e16, b: 1.0) -> 10000000000000000.0
    example Add(a: 1e16, b: 3.0) -> 10000000000000004.0
    example Round(a: 2.5) -> 3.0
    example Round(a: -2.5) -> -3.0
    example Conv(n: 9007199254740993) -> 9007199254740992.0
    example F32Mul(a: 0.1, b: 3.0) -> 0.30000001192092896
    example Add(a: 1.7976931348623157e308, b: 1e291) -> 1.7976931348623157e308

state Lab
    x: f64 = 0.0

event MulSub(a: f64, b: f64, c: f64)
event Add(a: f64, b: f64)
event Mul(a: f64, b: f64)
event Div(a: f64, b: f64)
event Sqrt(a: f64)
event Round(a: f64)
event Conv(n: i64)
event F32Mul(a: f64, b: f64)

# a * b - c is two roundings (no contraction): 0.1 * 10.0 rounds to 1.0, so
# the result is 0; a fused multiply-add would give 5.551115123125783e-17.
step Lab on MulSub(a: a, b: b, c: c) -> a * b - c
step Lab on Add(a: a, b: b) -> a + b
step Lab on Mul(a: a, b: b) -> a * b
step Lab on Div(a: a, b: b) -> a / b
step Lab on Sqrt(a: a) -> a.sqrt()
step Lab on Round(a: a) -> a.round()
step Lab on Conv(n: n) -> n as f64
step Lab on F32Mul(a: a, b: b) -> ((a as f32) * (b as f32)) as f64

spec/examples/58_float_keys.rce

Expected: accepted

module floatkeys

# 6.1 key identity: map keys follow state identity, so -0.0 and 0.0 are two
# keys (IEEE 754 totalOrder puts -0.0 first) and every target stores the
# same map, hence the same state hash.
intent "a tally keyed by float that keeps -0.0 and 0.0 apart"
    example Add(x: 0.0), Flip(x: 0.0), Add(x: 0.0) -> {-0.0: 1, 0.0: 2}
    example Add(x: 1.5), Flip(x: 2.5), Add(x: 1.5) -> {-2.5: 1, 1.5: 2}

state Tally
    m: Map[f64, i64] = {}

event Add(x: f64)
event Flip(x: f64)

step Tally on Add(x: x)
    m[x] = (m.get(x) catch 0) + 1
step Tally on Flip(x: x)
    let k = x * -1.0
    m[k] = (m.get(k) catch 0) + 1

items.name: law_fails.rce
items.html:
spec/examples/change/admission/law_fails.rce

Expected: requires change at the admit stage, rule W-LAW-1: line 5: W-LAW-1 law you_cant_win fails after 9 events (exhaustive, alphabet 4 complete, 86 states explored): the claim is false example Up, Up, Up, Up, Right, Right, Right, Right, Right -> won

# W-LAW-1: the walls on the far edges are missing, so the flag is reached after 9 events
intent "the board wraps, and the far-edge walls are missing"
    example Left, Left, Up -> not won
    example Up, Up, Up, Up -> y == 1
    law you_cant_win
        "no sequence of moves from the start reaches the flag"
        always not won

const W: u8 = 12
const H: u8 = 8
const ROOM: u8 = 3
const FLAG_X: u8 = 1
const FLAG_Y: u8 = 1

state Game
    x: u8 = 8
    y: u8 = 5
    won: bool = false

event Up
event Down
event Left
event Right

fn wall(x: u8, y: u8) -> bool
    let east = x == ROOM and y <= ROOM
    let south = x <= ROOM and y == ROOM
    let north = false
    let west = false
    return east or south or north or west

fn up(y: u8) -> u8
    if y == 0
        return H - 1
    return y - 1

fn down(y: u8) -> u8
    if y + 1 == H
        return 0
    return y + 1

fn left(x: u8) -> u8
    if x == 0
        return W - 1
    return x - 1

fn right(x: u8) -> u8
    if x + 1 == W
        return 0
    return x + 1

fn on_flag(x: u8, y: u8) -> bool
    return x == FLAG_X and y == FLAG_Y

step Game on Up if not wall(x, up(y))
    y = up(y)
    won = won or on_flag(x, y)
step Game on Down if not wall(x, down(y))
    y = down(y)
    won = won or on_flag(x, y)
step Game on Left if not wall(left(x), y)
    x = left(x)
    won = won or on_flag(x, y)
step Game on Right if not wall(right(x), y)
    x = right(x)
    won = won or on_flag(x, y)
